“better”, with a place structure (by the rules given above) of

{{dsp|example-random-id-pR5R}}
{{ind|example|better|example}}
{{judri|c12e15d11}}
:''z1 is better than z2 for xa2 by standard xa3 in amount z4''

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo place order|superlatives}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo place structure|superlatives}} We would expect the place structure of 
{{vla|xagrai}}, the superlative form, to somehow mirror that, given that comparatives and superlatives are comparable concepts, resulting in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Cc6J}}
{{judri|c12e15d12}}
:''xa1=t1 is the best of the set t4 for xa2 by standard xa3.''

The t2 place in 
{{vla|traji}}, normally filled by a property abstraction, is replaced by the seltau places, and the t3 place specifying the extremum of 

{{vla|traji}} (whether the most or the least, that is) is presumed by default to be 
“the most”.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo place order|superlatives as exceptions}} But the set against which the t1 place of 
{{vla|traji}} is compared is not the t2 place (which would make the place structure of 
{{vla|traji}} fully parallel to that of 
{{vla|zmadu}}), but rather the t4 place. Nevertheless, by a special exception to the rules of place ordering, the t4 place of 
{{vla|traji}}-based lujvo becomes the second place of the lujvo. Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFf1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFf1}}
{{judri|c12e15d13}}
:'''la djudis. cu citrai lo'i lobypli'''
:''Judy is the youngest of all Lojbanists.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFf4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFf4}}
{{judri|c12e15d14}}
:'''la .ainctain. cu balrai lo'i skegunka'''
:''Einstein was the greatest of all scientists.''

{{judri|section-gismu-place-structures}}
==Notes on gismu place structures==
{{ind|general-imported|place structure|gismu}}  {{ind|general-imported|gismu|place structures}} Unlike the place structures of lujvo, the place structures of gismu were assigned in a far less systematic way through a detailed case-by-case analysis and repeated reviews with associated changes. (The gismu list is now baselined, so no further changes are contemplated.) Nevertheless, certain regularities were imposed both in the choice of places and in the ordering of places which may be helpful to the learner and the lujvo-maker, and which are therefore discussed here.

{{ind|general-imported|gismu|place structures|rationale}} The choice of gismu places results from the varying outcome of four different pressures: brevity, convenience, metaphysical necessity, and regularity. (These are also to some extent the underlying factors in the lujvo place structures generated by the methods of this chapter.) The implications of each are roughly as follows:
*Brevity tends to remove places: the fewer places a gismu has, the easier it is to learn, and the less specific it is. As mentioned in 
[[#section-selecting-places|this section]], a brivla with fewer place structures is less specific, and generality is a virtue in gismu, because they must thoroughly blanket all of semantic space.
*Convenience tends to increase the number of places: if a concept can be expressed as a place of some existing gismu, there is no need to make another gismu, a lujvo or a fu'ivla for it.
*Metaphysical necessity can either increase or decrease places: it is a pressure tending to provide the 
“right number” of places. If something is part of the essential nature of a concept, then a place must be made for it; on the other hand, if instances of the concept need not have some property, then this pressure will tend to remove the place.
*Regularity is a pressure which can also either increase or decrease places. If a gismu has a given place, then gismu which are semantically related to it are likely to have the place also.

Here are some examples of gismu place structures, with a discussion of the pressures operating on them:

{{dsp|example-random-id-iu0B}}
{{judri|c12e16d1}}
{{vla|xekri}}: xe1 is black

{{ind|general-imported|color standards}} Brevity was the most important goal here, reinforced by one interpretation of metaphysical necessity. There is no mention of color standards here, as many people have pointed out; like all color gismu, 

{{vla|xekri}} is explicitly subjective. Objective color standards can be brought in by an appropriate BAI tag such as 

{{vla|ci'u}} ( 

“in system”; See [[#section-BAI|this section]]) or by making a lujvo.

{{dsp|example-random-id-cuYP}}
{{judri|c12e16d2}}
{{vla|jbena}}: j1 is born to j2 at time j3 and location j4

The gismu 
{{vla|jbena}} contains places for time and location, which few other gismu have: normally, the time and place at which something is done is supplied by a tense tag (See [[#chapter-tenses|this chapter]]). However, providing these places makes 
:{{jbo|le te jbena}} a simple term for 
“birthday” and 
:{{jbo|le ve jbena}} for 
“birthplace”, so these places were provided despite their lack of metaphysical necessity.

{{dsp|example-random-id-NTJn}}
{{judri|c12e16d3}}
{{vla|rinka}}: event r1 is the cause of event r2

{{ind|general-imported|melting}} The place structure of 
{{vla|rinka}} does not have a place for the agent, the one who causes, as a result of the pressure toward metaphysical necessity. A cause-effect relationship does not have to include an agent: an event (such as snow melting in the mountains) may cause another event (such as the flooding of the Nile) without any human intervention or even knowledge.

{{ind|general-imported|lujvo|as suppliers of agent place}} Indeed, there is a general tendency to omit agent places from most gismu except for a few such as 
{{vla|gasnu}} and 
{{vla|zukte}} which are then used as tertau in order to restore the agent place when needed: See [[#section-implicit-abstraction|this section]].

{{dsp|example-random-id-Atby}}
{{judri|c12e16d4}}
<definition>{{vla|cinfo}} :''c1 is a lion of species/breed c2''

{{ind|general-imported|diversified species}}  {{ind|general-imported|general terms}} The c2 place of 
{{vla|cinfo}} is provided as a result of the pressure toward regularity. All animal and plant gismu have such an x2 place; although there is in fact only one species of lion, and breeds of lion, though they exist, aren't all that important in talking about lions. The species/breed place must exist for such diversified species as dogs, and for general terms like 

{{vla|cinki}} (insect), and are provided for all other animals and plants as a matter of regularity.

{{ind|general-imported|gismu|place order|rationale}} Less can be said about gismu place structure ordering, but some regularities are apparent. The places tend to appear in decreasing order of psychological saliency or importance. There is an implication within the place structure of 
{{vla|klama}}, for example, that 
:{{jbo|lo klama}} (the one going) will be talked about more often, and is thus more important, than 
:{{jbo|lo se klama}} (the destination), which is in turn more important than 

:{{jbo|lo xe klama}} (the means of transport).

Some specific tendencies (not really rules) can also be observed. For example, when there is an agent place, it tends to be the first place. Similarly, when a destination and an origin point are mentioned, the destination is always placed just before the origin point. Places such as 

“under conditions” and 
“by standard”, which often go unfilled, are moved to near the end of the place structure.

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{judri|chapter-attitudinals}}
=Oooh! Arrgh! Ugh! Yecch! Attitudinal and Emotional Indicators=
{{image|xml:id="chapter-attitudinals-picture"|The picture for chapter 13|media/chapter-attitudinals.gif}}
{{judri|section-attitudinals-introduction}}
==What are attitudinal indicators?==

This chapter explains the various words that Lojban provides for expressing attitude and related notions. In natural languages, attitudes are usually expressed by the tone of voice when speaking, and (very imperfectly) by punctuation when writing. For example, the bare words

{{dsp|example-random-id-EWHQ}}
{{judri|c13e1d1}}
John is coming.

can be made, through tone of voice, to express the speaker's feeling of happiness, pity, hope, surprise, or disbelief. These fine points of tone cannot be expressed in writing. Attitudes are also expressed with various sounds which show up in print as oddly spelled words, such as the 

“Oooh!”, 
“Arrgh!”, 
“Ugh!”, and 
“Yecch!” in the title. These are part of the English language; people born to other languages use a different set; yet you won't find any of these words in a dictionary.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal indicators}} In Lojban, everything that can be spoken can also be written. Therefore, these tones of voice must be represented by explicit words known as 
“attitudinal indicators”, or just 

“attitudinals”. This rule seems awkward and clunky to English-speakers at first, but is an essential part of the Lojbanic way of doing things.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|placement for prevailing attitude}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|prevailing attitude}} The simplest way to use attitudinal indicators is to place them at the beginning of a text. In that case, they express the speaker's prevailing attitude. Here are some examples, correlated with the attitudes mentioned following 

{{linker|example-random-id-EWHQ}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFfd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFfd}}
{{judri|c13e1d2}}
{{ind|example|John is coming|example}}
:'''.ui la djan klama'''
:<code>[Whee!] John is coming!</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFFo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFFo}}
{{judri|c13e1d3}}
{{ind|example|John is coming|example}}
:'''.uu la djan klama'''
:<code>[Alas!] John is coming.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfFV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfFV}}
{{judri|c13e1d4}}
{{ind|example|John is coming|example}}
:'''.a'o la djan klama'''
:<code>[Hopefully] John is coming.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qffW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qffW}}
{{judri|c13e1d5}}
{{ind|example|John is coming|example}}
:'''.ue la djan klama'''
:<code>[Wow!] John is coming!</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfgA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfgA}}
{{judri|c13e1d6}}
{{ind|example|John is coming|example}}
:'''.ianai la djan klama'''
:<code>[Nonsense!] John is coming.</code>

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|.a'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|word-form for primary}} The primary Lojban attitudinals are all the cmavo of the form VV or V'V: one of the few cases where cmavo have been classified solely by their form. There are 39 of these cmavo: all 25 possible vowel pairs of the form V'V, the four standard diphthongs ( {{vla|.ai}}, 
{{vla|.au}}, 
{{vla|.ei}}, and 
{{vla|.oi}}), and the ten more diphthongs that are permitted only in these attitudinal indicators and in names and borrowings ( {{vla|.ia}}, 
{{vla|.ie}}, 
{{vla|.ii}}, 
{{vla|.io}}, 
{{vla|.iu}}, 
{{vla|.ua}}, 
{{vla|.ue}}, {{vla|.ui}}, 
{{vla|.uo}}, and 
{{vla|.uu}}). Note that each of these cmavo has a period before it, marking the pause that is mandatory before every word beginning with a vowel. Attitudinals, like most of the other kinds of indicators described in this chapter, belong to selma'o UI.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|compound}} Attitudinals can also be compound cmavo, of the types explained in Sections 4-8; 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfgA}} illustrates one such possibility, the compound attitudinal 
{{vla|.ianai}}. In attitudinals, 

:{{jbo|-nai}} indicates polar negation: the opposite of the simple attitudinal without the 
:{{jbo|-nai}}. Thus, as you might suppose, 
{{vla|.ia}} expresses belief, since 
{{vla|.ianai}} expresses disbelief.

{{ind|general-imported|indicators|types of}}  {{ind|general-imported|indicators}} In addition to the attitudinals, there are other classes of indicators: intensity markers, emotion categories, attitudinal modifiers, observationals, and discursives. All of them are grammatically equivalent, which is why they are treated together in this chapter.

Every indicator behaves in more or less the same way with respect to the grammar of the rest of the language. In general, one or more indicators can be inserted at the beginning of an utterance or after any word. Indicators at the beginning apply to the whole utterance; otherwise, they apply to the word that they follow. More details can be found in 
[[#section-scope|this section]].

Throughout this chapter, tables of indicators will be written in four columns. The first column is the cmavo itself. The second column is a corresponding English word, not necessarily a literal translation. The fourth column represents the opposite of the second column, and shows the approximate meaning of the attitudinal when suffixed with 
:{{jbo|-nai}}. The third column, which is sometimes omitted, indicates a neutral point between the second and fourth columns, and shows the approximate meaning of the attitudinal when it is suffixed with 
:{{jbo|-cu'i}}. The cmavo 

{{vla|cu'i}} belongs to selma'o CAI, and is explained more fully in 

[[#section-intensity-scale|this section]].

One flaw that the English glosses are particularly subject to is that in English it is often difficult to distinguish between expressing your feelings and talking about them, particularly with the limited resource of the written word. So the gloss for 

{{vla|.ui}} should not really be 
“happiness” but some sound or tone that expresses happiness. However, there aren't nearly enough of those that have unambiguous or obvious meanings in English to go around for all the many, many different emotions Lojban speakers can readily express.

Many indicators of CV'V form are loosely derived from specific gismu. The gismu should be thought of as a memory hook, not an equivalent of the cmavo. Such gismu are shown in this chapter between square brackets, thus: [gismu].

{{judri|section-pure-emotions}}
==Pure emotion indicators==
Attitudinals make no claim: they are expressions of attitude, not of facts or alleged facts. As a result, attitudinals themselves have no truth value, nor do they directly affect the truth value of a bridi that they modify. However, since emotional attitudes are carried in your mind, they reflect reactions to that version of the world that the mind is thinking about; this is seldom identical with the real world. At times, we are thinking about our idealized version of the real world; at other times we are thinking about a potential world that might or might not ever exist.

Therefore, there are two groups of attitudinals in Lojban. The 
“pure emotion indicators” express the way the speaker is feeling, without direct reference to what else is said. These indicators comprise the attitudinals which begin with 
{{lerfu|u}} or 
{{lerfu|o}} and many of those beginning with 
{{lerfu|i}}.

The cmavo beginning with {{lerfu|u}} are simple emotions, which represent the speaker's reaction to the world as it is, or as it is perceived to be.
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''.ua'''	discovery		confusion
'''.u'a'''	gain		loss
'''.ue'''	surprise	no surprise	expectation
'''.u'e'''	wonder		commonplace
'''.ui'''	happiness		unhappiness
'''.u'i'''	amusement		weariness
'''.uo'''	completion		incompleteness
'''.u'o'''	courage	timidity	cowardice
'''.uu'''	pity		cruelty
'''.u'u'''	repentance	lack of regret	innocence
</tabledata>

Here are some typical uses of the 
{{lerfu|u}} attitudinals:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFgi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFgi}}
{{judri|c13e2d1}}
:'''.ua mi facki fi le mi mapku'''
:<code>[Eureka!] I found my hat! [emphasizes the discovery of the hat]</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFgv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFgv}}
{{judri|c13e2d2}}
:'''.u'a mi facki fi le mi mapku'''
:<code>[Gain!] I found my hat! [emphasizes the obtaining of the hat]</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFh5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFh5}}
{{judri|c13e2d3}}
:'''.ui mi facki fi le mi mapku'''
:<code>[Yay!] I found my hat! [emphasizes the feeling of happiness]</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfHA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfHA}}
{{judri|c13e2d4}}
:'''.uo mi facki fi le mi mapku'''
:<code>[At last!] I found my hat! [emphasizes that the finding is complete]</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfHC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfHC}}
{{judri|c13e2d5}}
:'''.uu do cortu'''
:<code>[Pity!] You feel-pain. [expresses speaker's sympathy]</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfhT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfhT}}
{{judri|c13e2d6}}
:'''.u'u do cortu'''
:<code>[Repentance!] You feel-pain. [expresses that speaker feels guilty]</code>

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfHA}}, note that the attitudinal 
{{vla|.uo}} is translated by an English non-attitudinal phrase: 

“At last!” It is common for the English equivalents of Lojban attitudinals to be short phrases of this sort, with more or less normal grammar, but actually expressions of emotion.

In particular, both 
{{vla|.uu}} and 
{{vla|.u'u}} can be translated into English as 

“I'm sorry”; the difference between these two attitudes frequently causes confusion among English-speakers who use this phrase, leading to responses like 
“Why are you sorry? It's not your fault!”

It is important to realize that 
{{vla|.uu}}, and indeed all attitudinals, are meant to be used sincerely, not ironically. In English, the exclamation 
“Pity!” is just as likely to be ironically intended, but this usage does not extend to Lojban. Lying with attitudinals is (normally) as inappropriate to Lojban discourse as any other kind of lying: perhaps worse, because misunderstood emotions can cause even greater problems than misunderstood statements.

The following examples display the effects of 
{{vla|nai}} and 
{{vla|cu'i}} when suffixed to an attitudinal:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFiE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFiE}}
{{judri|c13e2d7}}
:'''.ue la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Surprise!] John comes.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfiI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfiI}}
{{judri|c13e2d8}}
:'''.uecu'i la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Ho hum.] John comes.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfin}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfin}}
{{judri|c13e2d9}}
:'''.uenai la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Expected!] John comes.</code>

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfin}}, John's coming has been anticipated by the speaker. In 

{{linker|example-random-id-qFiE}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfiI}}, no such anticipation has been made, but in 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfiI}} the lack-of-anticipation goes no further &ndash; in 
{{linker|example-random-id-qFiE}}, it amounts to actual surprise.

It is not possible to firmly distinguish the pure emotion words beginning with 
{{lerfu|o}} or 
{{lerfu|i}} from those beginning with 
{{lerfu|u}}, but in general they represent more complex, more ambivalent, or more difficult emotions.
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''.o'a'''	pride	modesty	shame
'''.o'e'''	closeness	detachment	distance
'''.oi'''	complaint/pain	doing OK	pleasure
'''.o'i'''	caution	boldness	rashness
'''.o'o'''	patience	mere tolerance	anger
'''.o'u'''	relaxation	composure	stress
</tabledata>

Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ch2s}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ch2s}}
{{judri|c13e2d10}}
:'''.oi la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Complaint!] John is coming.</code>

Here the speaker is distressed or discomfited over John's coming. The word 
{{vla|.oi}} is derived from the Yiddish word 
“oy” of similar meaning. It is the only cmavo with a Yiddish origin.

{{dsp|example-random-id-V8eD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-V8eD}}
{{judri|c13e2d11}}
:'''.o'onai la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Anger!] John is coming!</code>

Here the speaker feels anger over John's coming.

{{dsp|example-random-id-QCTs}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-QCTs}}
{{judri|c13e2d12}}
:'''.o'i la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Beware!] John is coming.</code>

Here there is a sense of danger in John's arrival.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfIR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfIR}}
{{judri|c13e2d13}}
:'''.o'ecu'i la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Detachment!] John is coming.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFJf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFJf}}
{{judri|c13e2d14}}
:'''.o'u la djan. klama'''
:<code>[Phew!] John is coming.</code>

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfIR}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qFJf}}, John's arrival is no problem: in the former example, the speaker feels emotional distance from the situation; in the latter example, John's coming is actually a relief of some kind.

The pure emotion indicators beginning with 
{{lerfu|i}} are those which could not be fitted into the 
{{lerfu|u}} or 
{{lerfu|o}} groups because there was a lack of room, so they are a mixed lot. 
{{vla|.ia}}, 
{{vla|i'a}}, 
{{vla|.ie}}, and 
{{vla|i'e}} do not appear here, as they belong in 

[[#section-propositional-emotions|this section]] instead.
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''.ii'''	fear	nervousness	security
'''.i'i'''	togetherness		privacy
'''.io'''	respect		disrespect
'''.i'o'''	appreciation		envy
'''.iu'''	love	no love lost	hatred
'''.i'u'''	familiarity		mystery
</tabledata>

Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFJV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFJV}}
{{judri|c13e2d15}}
:'''.ii smacu'''
:<code>[Fear!] [Observative:] a-mouse</code>
:''Eek! A mouse!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfK3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfK3}}
{{judri|c13e2d16}}
:'''la djan. .iu klama'''
:<code>John [love!] is coming.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfKX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfKX}}
{{judri|c13e2d17}}
:'''la djan. .ionai klama'''
:<code>John [disrespect!] is coming.</code>

{{linker|example-random-id-qFJV}} shows an attitude-colored observative; the attitudinal modifies the situation described by the observative, namely the mouse that is causing the emotion. Lojban-speaking toddlers, if there ever are any, will probably use sentences like 

{{linker|example-random-id-qFJV}} a lot.

{{linker|example-random-id-qfK3}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfKX}} use attitudinals that follow 
:{{jbo|la djan.}} rather than being at the beginning of the sentence. This form means that the attitude is attached to John rather than the event of his coming; the speaker loves or disrespects John specifically. Compare:

{{dsp|example-random-id-09oC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-09oC}}
{{judri|c13e2d18}}
:'''la djan. klama .iu'''
:<code>John is-coming [love!]</code>

where it is specifically the coming of John that inspires the feeling.

{{linker|example-random-id-qfKX}} is a compact way of swearing at John: you could translate it as 
“That good-for-nothing John is coming.”

{{judri|section-propositional-emotions}}
==Propositional attitude indicators==
{{ind|general-imported|hypothetical world}}  {{ind|general-imported|internal world}}  {{ind|general-imported|propositional|of attitudinals}}  {{ind|general-imported|indicators|placement of}} As mentioned at the beginning of 
[[#section-pure-emotions|this section]], attitudinals may be divided into two groups, the pure emotion indicators explained in that section, and a contrasting group which may be called the 
“propositional attitude indicators”. These indicators establish an internal, hypothetical world which the speaker is reacting to, distinct from the world as it really is. Thus we may be expressing our attitude towards 

“what the world would be like if ...”, or more directly stating our attitude towards making the potential world a reality.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|propositional effect on claim}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|propositional contrasted with emotional}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|emotional contrasted with propositional}} In general, the bridi paraphrases of pure emotions look (in English) something like 
“I'm going to the market, and I'm happy about it”. The emotion is present with the subject of the primary claim, but is logically independent of it. Propositional attitudes, though, look more like 
“I intend to go to the market”, where the main claim is logically subordinate to the intention: I am not claiming that I am actually going to the market, but merely that I intend to.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|i- series}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|e- series}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|a- series}} There is no sharp distinction between attitudinals beginning with 
{{lerfu|a}} and those beginning with 
{{lerfu|e}}; however, the original intent (not entirely realized due to the need to cram too many attitudes into too little space) was to make the members of the 
{{lerfu|a}}-series the purer, more attitudinal realizers of a potential world, while the members of the 
{{lerfu|e}}-series were more ambivalent or complex about the speaker's intention with regard to the predication. The relationship between the 
{{lerfu|a}}-series and the 
{{lerfu|e}}-series is similar to that between the 
{{lerfu|u}}-series and the 
{{lerfu|o}}-series, respectively. A few propositional attitude indicators overflowed into the 
{{lerfu|i}}-series as well.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|logical language and}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|propositional/emotional caveat}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|emotional/propositional caveat}} In fact, the entire distinction between pure emotions and propositional attitudes is itself a bit shaky: 

{{vla|u'u}} can be seen as a propositional attitude indicator meaning 

“I regret that ...”, and 
{{vla|a'e}} (discussed below) can be seen as a pure emotion meaning 
“I'm awake/aware”. The division of the attitudinals into pure-emotion and propositional-attitude classes in this chapter is mostly by way of explanation; it is not intended to permit firm rulings on specific points. Attitudinals are the part of Lojban most distant from the 
“logical language” aspect.

Here is the list of propositional attitude indicators grouped by initial letter, starting with those beginning with 
{{lerfu|a}}:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''.a'a'''	attentive	inattentive	avoiding
'''.a'e'''	alertness		exhaustion
'''.ai'''	intent	indecision	refusal
'''.a'i'''	effort	no real effort	repose
'''.a'o'''	hope		despair
'''.au'''	desire	indifference	reluctance
'''.a'u'''	interest	no interest	repulsion
</tabledata>

Some examples (of a parental kind):

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfLc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfLc}}
{{judri|c13e3d1}}
:'''.a'a do zgana le veltivni'''
:<code>[attentive] you observe the television-receiver.</code>
:''I'm noticing that you are watching the TV.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfMa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfMa}}
{{judri|c13e3d2}}
:'''.a'enai do ranji bacru'''
:<code>[exhaustion] you continuously utter.</code>
:''I'm worn out by your continuous talking.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFmF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFmF}}
{{judri|c13e3d3}}
:'''.ai mi benji do le ckana'''
:<code>[intent] I transfer you to-the bed.</code>
:''I'm putting you to bed.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfnb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfnb}}
{{judri|c13e3d4}}
:'''.a'i mi ba gasnu le nu do cikna binxo'''
:<code>[effort] I [future] am-the-actor-in the event-of you awake-ly become.</code>
:''It'll be hard for me to wake you up.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFPm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFPm}}
{{judri|c13e3d5}}
:'''.a'o mi kanryze'a ca le bavlamdei'''
:<code>[hope] I am-health-increased at-time the future-adjacent-day.</code>
:''I hope I feel better tomorrow!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfPV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfPV}}
{{judri|c13e3d6}}
:'''.au mi sipna'''
:<code>[desire] I sleep.</code>
:''I want to sleep.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFpy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFpy}}
{{judri|c13e3d7}}
:'''.a'ucu'i do pante'''
:<code>[no interest] you complain</code>
:''I have no interest in your complaints.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|.a'ucu'i}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.a'enai}}  (In a real-life situation, Examples 3.1-3.7 would also be decorated by various pure emotion indicators, certainly including 
:{{jbo|.oicai}}, but probably also 
:{{jbo|.iucai}}.)

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|rationale for}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|contrasted with bridi}} Splitting off the attitude into an indicator allows the regular bridi grammar to do what it does best: express the relationships between concepts that are intended, desired, hoped for, or whatever. Rephrasing these examples to express the attitude as the main selbri would make for unacceptably heavyweight grammar.

Here are the propositional attitude indicators beginning with 
{{lerfu|e}}, which stand roughly in the relation to those beginning with 
{{lerfu|a}} as the pure-emotion indicators beginning with 
{{lerfu|o}} do to those beginning with 
{{lerfu|u}}- they are more complex or difficult:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''.e'a'''	permission		prohibition
'''.e'e'''	competence		incompetence
'''.ei'''	obligation		freedom
'''.e'i'''	constraint	independence	resistance to constraint
'''.e'o'''	request		negative request
'''.e'u'''	suggestion	no suggestion	warning
</tabledata>

More examples (after a good night's sleep):

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFQ7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFQ7}}
{{judri|c13e3d8}}
{{ind|example|after sleep|example}}
:'''.e'a do sazri le karce'''
:<code>[permission] You drive the car.</code>
:''Sure, you can drive the car.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFR1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFR1}}
{{judri|c13e3d9}}
{{ind|example|after sleep|example}}
:'''.e'e mi lifri tu'a do'''
:<code>[competence] I experience something-related-to you</code>
:''I feel up to dealing with you.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfS1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfS1}}
{{judri|c13e3d10}}
{{ind|example|after sleep|example}}
:'''.ei mi tisygau le karce ctilyvau'''
:<code>[obligation] I fill the car-type-of petroleum-container.</code>
:''I should fill the car's gas tank.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfS7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfS7}}
{{judri|c13e3d11}}
{{ind|example|after sleep|example}}
:'''.e'o ko ko kurji'''
:<code>[request] You-imperative of-you-imperative take-care.</code>
:''Please take care of yourself!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFSC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFSC}}
{{judri|c13e3d12}}
{{ind|example|after sleep|example}}
:'''.e'u do klama le panka'''
:<code>[suggestion] You go to-the park.</code>
:''I suggest going to the park.''

Finally, the propositional attitude indicators beginning with 
{{lerfu|i}}, which are the overflow from the other sets:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''.ia'''	belief	skepticism	disbelief
'''.i'a'''	acceptance		blame
'''.ie'''	agreement		disagreement
'''.i'e'''	approval	non-approval	disapproval
</tabledata>

Still more examples (much, much later):

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfSU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfSU}}
{{judri|c13e3d13}}
:'''.ianai do pu pensi le nu tcica mi'''
:<code>[disbelief] You [past] think the event-of deceiving me.</code>
:''I can't believe you thought you could fool me.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfT6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfT6}}
{{judri|c13e3d14}}
:'''do .i'anai na xruti do le zdani'''
:<code>You [blame] did-not return you to-the house</code>
:''I blame you for not coming home.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qftC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qftC}}
{{judri|c13e3d15}}
:'''.ie mi na cusku lu'e le tcika be le nu xruti'''
:<code>[agreement] I did-not express a-symbol-for the time-of-day of the event-of (you return)</code>
:''It's true I didn't tell you when to come back.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFU7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFU7}}
{{judri|c13e3d16}}
:'''.i'enai do .i'e zukte'''

:<code>[disapproval] you [approval] act</code>
:''I don't approve of what you did, but I approve of you.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|.i'enai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.i'anai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.ianai}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-qFU7}} illustrates the use of a propositional attitude indicator, 
{{vla|i'e}}, in both the usual sense (at the beginning of the bridi) and as a pure emotion (attached to 

{{vla|do}}). The event expressed by the main bridi is disapproved of by the speaker, but the referent of the sumti in the x1 place (namely the listener) is approved of.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal|signaling as non-propositional}} To indicate that an attitudinal discussed in this section is not meant to indicate a propositional attitude, the simplest expedient is to split the attitudinal off into a separate sentence. Thus, a version of 
{{linker|example-random-id-qFQ7}} which actually claimed that the listener was or would be driving the car might be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-96qq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-96qq}}
{{judri|c13e3d17}}
:'''do sazri le karce .i .e'a'''
:<code>You drive the car. [Permission].</code>
:''You're driving (or will drive) the car, and that's fine.''

{{judri|section-intensity-scale}}
==Attitudes as scales==
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|neutral}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|negative}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|positive}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|scale of}} In Lojban, all emotions and attitudes are scales. These scales run from some extreme value (which we'll call 
“positive”) to an opposite extreme (which we'll call 
“negative”). In the tables above, we have seen three points on the scale: 
“positive”, neutral, and 
“negative”. The terms 
“positive” and 
“negative” are put into quotation marks because they are loaded words when applied to emotions, and the attitudinal system reflects this loading, which is a known cultural bias. Only two of the 
“positive” words, namely 
{{vla|.ii}} (fear) and 
{{vla|.oi}} (pain/complaint), represent emotions commonly thought of as less 
“virtuous” in most cases than their negative counterparts. But these two were felt to be instinctive, distinct, and very powerful emotions that needed to be expressible in a monosyllable when necessary, while their counterparts are less commonly expressed.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal scales|rationale for assignment}} (Why the overt bias? Because there are a lot of attitudinals and they will be difficult to learn as an entire set. By aligning our scales arbitrarily, we give the monosyllable 
{{vla|nai}} a useful meaning and make it easier for a novice to recognize at least the positive or negative alignment of an indicator, if not the specific word. Other choices considered were 
“random” orientation, which would have unknown biases and be difficult to learn, and orientation based on our guesses as to which scale orientations made the most frequent usages shorter, which would be biased in favor of American perceptions of 
“usefulness”. If bias must exist in our indicator set, it might as well be a known bias that eases learning, and in addition might as well favor a harmonious and positive world-view.)

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal scale|seven-position}}  {{ind|general-imported|emotional scale}} In fact, though, each emotional scale has seven positions defined, three 

“positive” ones (shown below on the left), three 
“negative” ones (shown below on the right), and a neutral one indicating that no particular attitude on this scale is felt. The following chart indicates the seven positions of the scale and the associated cmavo. All of these cmavo, except 
{{vla|nai}}, are in selma'o CAI.

<tabledata class="wikitable">
cai	sai	ru'e	cu'i	nairu'e	naisai	naicai
[carmi]	[tsali]	[ruble]	[cumki]
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|attitude|scalar}}  {{ind|general-imported|scalar attitude}} A scalar attitude is expressed by using the attitudinal word, and then following it by the desired scalar intensity. The bias creeps in because the 

“negative” emotions take the extra syllable 
{{vla|nai}} to indicate their negative position on the axis, and thus require a bit more effort to express.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal scale|usage}} Much of this system is optional. You can express an attitude without a scale indicator, if you don't want to stop and think about how strongly you feel. Indeed, for most attitudinals, we've found that either no scalar value is used, or 
{{vla|cai}} is used to indicate especially high intensity. Less often, 

{{vla|ru'e}} is used for a recognizably weak intensity, and 

{{vla|cu'i}} is used in response to the attitudinal question 

{{vla|pei}} (See [[#section-questions-empathy-contours|this section]]) to indicate that the emotion is not felt.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal|example of scale effect}} The following shows the variations resulting from intensity variation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfUc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfUc}}
{{judri|c13e4d1}}
{{ind|example|formal requirement|example}}
:'''.ei'''
:''I ought to (a non-specific obligation)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFUR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFUR}}
{{judri|c13e4d2}}
{{ind|example|formal requirement|example}}
:'''.eicai'''
:''I shall/must (an intense obligation or requirement, possibly a formal one)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfuy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfuy}}
{{judri|c13e4d3}}
{{ind|example|formal requirement|example}}
:'''.eisai'''
:''I should (a strong obligation or necessity, possibly an implied but not formal requirement)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfvL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfvL}}
{{judri|c13e4d4}}
{{ind|example|formal requirement|example}}
:'''.eiru'e'''
:''I might (a weak obligation &ndash; in English often mixed with permission and desire)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfvn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfvn}}
{{judri|c13e4d5}}
{{ind|example|formal requirement|example}}
:'''.eicu'i'''
:''No matter (no particular obligation)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFw3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFw3}}
{{judri|c13e4d6}}
{{ind|example|formal requirement|example}}
:'''.einai'''
:''I need not (a non-obligation)''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|.einai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.eicu'i}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.eiru'e}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.eisai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|.eicai}}
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal scale|stand-alone usage}} You can also utter a scale indicator without a specific emotion. This is often used in the language: in order to emphasize a point about which you feel strongly, you mark what you are saying with the scale indicator 
{{vla|cai}}. You could also indicate that you don't care using 

{{vla|cu'i}} by itself.

{{judri|section-attitudinal-space}}
==The space of emotions==
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal scale|as axis in emotion-space}} Each of the attitude scales constitutes an axis in a multi-dimensional space. In effect, given our total so far of 39 scales, we have a 39-dimensional space. At any given time, our emotions and attitudes are represented by a point in this 39-dimensional space, with the intensity indicators serving as coordinates along each dimension. A complete attitudinal inventory, should one decide to express it, would consist of reading off each of the scale values for each of the emotions, with the vector sum serving as a distinct single point, which is our attitude.

{{ind|general-imported|emotions|when expressed}}  {{ind|general-imported|emotions|insights}}  {{ind|general-imported|emotions|compound}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound emotions}} Now no one is going to ever utter a string of 100-odd attitudinals to express their emotions. If asked, we normally do not recognize more than one or two emotions at a time &ndash; usually the ones that are strongest or which most recently changed in some significant way. But the scale system provides some useful insights into a possible theory of emotion (which might be testable using Lojban), and incidentally explains how Lojbanists express compound emotions when they do recognize them.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal scale|neutral compared with positive + negative}} The existence of 39 scales highlights the complexity of emotion. We also aren't bound to the 39. There are modifiers described in 
[[#section-categories|this section]] that multiply the set of scales by an order of magnitude. You can also have mixed feelings on a scale, which might be expressed by 

{{vla|cu'i}}, but could also be expressed by using both the 

“positive” and 
“negative” scale emotions at once. One expression of 
“fortitude” might be 
:{{jbo|.ii.iinai}}- fear coupled with security.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|contrasted with rationalizations of emotion}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|order of}} Uttering one or more attitudinals to express an emotion reflects several things. We will tend to utter emotions in their immediate order of importance to us. We feel several emotions at once, and our expression reflects these emotions simultaneously, although their order of importance to us is also revealing &ndash; of our attitude towards our attitude, so to speak. There is little analysis necessary; for those emotions you feel, you express them; the 
“vector sum” naturally expresses the result. This is vital to their nature as attitudinals &ndash; if you had to stop and think about them, or to worry about grammar, they wouldn't be emotions but rationalizations.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|contrasted with bridi}} People have proposed that attitudinals be expressed as bridi just like everything else; but emotions aren't logical or analytical &ndash; saying 
“I'm awed” is not the same as saying 
“Wow!!!”. The Lojban system is intended to give the effects of an analytical system without the thought involved. Thus, you can simply feel in Lojban.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|design benefit}} A nice feature of this design is that you can be simple or complex, and the system works the same way. The most immediate benefit is in learning. You only need to learn a couple of the scale words and a couple of attitude words, and you're ready to express your emotions Lojbanically. As you learn more, you can express your emotions more thoroughly and more precisely, but even a limited vocabulary offers a broad range of expression.

{{judri|section-categories}}
==Emotional categories==
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal categories|rationale}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinal categories}}  {{ind|general-imported|emotional categories}} The Lojban attitudinal system was designed by starting with a long list of English emotion words, far too many to fit into the 39 available VV-form cmavo. To keep the number of cmavo limited, the emotion words in the list were grouped together by common features: each group was then assigned a separate cmavo. This was like making tanru in reverse, and the result is a collection of indicators that can be combined, like tanru, to express very complex emotions. Some examples in a moment.

The most significant 
“common feature” we identified was that the emotional words on the list could easily be broken down into six major groups, each of which was assigned its own cmavo:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ro'a'''	social	asocial	antisocial
'''ro'e'''	mental		mindless
'''ro'i'''	emotional		denying emotion
'''ro'o'''	physical		denying physical
'''ro'u'''	sexual		sexual abstinence
'''re'e'''	spiritual	secular	sacrilegious
</tabledata>

Using these, we were able to assign 
{{vla|o'u}} to mark a scale of what we might call 

“generalized comfort”. When you are comfortable, relaxed, satisfied, you express comfort with 
{{vla|o'u}}, possibly followed by a scale indicator to indicate how comfortable you are. The six cmavo given above allow you to turn this scale into six separate ones, should you wish.

{{ind|general|mental discomfort|example}}  {{ind|general|physical distress|example}}  {{ind|general|stress|example}}  {{ind|general|embarrassment|example}}  {{ind|general|spiritual discomfort|example}}  {{ind|general|sexual discomfort|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal categories|example of effect}} For example, embarrassment is a social discomfort, expressible as 

:{{jbo|.o'unairo'a}}. Some emotions that we label 
“stress” in English are expressed in Lojban with 
:{{jbo|.o'unairo'i}}. Physical distress can be expressed with 
:{{jbo|.o'unairo'o}}, which makes a nice groan if you say it with feeling. Mental discomfort might be what you feel when you don't know the answer to the test question, but feel that you should. Most adults can recall some instance where we felt sexual discomfort, 

:{{jbo|o'unairo'u}}. Spiritual discomfort, 
:{{jbo|o'unaire'e}}, might be felt by a church-goer who has wandered into the wrong kind of religious building.

Most of the time when expressing an emotion, you won't categorize it with these words. Emotional expressions should be quickly expressible without having to think about them. However, we sometimes have mixed emotions within this set, as for example emotional discomfort coupled with physical comfort or vice versa.

Coupling these six words with our 39 attitude scales, each of which has a positive and negative side, already gives you far more emotional expression words than we have emotional labels in English. Thus, you'll never see a Lojban-English emotional dictionary that covers all the Lojban possibilities. Some may be useless, but others convey emotions that probably never had a word for them before, though many have felt them ( 
:{{jbo|.eiro'u}}, for example &ndash; look it up).

{{ind|general|ro'anai|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|stand-alone categories}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|categories with nai}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|categories with scale markers}} You can use scale markers and 
{{vla|nai}} on these six category words, and you can also use category words without specifying the emotion. Thus, 
“I'm trying to concentrate” could be expressed simply as 
{{vla|ro'e}}, and if you are feeling anti-social in some non-specific way, 

{{vla|ro'anai}} will express it.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal categories|mnemonic for}} There is a mnemonic device for the six emotion categories, based on moving your arms about. In the following table, your hands begin above your head and move down your body in sequence.
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ro'a'''	hands above head	social
'''ro'e'''	hands on head	intellectual
'''ro'i'''	hands on heart	emotional
'''ro'o'''	hands on belly	physical
'''ro'u'''	hands on groin	sexual
'''re'e'''	hands moving around	spiritual
</tabledata>

The implicit metaphors 
“heart” for emotional and 
“belly” for physical are not really Lojbanic, but they work fine for English-speakers.

{{judri|section-modifiers}}
==Attitudinal modifiers==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ga'i'''	[galtu]	hauteur	equal rank	meekness
'''rank'''				lack of rank
'''le'o'''		aggressive	passive		defensive
'''vu'e'''	[vrude]	virtue (zabna)		sin (mabla)
'''se'i'''	[sevzi]	self-orientation		other-orientation
'''ri'e'''	[zifre]	release	restraint	control
'''fu'i'''	[frili]	with help	without help	with opposition
'''easily'''				with difficulty
'''be'u'''	lack/need	presence		satiation
'''need'''				satisfaction
'''se'a'''	[sevzi]	self-sufficiency		dependency
</tabledata>

{{ind|general|self-orientation|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal modifiers}} It turned out that, once we had devised the six emotion categories, we also recognized some other commonalities among emotions. These tended to fit nicely on scales of their own, but generally tend not to be thought of as separate emotions. Some of these are self-explanatory, some need to be placed in context. Some of these tend to go well with only a few of the attitudinals, others go with nearly all of them. To really understand these modifiers, try to use them in combination with one or two of the attitudinals found in 
[[#section-pure-emotions|this section]] and 
[[#section-propositional-emotions|this section]], and see what emotional pictures you can build:

The cmavo 
{{vla|ga'i}} expresses the scale used to indicate condescension or polite deference; it is not respect in general, which is 

{{vla|.io}}. Whatever it is attached to is marked as being below (for 
{{vla|ga'i}}) or above (for 

{{vla|ga'inai}}) the speaker's rank or social position. Note that it is always the referent, not the speaker or listener, who is so marked: in order to mark the listener, the listener must appear in the sentence, as with 

:{{jbo|doi ga'inai}}, which can be appended to a statement addressed to a social superior.

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ercd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ercd}}
{{judri|c13e7d1}}
{{ind|example|condescension|example}}
:'''ko ga'inai nenri klama le mi zdani'''
:<code>You-imperative [low-rank!] enter-type-of come-to my house.</code>
:''I would be honored if you would enter my residence.''

{{ind|general-imported|imperatives|attitude}} Note that imperatives in Lojban need not be imperious! Corresponding examples with 

{{vla|ga'icu'i}} and 
{{vla|ga'inai}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfWn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfWn}}
{{judri|c13e7d2}}
{{ind|example|deference|example}}
:'''ko ga'icu'i nenri klama le mi zdani'''
:<code>You-imperative [equal-rank!] enter-type-of come-to my house.</code>
:''Come on in to my place.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfwV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfwV}}
{{judri|c13e7d3}}
{{ind|example|inferior|example}}
:'''ko ga'i nenri klama le mi zdani'''
:<code>You-imperative [high-rank!] enter-type-of come-to my house.</code>
:''You! Get inside!''

Since 
{{vla|ga'i}} expresses the relative rank of the speaker and the referent, it does not make much sense to attach it to 

{{vla|mi}}, unless the speaker is using 
{{vla|mi}} to refer to a group (as in English 
“we”), or a past or future version of himself with a different rank.

It is also possible to attach 
{{vla|ga'i}} to a whole bridi, in which case it expresses the speaker's superiority to the event the bridi refers to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wgDV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wgDV}}
{{judri|c13e7d4}}
:'''ga'i le xarju pu citka'''
:<code>[High-rank!] the pig [past] eats</code>
:''The pig ate (which is an event beneath my notice).''

When used without being attached to any bridi, 
{{vla|ga'i}} expresses the speaker's superiority to things in general, which may represent an absolute social rank: 

:{{jbo|ga'icai}} is an appropriate opening word for an emperor's address from the throne.

The cmavo 
{{vla|le'o}} represents the scale of aggressiveness. We seldom overtly recognize that we are feeling aggressive or defensive, but perhaps in counseling sessions, a psychologist might encourage someone to express these feelings on this scale. And football teams could be urged on by their coach using 

:{{jbo|ro'ole'o}}. 
{{vla|le'o}} is also useful in threats as an alternative to 

:{{jbo|o'onai}}, which expresses anger.

{{ind|general|sinful|example}}  {{ind|general|virtue|example}}  {{ind|general|righteous indignation|example}}
The cmavo 
{{vla|vu'e}} represents ethical virtue or its absence. An excess of almost any emotion is usually somewhat 

“sinful” in the eyes of most ethical systems. On the other hand, we often feel virtuous about our feelings &ndash; what we call righteous indignation might be 

:{{jbo|o'onaivu'e}}. Note that this is distinct from lack of guilt: 
{{vla|.u'unai}}.

The cmavo 
{{vla|se'i}} expresses the difference between selfishness and generosity, for example (in combination with 

{{vla|.au}}):

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFxm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFxm}}
{{judri|c13e7d5}}
:'''.ause'i'''
:<code>[desire] [self]</code>
:''I want it!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfXq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfXq}}
{{judri|c13e7d6}}
:'''.ause'inai'''
:<code>[desire] [other]</code>
:''I want you to have it!''

In both cases, the English 
“it” is vague, reflecting the absence of a bridi. 
{{linker|example-random-id-qFxm}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qfXq}} are pure expressions of attitude. Analogously, 
:{{jbo|.uuse'i}} is self-pity, whereas 
:{{jbo|.uuse'inai}} is pity for someone else.

The modifier 
{{vla|ri'e}} indicates emotional release versus emotional control. 

“I will not let him know how angry I am”, you say to yourself before entering the room. The Lojban is much shorter:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Pwuv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Pwuv}}
{{judri|c13e7d7}}
:'''.o'onai ri'enai'''
:<code>[anger] [control]</code>

On the other hand, 
{{vla|ri'e}} can be used by itself to signal an emotional outburst.

The cmavo 
{{vla|fu'i}} may express a reason for feeling the way we do, as opposed to a feeling in itself; but it is a reason that is more emotionally determined than most. For example, it could show the difference between the mental discomfort mentioned in 

[[#section-categories|this section]] when it is felt on an easy test, as opposed to on a hard test. When someone gives you a back massage, you could use 
:{{jbo|.o'ufu'i}} to show appreciation for the assistance in your comfort.

The cmavo 
{{vla|be'u}} expresses, roughly speaking, whether the emotion it modifies is in response to something you don't have enough of, something you have enough of, or something you have too much of. It is more or less the attitudinal equivalent of the subjective quantifier cmavo 

{{vla|mo'a}}, 

{{vla|rau}}, and 

{{vla|du'e}} (these belong to selma'o PA, and are discussed in 

[[#section-indefinite-numbers|this section]]). For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-K4aV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-K4aV}}
{{judri|c13e7d8}}
{{ind|example|large meal|example}}
:'''.uiro'obe'unai'''
:<code>[Yay!] [physical] [Enough!]</code>

might be something you say after a large meal which you enjoyed.

Like all modifiers, 
{{vla|be'u}} can be used alone:

{{dsp|example-random-id-U3zm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-U3zm}}
{{judri|c13e7d9}}
:'''le cukta be'u cu zvati ma'''
:<code>The book [Needed!] is at-location [what sumti?]</code>
:<code>Where's the book? &ndash; I need it!</code>

Lastly, the modifier 
{{vla|se'a}} shows whether the feeling is associated with self-sufficiency or with dependence on others.

{{dsp|example-random-id-4S14}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4S14}}
{{judri|c13e7d10}}
:'''.e'ese'a'''
:<code>[I can!] [self-sufficient!]</code>
:''I can do it all by myself!''

is something a Lojban-speaking child might say. On the other hand,

{{dsp|example-random-id-Arv2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Arv2}}
{{judri|c13e7d11}}
:'''.e'ese'anai'''
:<code>[I can!] [dependent]</code>
:''I can do it if you help me.''

from the same child would indicate a (hopefully temporary) loss of self-confidence. It is also possible to negate the 
{{vla|e'e}} in 

{{linker|example-random-id-Pwuv}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-K4aV}}, leading to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-stdV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-stdV}}
{{judri|c13e7d12}}
:'''.e'enaise'a'''
:<code>[I can't!] [self-sufficient]</code>
:''I can't do it if you insist on “helping” me!''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-TIjf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TIjf}}
{{judri|c13e7d13}}
:'''.e'enaise'anai'''
:<code>[I can't!] [dependent]</code>
:''I can't do it by myself!''

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|complexity}} Some of the emotional expressions may seem too complicated to use. They might be for most circumstances. It is likely that most combinations will never get used. But if one person uses one of these expressions, another person can understand (as unambiguously as the expresser intends) what emotion is being expressed. Most probably as the system becomes well-known and internalized by Lojban-speakers, particular attitudinal combinations will come to be standard expressions (if not cliches) of emotion.

{{judri|section-compound-attitudinals}}
==Compound indicators==
{{ind|general-imported|indicators|meaning when compounded}}  {{ind|general-imported|indicators|grammar for compounding}} The grammar of indicators is quite simple; almost all facets are optional. You can combine indicators in any order, and they are still grammatical. The presumed denotation is additive; thus the whole is the sum of the parts regardless of the order expressed, although the first expressed is presumed most important to the speaker. Every possible string of UI cmavo has some meaning.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal indicator|unspecified}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinal indicators|conventions of interpretation}}  {{ind|general-imported|unspecified emotion}} Within a string of indicators, there will be conventions of interpretation which amount to a kind of second-order grammar. Each of the modifier words is presumed to modify an indicator to the left, if there is one. (There is an 
“unspecified emotion” word, 

{{vla|ge'e}}, reserved to ensure that if you want to express a modifier without a root emotion, it doesn't attach to and modify a previous but distinct emotional expression.)

{{ind|general-imported|unspecified level of emotion}}  {{ind|general-imported|unstated emotion}} For example, 
:{{jbo|.ieru'e}} expresses a weak positive value on the scale of agreement: the speaker agrees (presumably with the listener or with something else just stated), but with the least possible degree of intensity. But 
:{{jbo|.ie ge'eru'e}} expresses agreement (at an unspecified level), followed by some other unstated emotion which is felt at a weak level. A rough English equivalent of 

:{{jbo|.ie ge'eru'e}} might be 
“I agree, but ...” where the 
“but” is left hanging. (Again, attitudes aren't always expressed in English by English attitudinals.)

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal indicators|placement of scale in}} A scale variable similarly modifies the previous emotion word. You put the scale word for a root emotion word before a modifier, since the latter can have its own scale word. This merely maximizes the amount of information expressible. For example, 
:{{jbo|.oinaicu'i ro'ucai}} expresses a feeling midway between pain ( 
{{vla|.oi}}) and pleasure ( 
{{vla|.oinai}}) which is intensely sexual ( 
{{vla|ro'u}}) in nature.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|placement in sentences with &quot;nai&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinal indicators|placement of &quot;nai&quot; in}} The cmavo 
{{vla|nai}} is the most tightly bound modifier in the language: it always negates exactly one word &ndash; the preceding one. Of all the words used in indicator constructs, 
{{vla|nai}} is the only one with any meaning outside the indicator system. If you try to put an indicator between a non-indicator cmavo and its 
{{vla|nai}} negator, the 
{{vla|nai}} will end up negating the last word of the indicator. The result, though unambiguous, is not what you want. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-9BBA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9BBA}}
{{judri|c13e8d1}}
:'''mi .e .ui nai do'''
:<code>I and [Yay!] [Not!] you</code>

means 
“I and (unfortunately) you”, whereas

{{dsp|example-random-id-NBhW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NBhW}}
{{judri|c13e8d2}}
:'''mi .e nai .ui do'''
:<code>I and [Not!] [Yay!] you</code>

means 
“I but (fortunately) not you”. Attitudinal 
{{vla|nai}} expresses a 
“scalar negation”, a concept explained in 
[[#section-scalar-negation|this section]]; since every attitudinal word implies exactly one scale, the effect of 
{{vla|nai}} on each should be obvious.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|grammar of internal compounding}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|internal grammar|complete}} Thus, the complete internal grammar of UI is as follows, with each listed part optionally present or absent without affecting grammaticality, though it obviously would affect meaning.
'''attitudinal''' {{vla|nai}} '''intensity-word''' {{vla|nai}} '''modifier''' {{vla|nai}} '''intensity-word''' {{vla|nai}} (possibly repeated)

{{vla|ge'e}}, the non-specific emotion word, functions as an attitudinal. If multiple attitudes are being expressed at once, then in the 2nd or greater position, either 

{{vla|ge'e}} or a VV word must be used to prevent any modifiers from modifying the previous attitudinal.

{{judri|section-scope}}
==The uses of indicators==
{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|external grammar}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|grammar of placement in bridi}} The behavior of indicators in the 
“outside grammar” is nearly as simple as their internal structure. Indicator groupings are identified immediately after the metalinguistic erasers 

{{vla|si}}, 
{{vla|sa}}, and 
{{vla|su}} and some, though not all, kinds of quotations. The details of such interactions are discussed in 
[[#section-cmavo-interactions|this section]].

A group of indicators may appear anywhere that a single indicator may, except in those few situations (as in 
{{vla|zo}} quotation, explained in 
[[#section-more-quotations|this section]]) where compound cmavo may not be used.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|at beginning of text}} At the beginning of a text, indicators modify everything following them indefinitely: such a usage is taken as a raw emotional expression, and we normally don't turn off our emotions when we start and stop sentences. In every other place in an utterance, the indicator (or group) attaches to the word immediately to its left, and indicates that the attitude is being expressed concerning the object or concept to which the word refers.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|affecting whole grammatical structures}} If the word that an indicator (or group) attaches to is itself a cmavo which governs a grammatical structure, then the indicator construct pertains to the referent of the entire structure. There is also a mechanism, discussed in 
[[#section-attitudinal-scope|this section]], for explicitly marking the range of words to which an indicator applies.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|referent uncertainty}} More details about the uses of indicators, and the way they interact with other specialized cmavo, are given in 
[[#chapter-structure|this chapter]]. It is worth mentioning that real-world interpretation is not necessarily consistent with the formal scope rules. People generally express emotions when they feel them, with only a minimum of grammatical constraint on that expression; complexities of emotional expression are seldom logically analyzable. Lojban attempts to provide a systematic reference that could possibly be ingrained to an instinctive level. However, it should always be assumed that the referent of an indicator has some uncertainty.

{{ind|general-imported|multiple indicators}} For example, in cases of multiple indicators expressed together, the combined form has some ambiguity of interpretation. It is possible to interpret the second indicator as expressing an attitude about the first, or to interpret both as expressing attitudes about the common referent. For example, in

{{dsp|example-random-id-Rs6P}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Rs6P}}
{{judri|c13e9d1}}
:'''mi pu tavla do .o'onai .oi'''
:<code>I [past] talk-to you [Grrr!] [Oy!]</code>

can be interpreted as expressing complaint about the anger, in which case it means 
“Damn, I snapped at you”; or as expressing both anger and complaint about the listener, in which case it means 
“I told you, you pest!”

Similarly, an indicator after the final brivla of a tanru may be taken to express an attitude about the particular brivla placed there &ndash; as the rules have it &ndash; or about the entire bridi which hinges on that brivla. Remembering that indicators are supposedly direct expressions of emotion, this ambiguity is acceptable.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|benefit in written expression}} Even if the scope rules given for indicators turn out to be impractical or unintuitive for use in conversation, they are still useful in written expression. There, where you can go back and put in markers or move words around, the scope rules can be used in lieu of elaborate nuances of body language and intonation to convey the writer's intent.

{{judri|section-questions-empathy-contours}}
==Attitude questions; empathy; attitude contours==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''pei'''	attitude question		
'''dai'''	empathy		
'''bu'o'''	start emotion	continue emotion	end emotion
</tabledata>

You can ask someone how they are feeling with a normal bridi sentence, but you will get a normal bridi answer in response, one which may be true or false. Since the response to a question about emotions is no more logical than the emotion itself, this isn't appropriate.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal questions}} The word 
{{vla|pei}} is therefore reserved for attitude questions. Asked by itself, it captures all of the denotation of English 
“How are you?” coupled with 
“How do you feel?” (which has a slightly different range of usage).

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal answers|plausibility}} When asked in the context of discourse, 
{{vla|pei}} acts like other Lojban question words &ndash; it requests the respondent to 
“fill in the blank”, in this case with an appropriate attitudinal describing the respondent's feeling about the referent expression. As with other questions, plausibility is polite; if you answer with an irrelevant UI cmavo, such as a discursive, you are probably making fun of the questioner. (A 

{{vla|ge'e}}, however, is always in order &ndash; you are not required to answer emotionally. This is not the same as 

{{vla|.i'inai}}, which is privacy as the reverse of conviviality.)

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal questions|asking intensity}} Most often, however, the asker will use 
{{vla|pei}} as a place holder for an intensity marker. (As a result, 
{{vla|pei}} is placed in selma'o CAI, although selma'o UI would have been almost as appropriate. Grammatically, there is no difference between UI and CAI.) Such usage corresponds to a whole range of idiomatic usages in natural languages:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfXT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfXT}}
{{judri|c13e10d1}}
:'''.iepei'''
:<code>[agreement] [question]</code>
:''Do you agree?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfyA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfyA}}
{{judri|c13e10d2}}
:'''.iare'epei'''
:<code>[belief] [spiritual] [question]</code>
:''Are you a Believer?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFYC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFYC}}
{{judri|c13e10d3}}
:'''.aipei'''
:<code>[intention] [question]</code>
:''Are you going to do it?''

{{linker|example-random-id-qFYC}} might appear at the end of a command, to which the response

{{dsp|example-random-id-sKmg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sKmg}}
{{judri|c13e10d4}}
:'''.aicai'''
:<code>[intention] [maximal]</code>

corresponds to 
“Aye! Aye!” (hence the choice of cmavo).

{{dsp|example-random-id-ugFH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ugFH}}
{{judri|c13e10d5}}
:'''.e'apei'''
:<code>[permission] [question]</code>
:''Please, Mommy! Can I??''

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinal questions|asking about specific attitude}} Additionally, when 
{{vla|pei}} is used at the beginning of an indicator construct, it asks specifically if that construct reflects the attitude of the respondent, as in (asked of someone who has been ill or in pain):

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFYU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFYU}}
{{judri|c13e10d6}}
:'''pei.o'u'''
:<code>[question] [comfort]</code>
:''Are you comfortable?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfzc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfzc}}
{{judri|c13e10d7}}
:'''pei.o'ucu'i'''
:<code>[question] [comfort] [neutral]</code>
:''Are you no longer in pain?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qFzH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qFzH}}
{{judri|c13e10d8}}
:'''pei.o'usai'''
:<code>[question] [comfort] [strong]</code>
:''Are you again healthy?''

{{ind|general|sympathy|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|attitudes|empathy contrasted with sympathy}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|attributing emotion to others}} Empathy, which is not really an emotion, is expressed by the indicator 
{{vla|dai}}. (Don't confuse empathy with sympathy, which is 

:{{jbo|.uuse'inai}}.) Sometimes, as when telling a story, you want to attribute emotion to someone else. You can of course make a bridi claim that so-and-so felt such-and-such an emotion, but you can also make use of the attitudinal system by adding the indicator 

{{vla|dai}}, which attributes the preceding attitudinal to someone else &ndash; exactly whom, must be determined from context. You can also use 

{{vla|dai}} conversationally when you empathize, or feel someone else's emotion as if it were your own:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ny8w}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ny8w}}
{{judri|c13e10d9}}
{{ind|example|empathy|example}}
:'''.oiro'odai'''
:<code>[Pain!] [physical] [empathy]</code>
:''Ouch, that must have hurt!''

It is even possible to 
“empathize” with a non-living object:

{{dsp|example-random-id-M7Xf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-M7Xf}}
{{judri|c13e10d10}}
{{ind|example|ship sank|example}}
:'''le bloti .iidai .uu pu klama le xasloi'''
:<code>The ship [fear!] [empathy] [pity!] [past] goes-to the ocean-floor.</code>
:''Fearfully the ship, poor thing, sank.''

suggesting that the ship felt fear at its impending destruction, and simultaneously reporting the speaker's pity for it.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|non-speaker attitudes}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|exceptions}} Both 
{{vla|pei}} and 
{{vla|dai}} represent exceptions to the normal rule that attitudinals reflect the speaker's attitude.

{{ind|general-imported|attitudes|ceasing}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudes|beginning}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudes|continuing}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|contours}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudes|expressing changes in}} Finally, we often want to report how our attitudes are changing. If our attitude has not changed, we can just repeat the attitudinal. (Therefore, 
:{{jbo|.ui .ui .ui}} is not the same as 
:{{jbo|.uicai}}, but simply means that we are continuing to be happy.) If we want to report that we are beginning to feel, continuing to feel, or ceasing to feel an emotion, we can use the attitudinal contour cmavo 
{{vla|bu'o}}.

When attached to an attitudinal, 
{{vla|bu'o}} means that you are starting to have that attitude, 

{{vla|bu'ocu'i}} that you are continuing to have it, and 
{{vla|bu'onai}} that you are ceasing to have it. Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qfzq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qfzq}}
{{judri|c13e10d11}}
:'''.o'onai bu'o'''

:<code>[Anger!] [start emotion]</code>
:''I'm getting angry!''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qg0p}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qg0p}}
{{judri|c13e10d12}}
:'''.iu bu'onai .uinai'''
:<code>[Love!] [end emotion] [unhappiness!]</code>
:''I don't love you any more; I'm sad.''

Note the difference in effect between 
{{linker|example-random-id-qg0p}} and:

{{dsp|example-random-id-6EiY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6EiY}}
{{judri|c13e10d13}}
:'''mi ca ba'o prami do ja'e le nu mi badri'''
:<code>I [present] [cessitive] love you with-result the event-of (I am-sad).</code>
:''I no longer love you; therefore, I am sad.''

which is a straightforward bridi claim. 
{{linker|example-random-id-6EiY}} states that you have (or have had) certain emotions; 
{{linker|example-random-id-qg0p}} expresses those emotions directly.

{{judri|section-evidentials}}
==Evidentials==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ja'o'''		[jalge]		I conclude
'''ca'e'''				I define
'''ba'a'''	[balvi]	I expect	I experience	I remember
'''su'a'''	[sucta]	I generalize		I particularize
'''ti'e'''		[tirna]		I hear (hearsay)
'''ka'u'''		[kulnu]		I know by cultural means
'''se'o'''		[senva]		I know by internal experience
'''za'a'''		[zgana]		I observe
'''pe'i'''		[pensi]		I opine
'''ru'a'''		[sruma]		I postulate
'''ju'a'''		[jufra]		I state
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|inspiration for}}  {{ind|general-imported|evidentials|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|Láadan evidentials}}  {{ind|general-imported|American Indian languages and evidentials}}  {{ind|general-imported|Elgin|Suzette Haden and evidentials}} Now we proceed from the attitudinal indicators and their relatives to the other, semantically unrelated, categories of indicators. The indicators known as 

“evidentials” show how the speaker came to say the utterance; i.e. the source of the information or the idea. Lojban's list of evidentials was derived from lists describing several American Indian languages. Evidentials are also essential to the constructed language Láadan, designed by the linguist and novelist Suzette Haden Elgin. Láadan's set of indicators was drawn on extensively in developing the Lojban indicator system.

{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|in English}} It is important to realize, however, that evidentials are not some odd system used by some strange people who live at the other end of nowhere: although their English equivalents aren't single words, English-speakers have vivid notions of what constitutes evidence, and of the different kinds of evidence.

{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|scales}}  {{ind|general-imported|evidentials|grammar}} Like the attitudinal indicators, the evidentials belong to selma'o UI, and may be treated identically for grammatical purposes. Most of them are not usually considered scalar in nature, but a few have associated scales.

{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|rhetorical flavor}}  {{ind|general-imported|evidentials|indisputable bridi}}  {{ind|general-imported|indisputable bridi}} A bridi with an evidential in it becomes 
“indisputable”, in the sense that the speaker is saying 
“how it is with him or her”, which is beyond argument. Claims about one's own mental states may be true or false, but are hardly subject to other people's examination. If you say that you think, or perceive, or postulate such-and-such a predication, who can contradict you? Discourse that uses evidentials has therefore a different rhetorical flavor than discourse that does not; arguments tend to become what can be called dialogues or alternating monologues, depending on your prejudices.

{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|placement in bridi}} Evidentials are most often placed at the beginning of sentences, and are often attached to the 
{{vla|i}} that separates sentences in connected discourse. It is in the nature of an evidential to affect the entire bridi in which it is placed: like the propositional attitude indicators, they strongly affect the claim made by the main bridi.

{{ind|general|deduction|example}}  {{ind|general|thus|example}} A bridi marked by 
{{vla|ja'o}} is a conclusion by the speaker based on other (stated or unstated) information or ideas. Rough English equivalents of 
{{vla|ja'o}} are 
“thus” and 
“therefore”.

A bridi marked by 
{{vla|ca'e}} is true because the speaker says so. In addition to definitions of words, 

{{vla|ca'e}} is also appropriate in what are called performatives, where the very act of speaking the words makes them true. An English example is 

“I now pronounce you husband and wife”, where the very act of uttering the words makes the listeners into husband and wife. A Lojban translation might be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Po4T}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Po4T}}
{{judri|c13e11d1}}
{{ind|example|pronouncement|example}}
{{ind|example|husband and wife|example}}
:'''ca'e le re do cu simxu speni'''
:<code>[I define!] The two of-you are-mutual spouses.</code>

{{ind|general|remembered|example}}  {{ind|general|anticipated|example}}  {{ind|general-imported|evidentials|ba'a scale}} The three scale positions of 
{{vla|ba'a}}, when attached to a bridi, indicate that it is based on the speaker's view of the real world. Thus 

{{vla|ba'a}} means that the statement represents a future event as anticipated by the speaker; 

{{vla|ba'acu'i}}, a present event as experienced by the speaker; 

{{vla|ba'anai}}, a past event as remembered by the speaker. It is accidental that this scale runs from future to past instead of past to future.

{{dsp|example-random-id-B87W}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-B87W}}
{{judri|c13e11d2}}
{{ind|example|experienced|example}}
:'''ba'acu'i le tuple be mi cu se cortu'''
:<code>[I experience!] The leg of me is-the-locus-of-pain.</code>
:''My leg hurts.''

{{ind|general|induction|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|ja'o contrasted with su'a}}  {{ind|general-imported|evidentials|su'a contrasted with ja'o}} A bridi marked by 
{{vla|su'a}} is a generalization by the speaker based on other (stated or unstated) information or ideas. The difference between 
{{vla|su'a}} and 
{{vla|ja'o}} is that 
{{vla|ja'o}} suggests some sort of reasoning or deduction (not necessarily rigorous), whereas 

{{vla|su'a}} suggests some sort of induction or pattern recognition from existing examples (not necessarily rigorous).

{{ind|general|abduction|example}}
The opposite point of the scale, 
{{vla|su'anai}}, indicates abduction, or drawing specific conclusions from general premises or patterns.

{{ind|general-imported|discursives|su'a as}} This cmavo can also function as a discursive (See [[#section-discursives|this section]]), in which case 
{{vla|su'a}} means 
“abstractly” or 
“in general”, and 
{{vla|su'anai}} means “concretely” or “in particular”.

{{ind|general|hearsay|example}}
A bridi marked by {{vla|ti'e}} is relayed information from some source other than the speaker. There is no necessary implication that the information was relayed via the speaker's ears; what we read in a newspaper is an equally good example of {{vla|ti'e}}, unless we have personal knowledge of the content.

{{dsp|example-random-id-jiXV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jiXV}}
{{judri|c13e11d3}}
:'''ti'e la .uengas cu zergau'''
:<code>[I hear!] Wenga is-a-criminal-doer.</code>
:''I hear that Wenga is a crook.''

{{ind|general|cultural knowledge|example}}  {{ind|general|myth|example}} A bridi marked by 
{{vla|ka'u}} is one held to be true in the speaker's cultural context, as a matter of myth or custom, for example. Such statements should be agreed on by a community of people &ndash; you cannot just make up your own cultural context &ndash; although 

“objectivity” in the sense of actual correspondence with the facts is certainly not required.

{{ind|general|dream|example}}  {{ind|general|revelation|example}}
