{{ind|general-imported|evidentials|ka'u contrasted with se'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|evidentials|se'o contrasted with ka'u}} On the other hand, 
{{vla|se'o}} marks a bridi whose truth is asserted by the speaker as a result of an internal experience not directly available to others, such as a dream, vision, or personal revelation. In some cultures, the line between 

{{vla|ka'u}} and 
{{vla|se'o}} is fuzzy or even nonexistent.

{{ind|general-imported|observation evidential|contrasted with observative }}  {{ind|general-imported|observative|contrasted with observation evidential}} A bridi marked by 
{{vla|za'a}} is based on perception or direct observation by the speaker. This use of 

“observe” is not connected with the Lojban 
“observative”, or bridi with the first sumti omitted. The latter has no explicit aspect, and could be a direct observation, a conclusion, an opinion, or other aspectual point of view.

{{dsp|example-random-id-KEKa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KEKa}}
{{judri|c13e11d4}}
{{ind|example|observation|example}}
:'''za'a do tatpi'''
:<code>[I observe!] You are-tired.</code>
:''I see you are tired.''

A bridi marked by 
{{vla|pe'i}} is the opinion of the speaker. The form 

:{{jbo|pe'ipei}} is common, meaning 

“Is this your opinion?”. (Strictly, this should be 

:{{jbo|peipe'i}}, in accordance with the distinction explained in Examples 10.6-10.8, but since 
{{vla|pe'i}} is not really a scale, there is no real difference between the two orders.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-DcAG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DcAG}}
{{judri|c13e11d5}}
{{ind|example|opinion|example}}
{{ind|example|Carthage destroyed|example}}
:'''pe'i la kartagos. .ei se daspo'''
:<code>[I opine!] Carthage [obligation] is-destroyed.</code>
:''In my opinion, Carthage should be destroyed.''

{{ind|general-imported|e'u|compared with ru'a}}  {{ind|general-imported|ru'a|compared with e'u}} A bridi marked by 
{{vla|ru'a}} is an assumption made by the speaker. This is similar to one possible use of 

{{vla|e'u}}.

{{dsp|example-random-id-ydRN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ydRN}}
{{judri|c13e11d6}}
{{ind|example|assumption|example}}
{{ind|example|Livingston|example}}
:'''ru'a doi livinston.'''
:<code>Dr. Livingstone, I presume?</code>
:''(A rhetorical question: Stanley knew who he was.)''

{{ind|general|basis|example}}
Finally, the evidential 
{{vla|ju'a}} is used to avoid stating a specific basis for a statement. It can also be used when the basis for the speaker's statement is not covered by any other evidential. For the most part, using 

{{vla|ju'a}} is equivalent to using no evidential at all, but in question form it can be useful: 

:{{jbo|ju'apei}} means 

“What is the basis for your statement?” and serves as an evidential, as distinct from emotional, question.

{{judri|section-discursives}}
==Discursives==
{{ind|general-imported|discourse|expressing utterance relation to}}  {{ind|general-imported|utterance|expressing relation to discourse}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives|definition}} The term 
“discursive” is used for those members of selma'o UI that provide structure to the discourse, and which show how a given word or utterance relates to the whole discourse. To express these concepts in regular bridi would involve extra layers of nesting: rather than asserting that 
“I also came”, we would have to say 
“I came; furthermore, the event of my coming is an additional instance of the relationship expressed by the previous sentence”, which is intolerably clumsy. Typical English equivalents of discursives are words or phrases like 
“however”, 
“summarizing”, 
“in conclusion”, and 
“for example”.

{{ind|general-imported|discursives|as metalinguistic claims}}  {{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|contrasted with discursives}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives|contrasted with attitudinals}} Discursives are not attitudinals: they express no particular emotion. Rather, they are abbreviations for metalinguistic claims that reference the sentence or text they are found in.

{{ind|general-imported|discursives|placement in sentence}} Discursives are most often used at the beginning of sentences, often attached to the 
{{vla|i}} that separates sentences in running discourse, but can (like all other indicators) be attached to single words when it seems necessary or useful.

{{ind|general-imported|discursives for consecutive discourse}} The discursives discussed in this section are given in groups, roughly organized by function. First, the 
“consecutive discourse” group:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ku'i'''	[karbi]	however/but/in contrast
'''ji'a'''	[jmina]	additionally
'''si'a'''	[simsa]	similarly
'''mi'u'''	[mintu]	ditto
'''po'o'''		the only relevant case
</tabledata>

{{ind|general|too|example}}  {{ind|general|but|example}}  {{ind|general|ditto|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|go'i|contrasted with mi'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|mi'u|contrasted with go'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives for consecutive discourse|contrasted}} These five discursives are mutually exclusive, and therefore they are not usually considered as scales. The first four are used in consecutive discourse. The first, 
{{vla|ku'i}}, makes an exception to the previous argument. The second, 

{{vla|ji'a}}, adds weight to the previous argument. The third, 

{{vla|si'a}}, adds quantity to the previous argument, enumerating an additional example. The fourth, 

{{vla|mi'u}}, adds a parallel case to the previous argument, and can also be used in tables or the like to show that something is being repeated from the previous column. It is distinct from 

{{vla|go'i}} (of selma'o GOhA, discussed in 
[[#section-ri-gohi-series|this section]]), which is a non-discursive version of 
“ditto” that explicitly repeats the claim of the previous bridi.

Lastly, 
{{vla|po'o}} is used when there is no other comparable case, and thus corresponds to some of the uses of 

“only”, a word difficult to express in pure bridi form:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qG0v}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qG0v}}
{{judri|c13e12d1}}
{{ind|example|only|example}}
{{ind|example|hit nose|example}}
{{ind|example|hit cousin|example}}
:'''mi po'o darxi le mi tamne fo le nazbi'''
:<code>I [only] hit my cousin at-locus the nose.</code>
:''Only I (nobody else) hit my cousin on his nose.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qg21}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qg21}}
{{judri|c13e12d2}}
{{ind|example|only|example}}
{{ind|example|hit nose|example}}
{{ind|example|hit cousin|example}}
:'''mi darxi po'o le mi tamne fo le nazbi'''
:<code>I hit [only] my cousin at-locus the nose.</code>
:''I only hit my cousin on his nose (I did nothing else to him).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qg2f}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qg2f}}
{{judri|c13e12d3}}
{{ind|example|only|example}}
{{ind|example|hit nose|example}}
{{ind|example|hit cousin|example}}
:'''mi darxi le mi tamne po'o fo le nazbi'''
:<code>I hit my cousin [only] at-locus the nose.</code>
:''I hit only my cousin on his nose (no one else).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qG42}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qG42}}
{{judri|c13e12d4}}
{{ind|example|only|example}}
{{ind|example|hit nose|example}}
{{ind|example|hit cousin|example}}
:'''mi darxi le mi tamne fo le nazbi po'o'''
:<code>I hit my cousin at-locus the nose [only].</code>
:''I hit my cousin only on his nose (nowhere else).''

{{ind|general-imported|po'o|placement in sentence}} Note that 
“only” can go before or after what it modifies in English, but 
{{vla|po'o}}, as an indicator, always comes afterward.

Next, the 
“commentary on words” group:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''va'i [valsi]'''	in other words	in the same words
'''ta'u [tanru]'''	expanding a tanru	making a tanru
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|discursives|expressing how things are said}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives|word-level}} The discursives 
{{vla|va'i}} and 
{{vla|ta'u}} operate at the level of words, rather than discourse proper, or if you like, they deal with how things are said. An alternative English expression for 

{{vla|va'i}} is 
“rephrasing”; for 
{{vla|va'inai}}, 

“repeating”. Also compare 
{{vla|va'i}} with 
{{vla|ke'u}}, discussed below.

{{ind|general-imported|tanru|explicitly defining}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru|explicating}}  {{ind|general-imported|tanru|expanding}} The cmavo 
{{vla|ta'u}} is a discursive unique to Lojban; it expresses the particularly Lojbanic device of tanru. Since tanru are semantically ambiguous, they are subject to misunderstanding. This ambiguity can be removed by expanding the tanru into some semantically unambiguous structure, often involving relative clauses or the introduction of additional brivla. The discursive 

{{vla|ta'u}} marks the transition from the use of a brief but possibly confusing tanru to its fuller, clearer expansion; the discursive 

{{vla|ta'unai}} marks a transition in the reverse direction.

Next, the 
“commentary on discourse” group:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''li'a'''	[klina]	clearly		obscurely
''''''				obviously
'''ba'u'''	[banli]	exaggeration	accuracy	understatement
'''zo'o'''	humorously	dully		seriously
'''sa'e'''	[satci]	precisely speaking		loosely speaking
'''to'u'''	[tordu]	in brief		in detail
'''do'a'''	[dunda]	generously		parsimoniously
'''sa'u'''	[sampu]	simply		elaborating
'''pa'e'''	[pajni]	justice		prejudice
'''je'u'''	[jetnu]	truly		falsely
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|discourse|gesture markers}}  {{ind|general-imported|discourse|tone of voice markers}}  {{ind|general-imported|discourse|commentary on}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives|discourse commentary}} This group is used by the speaker to characterize the nature of the discourse, so as to prevent misunderstanding. It is well-known that listeners often fail to recognize a humorous statement and take it seriously, or miss an exaggeration, or try to read more into a statement than the speaker intends to put there. In speech, the tone of voice often provides the necessary cue, but the reader of ironic or understated or imprecise discourse is often simply clueless. As with the attitudinals, the use of these cmavo may seem fussy to new Lojbanists, but it is important to remember that 

{{vla|zo'o}}, for example, is the equivalent of smiling while you speak, not the equivalent of a flat declaration like 

“What I'm about to say is supposed to be funny.”

A few additional English equivalents: for {{vla|sa'enai}}, “roughly speaking” or “approximately speaking”; for 
{{vla|sa'unai}}, “furthermore”; for {{vla|to'u}}, “in short” or “skipping details”; for {{vla|do'a}}, “broadly construed”; for {{vla|do'anai}} (as you might expect), 
“narrowly construed”.

The cmavo {{vla|pa'e}} is used to claim (truly or falsely) that one is being fair or just to all parties mentioned, whereas 

{{vla|pa'enai}} admits (or proclaims) a bias in favor of one party.

{{ind|general|irony|example}}  {{ind|general|sarcasm|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|irony|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|sarcasm|expressing}} The scale of 
{{vla|je'u}} and 
{{vla|je'unai}} is a little different from the others in the group. By default, we assume that people speak the truth &ndash; or at least, that if they are lying, they will do their best to conceal it from us. So under what circumstances would 
{{vla|je'unai}} be used, or 
{{vla|je'u}} be useful? For one thing, 
{{vla|je'u}} can be used to mark a tautology: a sentence that is a truth of logic, like 
“All cats are cats.” Its counterpart 
{{vla|je'unai}} then serves to mark a logical contradiction. In addition, 
{{vla|je'unai}} can be used to express one kind of sarcasm or irony, where the speaker pretends to believe what he/she says, but actually wishes the listener to infer a contrary opinion. Other forms of irony can be marked with 

{{vla|zo'o}} (humor) or 

{{vla|.ianai}} (disbelief).

When used as a discursive, 
{{vla|su'a}} (See [[#section-evidentials|this section]]) belongs to this group.

Next, the “knowledge” group:

<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ju'o'''	[djuno]	certainly	uncertain	certainly not
'''la'a'''	[lakne]	probably		improbably
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|knowledge discursives|compared with propositional attitudes}}  {{ind|general-imported|propositional attitudes|compared with knowledge discursives}}  {{ind|general-imported|speaker's state of knowledge}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives|knowledge}}  {{ind|general-imported|knowledge discursives}} These two discursives describe the speaker's state of knowledge about the claim of the associated bridi. They are similar to the propositional attitudes of 

[[#section-propositional-emotions|this section]], as they create a hypothetical world. We may be quite certain that something is true, and label our bridi with 

{{vla|ju'o}}; but it may be false all the same.

Next, the 
“discourse management” group:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ta'o'''	[tanjo]	by the way		returning to point
'''ra'u'''	[ralju]	chiefly	equally	incidentally
'''mu'a'''	[mupli]	for example	omitting examples	end examples
'''zu'u'''	on the one hand			on the other hand
'''ke'u'''	[krefu]	repeating		continuing
'''da'i'''	supposing			in fact
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|flow of discourse|managing with discursives}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives for managing discourse flow}}  {{ind|general-imported|discursives|discourse management}} This final group is used to perform what may be called 
“managing the discourse”: providing reference points to help the listener understand the flow from one sentence to the next.

Other English equivalents of 
{{vla|ta'onai}} are 
“anyway”, 
“anyhow”, 
“in any case”, 
“in any event”, 
“as I was saying”, and 
“continuing”.

{{ind|general-imported|ra'u|scale of importance}}  {{ind|general-imported|importance of point|scale with ra'u}} The scale of 
{{vla|ra'u}} has to do with the importance of the point being, or about to be, expressed: 

{{vla|ra'u}} is the most important point, {{vla|ra'ucu'i}} is a point of equal importance, and {{vla|ra'unai}} is a lesser point. Other English equivalents of 
{{vla|ra'u}} are “above all” and 
“primarily”.

{{ind|general-imported|ke'u|contrasted with va'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|va'i|contrasted with ke'u}} The cmavo 
{{vla|ke'u}} is very similar to {{vla|va'i}}, although {{vla|ke'unai}} and {{vla|va'inai}} are quite different. Both {{vla|ke'u}} and {{vla|va'i}} indicate that the same idea is going to be expressed using different words, but the two cmavo differ in emphasis. Using 
{{vla|ke'u}} emphasizes that the content is the same; using {{vla|va'i}} emphasizes that the words are different. Therefore, {{vla|ke'unai}} shows that the content is new (and therefore the words are also); {{vla|va'inai}} shows that the words are the same (and therefore so is the content). One English equivalent of 

{{vla|ke'unai}} is “furthermore”.

{{ind|general-imported|if|expressing real world}}  {{ind|general-imported|if|expressing hypothetical world}}  {{ind|general-imported|hypothetical world point of view}}  {{ind|general-imported|real world point of view}} The discursive 
{{vla|da'i}} marks the discourse as possibly taking a non-real-world viewpoint ( 

“Supposing that”, 
“By hypothesis”), whereas 
{{vla|da'inai}} insists on the real-world point of view ( 
“In fact”, 
“In truth”, 
“According to the facts”). A common use of 
{{vla|da'i}} is to distinguish between:

{{dsp|example-random-id-v6BU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-v6BU}}
{{judri|c13e12d5}}
{{ind|example|pregnant sister|example}}
{{ind|example|sister pregnant|example}}
:'''ganai da'i do viska le mi citno mensi gi ju'o do djuno le du'u ri pazvau'''
:<code>If you [hypothetical] see my young sister, then [certain] you know that she is-pregnant.</code>
:''If you were to see my younger sister, you would certainly know she is pregnant.''

{{ind|general-imported|hypothetical world|contrasted with real world|example}} {{ind|general-imported|real world|contrasted with hypothetical world|example}} and:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Sach}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Sach}}
{{judri|c13e12d6}}
{{ind|example|pregnant sister|example}}
{{ind|example|sister pregnant|example}}
:'''ganai da'inai do viska le mi citno mensi gi ju'o do djuno le du'u ri pazvau'''
:<code>If you [factual] see my young sister, then [certainty] you know that she is-pregnant.</code>
:''If you saw my younger sister, you would certainly know she is pregnant.''

It is also perfectly correct to omit the discursive altogether, and leave the context to indicate which significance is meant. (Chinese always leaves this distinction to the context: the Chinese sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-rxfh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rxfh}}
{{judri|c13e12d7}}
:'''ru'''

is the equivalent of either 
{{linker|example-random-id-v6BU}} or 
{{linker|example-random-id-Sach}}.)

{{judri|section-miscellanious}}
==Miscellaneous indicators==
Some indicators do not fall neatly into the categories of attitudinal, evidential, or discursive. This section discusses the following miscellaneous indicators:
<tabledata class="wikitable">
'''ki'a'''		metalinguistic confusion
'''na'i'''		metalinguistic negator
'''jo'a'''		metalinguistic affirmer
'''li'o'''		omitted text (quoted material)
'''sa'a'''		material inserted by editor/narrator
'''xu'''		true-false question
'''pau'''	question premarker	rhetorical question
'''pe'a'''	figurative language	literal language
'''bi'u'''	new information	old information
'''ge'e'''		non-specific indicator
</tabledata>

{{ind|general-imported|confusion about what was said}}  {{ind|general-imported|confusion|metalinguistic}} The cmavo 
{{vla|ki'a}} is one of the most common of the miscellaneous indicators. It expresses metalinguistic confusion; i.e. confusion about what has been said, as opposed to confusion not tied to the discourse (which is 
{{vla|.uanai}}). The confusion may be about the meaning of a word or of a grammatical construct, or about the referent of a sumti. One of the uses of English 
“which” corresponds to 
{{vla|ki'a}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gWFX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gWFX}}
{{judri|c13e13d1}}
{{ind|example|huh?|example}}
:'''mi nelci le ctuca'''
:'''.i le ki'a ctuca'''
:''I like the teacher''
:''Which teacher?''

Here, the second speaker does not understand the referent of the sumti 
:{{jbo|le ctuca}}, and so echoes back the sumti with the confusion marker.

{{ind|general-imported|invalid speech|marking as error with na'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|error marking|metalinguistic}} The metalinguistic negation cmavo 

{{vla|na'i}} and its opposite 
{{vla|jo'a}} are explained in full in 

[[#chapter-negation|this chapter]]. In general, 
{{vla|na'i}} indicates that there is something wrong with a piece of discourse: either an error, or a false underlying assumption, or something else of the sort. The discourse is invalid or inappropriate due to the marked word or construct.

{{ind|general-imported|valid speech|marking as error with jo'a}} Similarly, 
{{vla|jo'a}} marks something which looks wrong but is in fact correct. These two cmavo constitute a scale, but are kept apart for two reasons: 

:{{jbo|na'inai}} means the same as 
{{vla|jo'a}}, but would be too confusing as an affirmation; 

:{{jbo|jo'anai}} means the same as 
{{vla|na'i}}, but is too long to serve as a convenient metalinguistic negator.

{{ind|general-imported|partial quotation}}  {{ind|general-imported|fragmentary text}} The next two cmavo are used to assist in quoting texts written or spoken by others. It is often the case that we wish to quote only part of a text, or to supply additional material either by way of commentary or to make a fragmentary text grammatical. The cmavo 

{{vla|li'o}} serves the former function. It indicates that words were omitted from the quotation. What remains of the quotation must be grammatical, however, as 

{{vla|li'o}} does not serve any grammatical function. It cannot, for example, take the place of a missing selbri in a bridi, or supply the missing tail of a description sumti: 

:{{false|le li'o}} in isolation is not grammatical.

{{ind|general-imported|sa'a|interaction with to'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|sa'a|interaction with sei}}  {{ind|general-imported|sa'a|interaction with li'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|editorial insertion|with &quot;sa'a}} The cmavo 
{{vla|sa'a}} indicates in a quotation that the marked word or construct was not actually expressed, but is inserted for editorial, narrative, or grammatical purposes. Strictly, even a 

{{vla|li'o}} should appear in the form 

:{{jbo|li'osa'a}}, since the 
{{vla|li'o}} was not part of the original quotation. In practice, this and other forms which are already associated with metalinguistic expressions, such as 

{{vla|sei}} (of selma'o SEI) or 
{{vla|to'i}} (of selma'o TO) need not be marked except where confusion might result.

{{ind|general-imported|sa'a|editorial insertion of text already containing sa'a}}  {{ind|general-imported|editorial insertion|of text already containing sa'a}} In the rare case that the quoted material already contains one or more instances of 
{{vla|sa'a}}, they can be changed to 

:{{jbo|sa'asa'a}}.

{{ind|general-imported|questions|with &quot;xu&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|yes/no questions}} The cmavo 
{{vla|xu}} marks truth questions, which are discussed in detail in 
[[#section-truth-questions|this section]]. In general, 
{{vla|xu}} may be translated 
“Is it true that ... ?” and questions whether the attached bridi is true. When 
{{vla|xu}} is attached to a specific word or construct, it directs the focus of the question to that word or construct.

{{ind|general-imported|questions|marking in advance}} Lojban question words, unlike those of English, frequently do not stand at the beginning of the question. Placing the cmavo 
{{vla|pau}} at the beginning of a bridi helps the listener realize that the bridi is a question, like the symbol at the beginning of written Spanish questions that looks like an upside-down question mark. The listener is then warned to watch for the actual question word.

{{ind|general-imported|questions|rhetorical}}  {{ind|general-imported|rhetorical question}}  {{ind|general-imported|pau|placement in sentence}} Although 
{{vla|pau}} is grammatical in any location (like all indicators), it is not really useful except at or near the beginning of a bridi. Its scalar opposite, 

{{vla|paunai}}, signals that a bridi is not really a question despite its form. This is what we call in English a rhetorical question: an example appears in the English text near the beginning of 

[[#section-evidentials|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|figurative speech}} The cmavo 
{{vla|pe'a}} is the indicator of figurative speech, indicating that the previous word should be taken figuratively rather than literally:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rXiR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rXiR}}
{{judri|c13e13d2}}
{{ind|example|blue|as sad|example}}
:'''mi viska le blanu pe'a zdani'''
:<code>I see the blue [figurative] house.</code>
:''I see the “blue” house.''

Here the house is not blue in the sense of color, but in some other sense, whose meaning is entirely culturally dependent. The use of 
{{vla|pe'a}} unambiguously marks a cultural reference: 

{{vla|blanu}} in 
{{linker|example-random-id-rXiR}} could mean 
“sad” (as in English) or something completely different.

{{ind|general-imported|literally}} The negated form, 
:{{jbo|pe'anai}}, indicates that what has been said is to be interpreted literally, in the usual way for Lojban; natural-language intuition is to be ignored.

{{ind|general|heartburn|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|culturally dependent lujvo}}  {{ind|general-imported|figurative lujvo|place structure}}  {{ind|general-imported|figurative lujvo}}  {{ind|general-imported|lujvo|place structure of figurative lujvo}} Alone among the cmavo of selma'o UI, 
{{vla|pe'a}} has a rafsi, namely 

{{raf|pev}}. This rafsi is used in forming figurative (culturally dependent) lujvo, whose place structure need have nothing to do with the place structure of the components. Thus 
{{vla|risnyjelca}} (heart burn) might have a place structure like:

:''x1 is the heart of x2, burning in atmosphere x3 at temperature x4''
whereas 
{{vla|pevrisnyjelca}}, explicitly marked as figurative, might have the place structure:

:''x1 is indigestion/heartburn suffered by x2''
which obviously has nothing to do with the places of either 
{{vla|risna}} or 
{{vla|jelca}}.

{{ind|general|an|example}}  {{ind|general|a|example}}  {{ind|general|the|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|a/an|contrasted with the}}  {{ind|general-imported|the|contrasted with a/an}} The uses of 
{{vla|bi'u}} and {{vla|bi'unai}} correspond to one of the uses of the English articles “the” and “a/an”. An English-speaker telling a story may begin with 
“I saw a man who ...”. Later in the story, the same man will be referred to with the phrase 
“the man”. Lojban does not use its articles in the same way: both “a man” and “the man” would be translated {{jbo|le nanmu}}, since the speaker has in mind a specific man. However, the first use might be marked {{jbo|le bi'u nanmu}}, to indicate that this is a new man, not mentioned before. Later uses could correspondingly be tagged {{jbo|le bi'unai nanmu}}.

Most of the time, the distinction between {{vla|bi'u}} and {{vla|bi'unai}} need not be made, as the listener can infer the right referent. However, if a different man were referred to still later in the story, {{jbo|le bi'u nanmu}} would clearly show that this man was different from the previous one.

{{ind|general-imported|attitude|avoidance of expression}} Finally, the indicator 
{{vla|ge'e}} has been discussed in 

[[#section-compound-attitudinals|this section]] and 
[[#section-questions-empathy-contours|this section]]. It is used to express an attitude which is not covered by the existing set, or to avoid expressing any attitude.

Another use for 
{{vla|ge'e}} is to explicitly avoid expressing one's feeling on a given scale; in this use, it functions like a member of selma'o CAI: 

:{{jbo|.iige'e}} means roughly 
“I'm not telling whether I'm afraid or not.”

{{ind|general-imported|indirect question}}

<tabledata class="wikitable">
{{c|kau}}	indirect question
</tabledata>

This cmavo is explained in detail in 
[[#section-indirect-questions|this section]]. It marks the word it is attached to as the focus of an indirect question:

{{dsp|example-random-id-umCQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-umCQ}}
{{judri|c13e13d3}}
:'''mi djuno le du'u dakau klama le zarci'''
:<code>I know the statement-that somebody [indirect ?] goes to-the store.</code>
:''I know who goes to the store.''

{{judri|section-vocative-scales}}
==Vocative scales==
{{ind|lojban-word-imported|COI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|direct address}}  {{ind|general-imported|&quot;la&quot;|contrasted with vocatives}}  {{ind|general-imported|vocatives|contrasted with &quot;la&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|vocatives|definition}} 
“Vocatives” are words used to address someone directly; they precede and mark a name used in direct address, just as 

{{vla|la}} (and the other members of selma'o LA) mark a name used to refer to someone. The vocatives actually are indicators &ndash; in fact, discursives &ndash; but the need to tie them to names and other descriptions of listeners requires them to be separated from selma'o UI. But like the cmavo of UI, the members of selma'o COI can be 
“negated” with 
{{vla|nai}} to get the opposite part of the scale.

{{ind|general-imported|vocatives|rationale for redundancy}}  {{ind|general-imported|redundancy|effect on vocative design}} Because of the need for redundancy in noisy environments, the Lojban design does not compress the vocatives into a minimum number of scales. Doing so would make a non-redundant 

{{vla|nai}} too often vital to interpretation of a protocol signal, as explained later in this section.

{{ind|general-imported|vocatives|grammar overview}} The grammar of vocatives is explained in 
[[#section-vocative-syntax|this section]]; but in brief, a vocative may be followed by a name (without 
{{vla|la}}), a description (without 
{{vla|le}} or its relatives), a complete sumti, or nothing at all (if the addressee is obvious from the context). There is an elidable terminator, 
{{vla|do'u}} (of selma'o DOhU) which is almost never required unless no name (or other indication of the addressee) follows the vocative.

{{ind|general-imported|vocatives|and definition of &quot;you&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|you|defining}} Using any vocative except 
{{vla|mi'e}} (explained below) implicitly defines the meaning of the pro-sumti 
{{vla|do}}, as the whole point of vocatives is to specify the listener, or at any rate the desired listener &ndash; even if the desired listener isn't listening! We will use the terms 
“speaker” and 
“listener” for clarity, although in written Lojban the appropriate terms would be 
“writer” and 
“reader”.

{{ind|general-imported|vocatives|notation convention symbol &quot;X&quot;}} In the following list of vocatives, the translations include the symbol X. This represents the name (or identifying description, or whatever) of the listener.

{{ind|general-imported|doi|effect on pause before name}}  {{ind|general-imported|pause before name|effect of doi}} The cmavo 
{{vla|doi}} is the general-purpose vocative. Unlike the cmavo of selma'o COI, explained below, 
{{vla|doi}} can precede a name directly without an intervening pause. It is not considered a scale, and 
:{{false|doinai}} is not grammatical. In general, 
{{vla|doi}} needs no translation in English (we just use names by themselves without any preceding word, although in poetic styles we sometimes say 
“Oh X”, which is equivalent to 
{{vla|doi}}). One may attach an attitudinal to 
{{vla|doi}} to express various English vocatives. For example, 
:{{jbo|doi .io}} means 
“Sir/Madam!”, whereas 
:{{jbo|doi .ionai}} means “You there!”.

{{ind|general-imported|COI selma'o|effect on pause before name}}  {{ind|general-imported|pause before name|effect of vocatives of COI}} All members of selma'o COI require a pause when used immediately before a name, in order to prevent the name from absorbing the COI word. This is unlike selma'o DOI and LA, which do not require pauses because the syllables of these cmavo are not permitted to be embedded in a Lojban name. When calling out to someone, this is fairly natural, anyway. 
“Hey! John!” is thus a better translation of 
:{{jbo|ju'i .djan.}} than 

“Hey John!”. No pause is needed if the vocative reference is something other than a name, as in the title of the Lojban journal, 
:{{jbo|ju'i lobypli}}.

(Alternatively, 
{{vla|doi}} can be inserted between the COI cmavo and the name, making a pause unnecessary: 
:{{jbo|coi doi djan.}})

:{{c|coi}}
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">greetings</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“Hello, X”; 
“Greetings, X”; indicates a greeting to the listener.
</description>

:{{c|co'o}}
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">partings</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“Good-bye, X”; indicates parting from immediate company by either the speaker or the listener. 
{{vla|coico'o}} means 
“greeting in passing”.
</description>

:{{c|ju'i}}
<gismu>[jundi]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">attention</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="cu'i">at ease</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">ignore me/us</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“Attention/Lo/Hark/Behold/Hey!/Listen, X”; indicates an important communication that the listener should listen to.
</description>

:{{c|nu'e}}
<gismu>[nupre]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">promise</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="cu'i">release promise</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">non-promise</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“I promise, X”; indicates a promise to the listener. In some contexts, 
{{vla|nu'e}} may be prefixed to an oath or other formal declaration.
</description>

:{{c|ta'a}}
<gismu>[tavla]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">interruption</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“I interrupt, X”, 
“I desire the floor, X”; a vocative expression to (possibly) interrupt and claim the floor to make a statement or expression. This can be used for both rude and polite interruptions, although rude interruptions will probably tend not to use a vocative at all. An appropriate response to an interruption might be 
{{vla|re'i}} (or 
{{vla|re'inai}} to ignore the interruption).
</description>

:{{c|pe'u}}
<gismu>[cpedu]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">request</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">
{{ind|general-imported|e'o|contrasted with pe'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|pe'u|contrasted with e'o}} 
“Please, X”; indicates a request to the listener. It is a formal, non-attitudinal, equivalent of 
{{vla|e'o}} with a specific recipient being addressed. On the other hand, 
{{vla|e'o}} may be used when there is no specific listener, but merely a 
“sense of petition floating in the air”, as it were.
</description>

:{{c|ki'e}}
<gismu>[ckire]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">appreciation</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">gratitude</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">disappreciation</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">ingratitude</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

{{ind|general|thank you|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|politeness|you're welcome}}  {{ind|general-imported|politeness|thank you and you're welcome}} 
“Thank you, X”; indicates appreciation or gratitude toward the listener. The usual response is 
{{vla|je'e}}, but 
{{vla|fi'i}} is appropriate on rare occasions: see the explanation of 
{{vla|fi'i}}.
</description>

:{{c|fi'i}}
<gismu>[friti]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">welcome</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">offering</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">unwelcome</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">inhospitality</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

{{ind|general|hospitality|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|you're welcome|je'e contrasted with fi'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|you're welcome|fi'i contrasted with je'e}} 
“At your service, X”; 
“Make yourself at home, X”; offers hospitality (possibly in response to thanks, but not necessarily) to the listener. Note that 
{{vla|fi'i}} is 
<emphasis>not</emphasis> the equivalent of American English 
“You're welcome” as a mechanical response to 
“Thank you”; that is 
{{vla|je'e}}, as noted below.
</description>

:{{c|be'e}}
<gismu>[benji]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">request to send</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">
{{ind|general-imported|telephone conversation|hello}} 
“Request to send to X”; indicates that the speaker wishes to express something, and wishes to ensure that the listener is listening. In a telephone conversation, can be used to request the desired conversant(s). A more colloquial equivalent is 
“Hello? Can I speak to X?”.
</description>

:{{c|re'i}}
<gismu>[bredi]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">ready to receive</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">not ready</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“Ready to receive, X”; indicates that the speaker is attentive and awaiting communication from the listener. It can be used instead of 
{{vla|mi'e}} to respond when called to the telephone. The negative form can be used to prevent the listener from continuing to talk when the speaker is unable to pay attention: it can be translated 
“Hold on!” or 
“Just a minute”.
</description>

:{{c|mu'o}}
<gismu>[mulno]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">completion of utterance</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">more to follow</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“Over, X”; indicates that the speaker has completed the current utterance and is ready to hear a response from the listener. The negative form signals that the pause or non-linguistic sound which follows does not represent the end of the current utterance: more colloquially, 
“I'm not done talking!”
</description>

:{{c|je'e}}
<gismu>[jimpe]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">successful receipt</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">unsuccessful receipt</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

{{ind|general|roger|example}}
{{ind|general-imported|politeness|you're welcome}} 
“Roger, X!”, 
“I understand”; acknowledges the successful receipt of a communication from the listener. The negative form indicates failure to receive correctly, and is usually followed by 
{{vla|ke'o}}. The colloquial English equivalents of 
{{vla|je'e}} and 
{{vla|je'enai}} are the grunt typically written 
“uh-huh” and 
“What?/Excuse me?”. 
{{vla|je'e}} is also used to mean 
“You're welcome” when that is a response to 
“Thank you”.
</description>

:{{c|vi'o}}
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">will comply</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">will not comply</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">
{{ind|general-imported|vi'o|contrasted with je'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|je'e|contrasted with vi'o}} 
“Wilco, X”, 
“I understand and will comply”. Similar to 
{{vla|je'e}} but signals an intention (similar to 
{{vla|.ai}}) to comply with the other speaker's request. This cmavo is the main way of saying 
“OK” in Lojban, in the usual sense of 
“Agreed!”, although 
{{vla|.ie}} carries some of the same meaning. The negative form indicates that the message was received but that you will not comply: a very colloquial version is 
“No way!”.
</description>

:{{c|ke'o}}
<gismu>[krefu]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">please repeat</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">no repeat needed</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">
{{ind|general-imported|ki'a|compared to ke'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke'o|compared to ki'a}} 
“What did you say, X?”; a request for repetition or clarification due to unsuccessful receipt or understanding. This is the vocative equivalent of 
{{vla|ki'a}}, and is related to 
{{vla|je'enai}}. The negative form may be rendered 
“Okay, already; I get the point!”
</description>

:{{c|fe'o}}
<gismu>[fanmo]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">end of communication</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">not done</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">

“Over and out, X”; indicates completion of statement(s) and communication directed at the identified person(s). Used to terminate a letter if a signature is not required because the sender has already been identified (as in memos). The negative form means 
“Wait, hold it, we're not done!” and differs from 
{{vla|mu'onai}} in that it means more exchanges are to follow, rather than that the current exchange is incomplete.
</description>

{{ind|general-imported|fa'o|contrasted with fe'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|fe'o|contrasted with fa'o}} Do not confuse 
{{vla|fe'o}} with 
{{vla|fa'o}} (selma'o FAhO) which is a mechanical, extra-grammatical signal that a text is complete. One may say 
{{vla|fe'o}} to one participant of a multi-way conversation and then go on speaking to the others.

:{{c|mi'e}}
<gismu>[cmavo: mi]</gismu>
<attitudinal-scale point="sai">self-identification</attitudinal-scale>
<attitudinal-scale point="nai">non-identification</attitudinal-scale>
<description role="long">
{{ind|general-imported|me|explicitly specifying}}  {{ind|general-imported|mi'e|contrasted with other members of COI}}  {{ind|general-imported|introduce oneself}} 
“And I am X”; a generalized self-vocative. Although grammatically just like the other members of selma'o COI, 
{{vla|mi'e}} is quite different semantically. In particular, rather than specifying the listener, the person whose name (or description) follows 
{{vla|mi'e}} is taken to be the speaker. Therefore, using 
{{vla|mi'e}} specifies the meaning of the pro-sumti 
{{vla|mi}}. It can be used to introduce oneself, to close letters, or to identify oneself on the telephone.
</description>

{{ind|general-imported|mi'e|effect of ordering multiple COI}}  {{ind|general-imported|COI selma'o|ordering multiple with mi'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|closings|letter}} This cmavo is often combined with other members of COI: 
:{{jbo|fe'omi'e}} would be an appropriate closing at the end of a letter; 

:{{jbo|re'imi'e}} would be a self-vocative used in delayed responses, as when called to the phone, or possibly in a roll-call. As long as the 

{{vla|mi'e}} comes last, the following name is that of the speaker; if another COI cmavo is last, the following name is that of the listener. It is not possible to name both speaker and listener in a single vocative expression, but this fact is of no importance, because wherever one vocative expression is grammatical, any number of consecutive ones may appear.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|mi'enai}} The negative form denies an identity which someone else has attributed to you; 
:{{jbo|mi'enai .djan.}} means that you are saying you are not John.

{{ind|general-imported|protocol|using vocatives}}  {{ind|general-imported|protocol|computer communications using COI}}  {{ind|general-imported|protocol|parliamentary using COI}} Many of the vocatives have been listed with translations which are drawn from radio use: 
“roger”, 

“wilco”, 
“over and out”. This form of translation does not mean that Lojban is a language of CB enthusiasts, but rather that in most natural languages these forms are so well handled by the context that only in specific domains (like speaking on the radio) do they need special words. In Lojban, dependence on the context can be dangerous, as speaker and listener may not share the right context, and so the vocatives provide a formal protocol for use when it is appropriate. Other appropriate contexts include computer communications and parliamentary procedure: in the latter context, the protocol question {{jbo|ta'apei}} would mean “Will the speaker yield?”

{{judri|section-sample-dialogue}}
==A sample dialogue==
The following dialogue in Lojban illustrates the uses of attitudinals and protocol vocatives in conversation. The phrases enclosed in {{jbo|sei ... se'u}} indicate the speaker of each sentence.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qg4j}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qg4j}}
{{judri|c13e15d1}}
:'''la rik. .e la .alis. nerkla le kafybarja'''
:<code>Rick and Alice in-go to-the coffee-bar.</code>
:''Rick and Alice go into the coffee bar.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qG4V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qG4V}}
{{judri|c13e15d2}}
:'''.i sei la rik. cusku se'u ta'a ro zvati be ti mi baza speni ti .iu'''
:<code>[Comment] Rick says, [end-comment] [Interrupt] all at this-place, I [future] [medium] am-spouse-to this-one [love].</code>
:''Rick said, “Sorry to break in, everybody. Pretty soon I'm getting married to my love here.”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qG5K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qG5K}}
{{judri|c13e15d3}}
:'''.i sei la djordj. cusku se'u .a'o ko gleki doi ma'''
:<code>[Comment] George says, [end-comment] [Hope] [You-imperative] are-happy, O [who?].</code>
:''George said, “I hope you'll be happy, um, ...?”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qG74}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qG74}}
{{judri|c13e15d4}}
:'''.i sei la pam. cusku se'u pe'u .alis. xu mi ba terfriti le nunspenybi'o'''
:<code>[Comment] Pam says, [end-comment] [Please] Alice, [Is it true?] I [future] receive-offer-of the event-of-spouse-becoming?</code>
:''Pam said, “Please, Alice, am I going to be invited to the wedding?”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qg8r}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qg8r}}
{{judri|c13e15d5}}
:'''.i sei la mark. cusku se'u coi baza speni a'o le re do lifri le ka gleki'''
:<code>[Comment] Mark says, [end-comment] [Greetings] [future] [medium] spouse(s), [Hope] the two of-you experience the-property-of being-happy</code>
:''Mark said, “Hello, spouses-to-be. I hope both of you will be very happy.”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qG8R}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qG8R}}
{{judri|c13e15d6}}
:'''.i sei la rik. cusku se'u mi'e .rik. doi terpreti'''
:<code>[Comment] Rick says, [end-comment] [I am] Rick, O questioners.</code>
:''Rick said, “My name is Rick, for those of you who want to know.”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qg9C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qg9C}}
{{judri|c13e15d7}}
:'''.i sei la .alis. cusku se'u nu'e .pam. .o'ero'i do ba zvati'''
:<code>[Comment] Alice says, [end-comment] [Promise-to] Pam, [closeness] [emotional] you [future] are-at.</code>
:''Alice said, “I promise you'll be there, Pam honey.”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGad}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGad}}
{{judri|c13e15d8}}
:'''.i sei la fred. cusku se'u .uinaicairo'i mi ji'a prami la .alis. fe'o .rik.'''
:<code>[Comment] Fred says, [end-comment] [Happy] [not] [emphatic] [emotional] I [additionally] love Alice. [Over and out to] Rick.</code>
<natlang>
“I love Alice too,” said Fred miserably. 
“Have a nice life, Rick.”</natlang>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGBG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGBG}}
{{judri|c13e15d9}}
:'''.i la fred. cliva'''
:<code>Fred leaves.</code>
:''And he left.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGbn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGbn}}
{{judri|c13e15d10}}
:'''.i sei la rik. cusku se'u fi'i ro zvati ko pinxe pa ckafi fi'o pleji mi'''
:<code>[Comment] Rick says, [end-comment] [Welcome-to] all at-place, [You-imperative] drink one coffee with-payer me.</code>
:''Rick said, raising his voice, “A cup of coffee for the house, on me.”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGbT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGbT}}

:'''.i sei la pam. cusku se'u be'e selfu'''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGBz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGBz}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGcT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGcT}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgDV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgDV}}

:''“Gotcha”, said the waiter.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGdy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGdy}}

:'''.i sei la rik. cusku se'u ki'e .pam.'''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgFH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgFH}}

:'''.i sei la pam. cusku se'u je'e'''
:<code>[Comment] Pam says, [end-comment] [Acknowledge].</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGfT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGfT}}
{{judri|c13e15d17}}
:'''.i sei la djan. cusku se'u .y. mi .y. mutce spopa .y. le nu le speni si .y. ba speni .y. .y. su .yyyyyy. mu'o'''

:''John said, “I, er, a lotta, uh, marriage, upcoming marriage, .... Oh, forget it. Er, later.”''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qggJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qggJ}}

:<code>[Comment] George says, [end-comment] [Repeat O] John [humor].</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGGv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGGv}}

{{judri|section-attitudinals-conclusion}}
==Tentative conclusion==
{{ind|general-imported|indicators|ramifications}}  {{ind|general-imported|aliens|communication with}}  {{ind|general-imported|Kzinti|communication with}} The exact ramifications of the indicator system in actual usage are unknown. There has never been anything like it in natural language before. The system provides great potential for emotional expression and transcription, from which significant Sapir-Whorf effects can be anticipated. When communicating across cultural boundaries, where different indicators are often used for the same emotion, accidental offense can be avoided. If we ever ran into an alien race, a culturally neutral language of emotion could be vital. (A classic example, taken from the science fiction of Larry Niven, is to imagine speaking Lojban to the carnivorous warriors called Kzinti, noting that a human smile bares the teeth, and could be seen as an intent to attack.) And for communicating emotions to computers, when we cannot identify all of the signals involved in subliminal human communication (things like body language are also cultural), a system like this is needed.

{{ind|general-imported|indicators|rationale for selection}} We have tried to err on the side of overkill. There are distinctions possible in this system that no one may care to make in any culture. But it was deemed more neutral to overspecify and let usage decide, than to choose a limited set and constrain emotional expression. For circumstances in which even the current indicator set is not enough, it is possible using the cmavo 
{{vla|sei}}, explained in 
[[#section-parentheses|this section]], to create metalinguistic comments that act like indicators.

{{ind|general-imported|indicators|evolutionary development of}} We envision an evolutionary development. At this point, the system is little more than a mental toy. Many of you who read this will try playing around with various combinations of indicators, trying to figure out what emotions they express and when the expressions might be useful. You may even find an expression for which there currently is no good English word and start using it. Why not, if it helps you express your feelings?

There will be a couple dozen of these used pretty much universally &ndash; mostly just simple attitudinals with, at most, intensity markers. These are the ones that will quickly be expressed at the subconscious level. But every Lojbanist who plays with the list will bring in a couple of new words. Poets will paint emotional pictures, and people who identify with those pictures will use the words so created for their own experiences.

Just as a library of tanru is built up, so will a library of attitudes be built. Unlike the tanru, though, the emotional expressions are built on some fairly nebulous root emotions &ndash; words that cannot be defined with the precision of the gismu. The emotion words of Lojban will very quickly take on a life of their own, and the outline given here will evolve into a true system of emotions.

{{ind|general-imported|emotions|research using indicators}}  {{ind|general-imported|emotions|recording using indicators}} There are several theories as to the nature of emotion, and they change from year to year as we learn more about ourselves. Whether or not Lojban's additive/scalar emotional model is an accurate model for human emotions, it does support the linguistic needs for expressing those emotions. Researchers may learn more about the nature of human emotions by exploring the use of the system by Lojban speakers. They also may be able to use the Lojban system as a means for more clearly recording emotions.

{{ind|general-imported|emotions|cultural bias of expression}} The full list of scales and attitudes will probably not be used until someone speaks the language from birth. Until then, people will use the attitudes that are important to them. In this way, we counter cultural bias &ndash; if a culture is prone to recognizing and/or expressing certain emotions more than others, its members will use only those out of the enormous set available. If a culture hides certain emotions, its members simply won't express them.

{{ind|general-imported|Sapir-Whorf effects|and emotional indicators}} Perhaps native Lojban speakers will be more expressively clear about their emotions than others. Perhaps they will feel some emotions more strongly than others in ways that can be correlated with the word choices; any difference from the norms of other cultures could be significant. Psychologists have devised elaborate tests for measuring attitudes and personality; this may be the easiest area in which to detect any systematic cultural effect of the type sought to confirm Sapir-Whorf, simply because we already have tools in existence to test it. Because Lojban is unique among languages in having such extensive and expressive indicators, it is likely that a Sapir-Whorf effect will occur and will be recognized.

It is unlikely that we will know the true potential of a system like this one until and unless we have children raised entirely in a multi-cultural Lojban-speaking environment. We learn too many cultural habits in the realm of emotional communication “at our mother's knee”. Such children will have a Lojban system that has stronger reinforcement than any typical culture system. The second generation of such children, then, could be said to be the start of a true Lojbanic culture.

{{ind|general-imported|emotional indicators|noticeable effects of}} We shouldn't need to wait that long to detect significant effects. Emotion is so basic to our lives that even a small change or improvement in emotional communication would have immediately noticeable effects. Perhaps it will be the case that the most important contribution of our 
“logical language” will be in the non-logical realm of emotion!

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{judri|chapter-connectives}}
=If Wishes Were Horses: The Lojban Connective System=
{{image|xml:id="chapter-connectives-picture"|The picture for chapter 14|media/chapter-connectives.gif}}
{{judri|section-connectives-introduction}}
==Logical connection and truth tables==

{{ind|general-imported|truth functions}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical language|truth functions}} Lojban is a logical language: the name of the language itself means 

“logical language”. The fundamentals of ordinary logic (there are variant logics, which aren't addressed in this book) include the notions of a “sentence” (sometimes called a “statement” or “proposition”), which asserts a truth or falsehood, and a small set of “truth functions”, which combine two sentences to create a new sentence. The truth functions have the special characteristic that the truth value (that is, the truth or falsehood) of the results depends only on the truth value of the component sentences. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-mJ6y}}
{{judri|c14e1d1}}
{{ind|example|man or woman|example}}
John is a man or James is a woman.

is true if 
“John is a man” is true, or if 
“James is a woman” is true. If we know whether John is a man, and we know whether James is a woman, we know whether 
“John is a man or James is a woman” is true, provided we know the meaning of 
“or”. Here 
“John is a man” and 
“James is a woman” are the component sentences.

{{ind|general-imported|negating a sentence|and truth value}} We will use the phrase “negating a sentence” to mean changing its truth value. An English sentence may always be negated by prefixing 

“It is false that ...”, or more idiomatically by inserting 
“not” at the right point, generally before the verb. 
“James is not a woman” is the negation of 
“James is a woman”, and vice versa. Recent slang can also negate a sentence by following it with the exclamation 
“Not!”

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives}} Words like 
“or” are called “logical connectives”, and Lojban has many of them, as befits a logical language. This chapter is mostly concerned with explaining the forms and uses of the Lojban logical connectives. There are a number of other logical connectives in English such as “and”, “and/or”, “if”, “only if”, “whether or not”, and others; however, not every use of these English words corresponds to a logical connective. This point will be made clear in particular cases as needed. The other English meanings are supported by different Lojban connective constructs.

The Lojban connectives form a system (as the title of this chapter suggests), regular and predictable, whereas natural-language connectives are rather less systematic and therefore less predictable.

{{ind|general-imported|truth table|explanation}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth functions|16 possible}} There exist 16 possible different truth functions. A truth table is a graphical device for specifying a truth function, making it clear what the value of the truth function is for every possible value of the component sentences. Here is a truth table for 

“or”:

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<td>first</td>
<td>second</td>
<td>result</td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tr>
<td>True</td>
<td>True</td>
<td>True</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>True</td>
<td>False</td>
<td>True</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>False</td>
<td>True</td>
<td>True</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>False</td>
<td>False</td>
<td>False</td>
</tr>
</table>
This table means that if the first sentence stated is true, and the second sentence stated is true, then the result of the truth function is also true. The same is true for every other possible combination of truth values except the one where both the first and the second sentences are false, in which case the truth value of the result is also false.

Suppose that 
“John is a man” is true (and 
“John is not a man” is false), and that 
“James is a woman” is false (and 
“James is not a woman” is true). Then the truth table tells us that

:''“John is a man, or James is not a woman”             (true   true )  is true''
:''“John is a man, or James is a woman”                 (true , false)  is true''
:''“John is not a man, or James is not a woman”         (false, true )  is true''
:''“John is not a man, or James is a woman”             (false, false)  is false''

{{ind|general-imported|&quot;or&quot;|&quot;and/or&quot; contrasted with &quot;either … or … but not both&quot;}} Note that the kind of 
“or” used in this example can also be expressed (in formal English) with 
“and/or”. There is a different truth table for the kind of “or” that means “either ... or ... but not both”.

{{ind|general-imported|truth tables|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth tables|abbreviated format}} To save space, we will write truth tables in a shorter format henceforth. Let the letters T and F stand for True and False. The rows will always be given in the order shown above: TT, TF, FT, FF for the two sentences. Then it is only necessary to give the four letters from the result column, which can be written TTTF, as can be seen by reading down the third column of the table above. So TTTF is the abbreviated truth table for the 

“or” truth function. Here are the 16 possible truth functions, with an English version of what it means to assert that each function is, in fact, true ( 
“first” refers to the first sentence, and 
“second” to the second sentence):

{{ind|general-imported|truth tables|list of 16 in abbreviated form}}
<table>
<tr>
<td>TTTT</td><td>(always true)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TTTF</td><td>first is true and/or second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TTFT</td><td>first is true if second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TTFF</td><td>first is true whether or not second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFTT</td><td>first is true only if second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFTF</td><td>whether or not first is true, second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFFT</td><td>first is true if and only if second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFFF</td><td>first is true and second is true</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>FTTT</td><td>first and second are not both true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTTF</td><td>first or second is true, but not both.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTFT</td><td>whether or not first is true, second is false.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTFF</td><td>first is true, but second is false.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFTT</td><td>first is false whether or not second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFTF</td><td>first is false, but second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFFT</td><td>neither first nor second is true.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFFF</td><td>(always false)</td>
</tr>
</table>
Skeptics may work out the detailed truth tables for themselves.

{{judri|section-four-basics}}
==The Four basic vowels==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|relation to truth functions}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth functions|relation to logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth functions|fundamental 4 in Lojban}} Lojban regards four of these 16 truth functions as fundamental, and assigns them the four vowels A, E, O, and U. These letters do not represent actual cmavo or selma'o, but rather a component vowel from which actual logical-connective cmavo are built up, as explained in the next section. Here are the four vowels, their truth tables, and rough English equivalents:

{{ind|general-imported|fancy U|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|fancy O|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|fancy E|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|fancy A|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|truth tables|for 4 fundamental Lojban truth functions}}
<table>
<tr>
<td>A</td>
<td>TTTF</td>
<td>or, and/or</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>E</td>
<td>TFFF</td>
<td>and</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>O</td>
<td>TFFT</td>
<td>if and only if</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>U</td>
<td>TTFF</td>
<td>whether or not</td>
</tr>
</table>
More precisely:

:'''A is true if either or both sentences are true'''
:'''E is true if both sentences are true, but not otherwise'''
:'''O is true if the sentences are both true or both false'''
:'''U is true if the first sentence is true, regardless of the truth value of the second sentence'''

{{ind|general-imported|truth functions|creating all 16 with Lojban's basic set}} With the four vowels, the ability to negate either sentence, and the ability to exchange the sentences, as if their order had been reversed, we can create all of the 16 possible truth functions except TTTT and FFFF, which are fairly useless anyway. The following table illustrates how to create each of the 14 remaining truth functions:

<table>
<tr>
<td>TTTF</td><td>A</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TTFT</td><td>A with second sentence negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TTFF</td><td>U</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFTT</td><td>A with first sentence negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFTF</td><td>U with sentences exchanged</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFFT</td><td>O</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>TFFF</td><td>E</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>FTTT</td><td>A with both sentences negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTTF</td><td>O with either first or second negated (not both)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTFT</td><td>U with sentences exchanged and then second negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FTFF</td><td>E with second sentence negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFTT</td><td>U with first sentence negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFTF</td><td>E with first sentence negated</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FFFT</td><td>E with both sentences negated</td>
</tr>
</table>
{{ind|general-imported|truth functions|commutative}}  {{ind|general-imported|commutative truth functions}} Note that exchanging the sentences is only necessary with U. The three other basic truth functions are commutative; that is, they mean the same thing regardless of the order of the component sentences. There are other ways of getting some of these truth tables; these just happen to be the methods usually employed.

{{judri|section-six-types}}
==The six types of logical connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|rationale for multiple sets in grammar}} In order to remain unambiguous, Lojban cannot have only a single logical connective for each truth function. There are many places in the grammar of the language where logical connection is permitted, and each must have its appropriate set of connectives. If the connective suitable for sumti were used to connect selbri, ambiguity would result.

Consider the English sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ptgf}}
{{judri|c14e3d1}}
{{ind|example|window|example}}
Mary went to the window and ...

where the last word could be followed by 
“the door”, a noun phrase, or by 
“saw the horses”, a sentence with subject omitted, or by 
“John went to the door”, a full sentence, or by one of a variety of other English grammatical constructions. Lojban cannot tolerate such grammatical looseness.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|selma'o|enumerated}} Instead, there are a total of five different selma'o used for logical connection: A, GA, GIhA, GUhA, and JA. Each of these includes four cmavo, one based on each of the four vowels, which is always the last vowel in the cmavo. In selma'o A, the vowel is the entire cmavo.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|cmavo|format for each selma'o}} Thus, in selma'o A, the cmavo for the function A is {{vla|a}}. (Do not confuse A, which is a selma'o, with A, which is a truth function, or {{vla|a}}, which is a cmavo.) Likewise, the cmavo for E in selma'o GIhA is {{vla|gi'e}}, and the cmavo for U in selma'o GA is {{vla|gu}}. This systematic regularity makes the cmavo easier to learn.

{{ind|general-imported|compound logical connectives|components}} Obviously, four cmavo are not enough to express the 14 truth functions explained in 
[[#section-connectives-introduction|this section]]. Therefore, compound cmavo must be used. These compound cmavo follow a systematic pattern: each has one cmavo from the five logical connection selma'o at its heart, and may also contain one or more of the auxiliary cmavo 
{{vla|se}}, 
{{vla|na}}, or 
{{vla|nai}}. Which auxiliaries are used with which logical connection cmavo, and with what grammar and meaning, will be explained in the following sections. The uses of each of these auxiliary cmavo relates to its other uses in other parts of Lojban grammar.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|jek|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|ek|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|-ek|in name for logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound logical connectives|naming convention}} For convenience, each of the types of compound cmavo used for logical connection is designated by a Lojban name. The name is derived by changing the final 
“-A” of the selma'o name to 
“-ek”; the reasons for using 
“-ek” are buried deep in the history of the Loglan Project. Thus, compound cmavo based on selma'o A are known as eks, and those based on selma'o JA are known as jeks. (When writing in English, it is conventional to use 
“eks” as the plural of “ek”.) When the term “logical connective” is used in this chapter, it refers to one or more of these kinds of compound cmavo.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijek|definition}} Why does the title of this section refer to 
“six types” when there are only five selma'o? A jek may be preceded by 
{{vla|i}}, the usual Lojban cmavo for connecting two sentences. The compound produced by 
{{vla|i}} followed by a jek is known as an ijek. It is useful to think of ijeks as a sixth kind of logical connective, parallel to eks, jeks, geks, giheks, and guheks.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijoik|as name for compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|joigik|as name for compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|joik|as name for compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|gik|as name for compound cmavo}} There also exist giks, joiks, ijoiks, and joigiks, which are not logical connectives, but are other kinds of compound cmavo which will be introduced later.

{{judri|section-bridi-connection}}
==Logical connection of bridi==
{{ind|general-imported|bridi|logical connective for}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijek logical connectives|connecting bridi}} Now we are ready to express 
{{linker|example-random-id-mJ6y}} in Lojban! The kind of logical connective which is placed between two Lojban bridi to connect them logically is an ijek:

{{dsp|example-random-id-h2hN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-h2hN}}
{{judri|c14e4d1}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ija la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man or James is-a-woman.</code>

Here we have two separate Lojban bridi, {{jbo|la djan. nanmu}} and {{jbo|la djeimyz. ninmu}}. These bridi are connected by {{vla|.i}}{{vla|ja}}, the ijek for the truth function A. The {{vla|i}} portion of the ijek tells us that we are dealing with separate sentences here. Similarly, we can now say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGiu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGiu}}
{{judri|c14e4d2}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ije la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man and James is-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGIu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGIu}}
{{judri|c14e4d3}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ijo la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man if-and-only-if James is-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgJC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgJC}}
{{judri|c14e4d4}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .iju la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man whether-or-not James is-a-woman.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|bridi|logical connection with negation}} To obtain the other truth tables listed in 

[[#section-four-basics|this section]], we need to know how to negate the two bridi which represent the component sentences. We could negate them directly by inserting 
{{vla|na}} before the selbri, but Lojban also allows us to place the negation within the connective itself.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}} To negate the first or left-hand bridi, prefix 
{{vla|na}} to the JA cmavo but after the 
{{vla|i}}. To negate the second or right-hand bridi, suffix 
:{{jbo|-nai}} to the JA cmavo. In either case, the negating word is placed on the side of the connective that is closest to the bridi being negated.

So to express the truth table FTTF, which requires O with either of the two bridi negated (not both), we can say either:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgKB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgKB}}
{{judri|c14e4d5}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .inajo la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-not-a-man if-and-only-if James is-a-woman.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgLH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgLH}}
{{judri|c14e4d6}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ijonai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is a man if-and-only-if James is-not-a-woman</code>

The meaning of both 
{{linker|example-random-id-qgKB}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qgLH}} is the same as that of:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1Kp9}}
{{judri|c14e4d7}}
John is a man or James is a woman, but not both.

Here is another example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-FXSC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-FXSC}}
{{judri|c14e4d8}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ijanai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-a-man or James is-not-a-woman.</code>
:''John is a man if James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|if|English usage contrasted with Lojban logical connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|if|meaning in logical connections}} How's that again? Are those two English sentences in 
{{linker|example-random-id-FXSC}} really equivalent? In English, no. The Lojban TTFT truth function can be glossed 
“A if B”, but the 
“if” does not quite have its English sense. 
{{linker|example-random-id-FXSC}} is true so long as John is a man, even if James is not a woman; likewise, it is true just because James is not a woman, regardless of John's gender. This kind of 
“if-then” is technically known as a 
“material conditional”.

Since James is not a woman (by our assertions in 
[[#section-connectives-introduction|this section]]), the English sentence 
“John is a man if James is a woman” seems to be neither true nor false, since it assumes something which is not true. It turns out to be most convenient to treat this 
“if” as TTFT, which on investigation means that 
{{linker|example-random-id-FXSC}} is true. 
{{linker|example-random-id-EdY5}}, however, is equally true:

{{dsp|example-random-id-EdY5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-EdY5}}
{{judri|c14e4d9}}
:'''la djan. ninmu .ijanai la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''John is a woman if James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|false statement|implications of}}  {{ind|general-imported|principle of consistency|of logical-if statements}} This can be thought of as a principle of consistency, and may be paraphrased as follows: 

“If a false statement is true, any statement follows from it.” All uses of English “if” must be considered very carefully when translating into Lojban to see if they really fit this Lojban mold.

{{ind|general-imported|only if|compared with if … then}}  {{ind|general-imported|if … then|compared with only if}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-9CCS}}, which uses the TFTT truth function, is subject to the same rules: the stated gloss of TFTT as 
“only if” works naturally only when the right-hand bridi is false; if it is true, the left-hand bridi may be either true or false. The last gloss of 
{{linker|example-random-id-9CCS}} illustrates the use of 
“if ... then” as a more natural substitute for “only if”.

{{dsp|example-random-id-9CCS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9CCS}}
{{judri|c14e4d10}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .inaja la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>John is-not-a-man or James is-a-woman.</code>
:''John is a man only if James is a woman.''
:''If John is a man, then James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|se|in logical connective to exchange sentences}} The following example illustrates the use of 
{{vla|se}} to, in effect, exchange the two sentences. The normal use of 
{{vla|se}} is to (in effect) transpose places of a bridi, as explained in 
[[#section-place-conversion|this section]].

{{dsp|example-random-id-z43X}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-z43X}}
{{judri|c14e4d11}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .iseju la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''Whether or not John is a man, James is a woman.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|general-imported|na|order in logical connectives with se}}  {{ind|general-imported|se|order in logical connectives with na}} If both 
{{vla|na}} and 
{{vla|se}} are present, which is legal but never necessary, 
{{vla|na}} would come before 
{{vla|se}}.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|I selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijeks|syntax of}} The full syntax of ijeks, therefore, is:

{{grammar|.i [na] [se] JA [nai]}}
where the cmavo in brackets are optional.

{{judri|section-forethought-bridi-connection}}
==Forethought bridi connection==

{{ind|general-imported|forethought connectives|contrasted with afterthought connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought connectives|contrasted with forethought connectives}} Many concepts in Lojban are expressible in two different ways, generally referred to as 
“afterthought” and 
“forethought”. 
[[#section-bridi-connection|this section]] discussed what is called 
“afterthought bridi logical connection”. The word 

“afterthought” is used because the connective cmavo and the second bridi were added, as it were, afterwards and without changing the form of the first bridi. This form might be used by someone who makes a statement and then wishes to add or qualify that statement after it has been completed. Thus,

{{dsp|example-random-id-dp8V}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-dp8V}}
{{judri|c14e5d1}}
:'''la djan. nanmu'''

is a complete bridi, and adding an afterthought connection to make

{{dsp|example-random-id-7h3s}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7h3s}}
{{judri|c14e5d2}}
:'''la djan. nanmu .ija la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''John is a man or James is a woman (or both)''

provides additional information without requiring any change in the form of what has come before; changes which may not be possible or practical, especially in speaking. (The meaning, however, may be changed by the use of a negating connective.) Afterthought connectives make it possible to construct all the important truth-functional relationships in a variety of ways.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought bridi connectives|contrasted with forethought bridi connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought bridi connectives|contrasted with afterthought bridi connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|gek bridi connectives|contrasted with ijeks}}  {{ind|general-imported|ijek bridi connectives|contrasted with geks}}  {{ind|general-imported|gek|definition}} In forethought style the speaker decides in advance, before expressing the first bridi, that a logical connection will be expressed. Forethought and afterthought connectives are expressed with separate selma'o. The forethought logical connectives corresponding to afterthought ijeks are geks:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mYeS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mYeS}}
{{judri|c14e5d3}}
:'''ga la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''Either John is a man or James is a woman (or both).''

{{vla|ga}} is the cmavo which represents the 
A truth function in selma'o GA. The word 
{{vla|gi}} does not belong to GA at all, but constitutes its own selma'o: it serves only to separate the two bridi without having any content of its own. The English translation of 
{{vla|ga}}&hellip;{{vla|gi}} is 
“either ... or”, but in the English form the truth function is specified both by the word 
“either” and by the word 
“or”: not so in Lojban.

{{ind|general-imported|i|regarding forethought bridi connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought bridi connection|as grammatically one sentence}} Even though two bridi are being connected, geks and giks do not have any 

{{vla|i}} in them. The forethought construct binds up the two bridi into a single sentence as far as the grammar is concerned.

Some more examples of forethought bridi connection are:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGLh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGLh}}
{{judri|c14e5d4}}
:'''ge la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''(It is true that) both John is a man and James is a woman.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgMN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgMN}}
{{judri|c14e5d5}}
:'''gu la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:''It is true that John is a man, whether or not James is a woman.''

It is worth emphasizing that 
{{linker|example-random-id-qgMN}} does not assert that James is (or is not) a woman. The 
{{vla|gu}} which indicates that 
:{{jbo|la djeimyz. ninmu}} may be true or false is unfortunately rather remote from the bridi thus affected.

Perhaps the most important of the truth functions commonly expressed in forethought is TFTT, which can be paraphrased as 
“if ... then ...”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Xcg1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Xcg1}}
{{judri|c14e5d6}}
:'''ganai la djan. nanmu gi la djeimyz. ninmu'''
:<code>Either John is not a man, or James is a woman.</code>
:''If John is a man, then James is a woman.''

{{ind|general-imported|nai|placement in afterthought bridi connection contrasted with forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|nai|placement in forethought bridi connection contrasted with afterthought}} Note the placement of the 
{{vla|nai}} in 
{{linker|example-random-id-Xcg1}}. When added to afterthought selma'o such as JA, a following 
{{vla|nai}} negates the second bridi, to which it is adjacent. Since GA cmavo precede the first bridi, a following 
{{vla|nai}} negates the first bridi instead.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|negated first sentence as a potential problem for understanding}} Why does English insist on forethought in the translation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-Xcg1}}? Possibly because it would be confusing to seemingly assert a sentence and then make it conditional (which, as the Lojban form shows, involves a negation). Truth functions which involve negating the first sentence may be confusing, even to the Lojbanic understanding, when expressed using afterthought.

{{ind|general-imported|if … then|logical connectives contrasted with other translations}} It must be reiterated here that not every use of English 
“if ... then” is properly translated by 

{{vla|.i}}{{vla|na}}{{vla|ja}} or
