:{{jbo|mi jo'u do}} would be two individuals, not a mass, therefore 

{{vla|jo'u}} is not applicable; 

{{vla|joi}} would be the correct connective.

{{ind|general-imported|connective answers|non-logical}}  {{ind|general-imported|connective questions|non-logical}} There is no joik question cmavo as such; however, joiks and ijoiks may be uttered in isolation in response to a logical connective question, as in the following exchange:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGSm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGSm}}
{{judri|c14e15d12}}
:'''do djica tu'a loi ckafi ji loi tcati'''
:<code>You desire something-about a-mass-of coffee [what connective?] a-mass-of tea?</code>
:''Do you want coffee or tea?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgsp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgsp}}
{{judri|c14e15d13}}
{{ind|example|ugh|example}}
{{ind|example|coffee mixed with tea|example}} 
:'''joi'''
:<code>Mixed-mass-and.</code>
:''Both as a mass (i.e, mixed together).''

Ugh. (Or in Lojban: {{vla|.a'u}}{{vla|nai}}{{vla|sai}}{{vla|ro'o}}.)

{{judri|section-non-logical-continued-continued}}
==Interval connectives and forethought non-logical connection==

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|expressed as endpoints}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|intervals}} In addition to the non-logical connectives of selma'o JOI explained in 
[[#section-non-logical-connectives|this section]] and 
[[#section-non-logical-continued|this section]], there are three other connectives which can appear in joiks: 
{{vla|bi'i}}, 
{{vla|bi'o}}, and 
{{vla|mi'i}}, all of selma'o BIhI. The first two cmavo are used to specify intervals: abstract objects defined by two endpoints. The cmavo 

{{vla|bi'i}} is correct if the endpoints are independent of order, whereas 
{{vla|bi'o}} or 
{{vla|se}}{{vla|bi'o}} are used when order matters.

An example of 
{{vla|bi'i}} in sumti connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sHhA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sHhA}}
{{judri|c14e16d1}}
{{ind|example|between Dresden and Frankfurt|example}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. bi'i la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand-on-surface Dresden [interval] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt.''

{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|un-ordered intervals}} In 
{{linker|example-random-id-sHhA}}, it is all the same whether I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt or between Frankfurt and Dresden, so 

{{vla|bi'i}} is the appropriate interval connective. The sumti 
:{{jbo|la drezdn. bi'i la frankfurt.}} falls into the x2 place of 
{{vla|sanli}}, which is the surface I stand on; the interval specifies that surface by its limits. (Obviously, I am not standing on the whole of the interval; the x2 place of 
{{vla|sanli}} specifies a surface which is typically larger in extent than just the size of the stander's feet.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-rYv4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rYv4}}
{{judri|c14e16d2}}
{{ind|example|from one to two o'clock|example}}
:'''mi cadzu ca la pacac. bi'o la recac.'''
:<code>I walk simultaneous-with First-hour [ordered-interval] Second-hour.</code>
:''I walk from one o'clock to two o'clock.''

{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|ordered intervals}} In 
{{linker|example-random-id-rYv4}}, on the other hand, it is essential that 
:{{jbo|la pacac.}} comes before 
:{{jbo|la recac.}}; otherwise we have an 11-hour (or 23-hour) interval rather than a one-hour interval. In this use of an interval, the whole interval is probably intended, or at least most of it.

{{linker|example-random-id-rYv4}} is equivalent to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qqIr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qqIr}}
{{judri|c14e16d3}}
:'''mi cadzu ca la recac. sebi'o la pacac.'''
:<code>I walk simultaneous-with Second-hour [reverse] [ordered] First-hour.</code>

English cannot readily express 
{{vla|se}}{{vla|bi'o}}, but its meaning can be understood by reversing the two sumti.

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|expressed as center and distance}} The third cmavo of selma'o BIhI, namely 
{{vla|mi'i}}, expresses an interval seen from a different viewpoint: not a pair of endpoints, but a center point and a distance. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wm5E}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wm5E}}
{{judri|c14e16d4}}
{{ind|example|bomb destroyed fifty miles|example}}
:'''le jbama pu daspo la .uacintyn. mi'i lo minli be li muno'''
:<code>The bomb [past] destroys Washington [center] what-is measured-in-miles by 50.</code>
:''The bomb destroyed Washington and fifty miles around.''

Here we have an interval whose center is Washington and whose distance, or radius, is fifty miles.

{{ind|general-imported|endpoints|inclusion in interval}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|inclusion of endpoints}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|open}}  {{ind|general-imported|interval|closed}}  {{ind|general-imported|open interval}}  {{ind|general-imported|closed interval}} In 
{{linker|example-random-id-sHhA}}, is it possible that I am standing in Dresden (or Frankfurt) itself? Yes. The connectives of selma'o BIhI are ambiguous about whether the endpoints themselves are included in or excluded from the interval. Two auxiliary cmavo 
{{vla|ga'o}} and 
{{vla|ke'i}} (of cmavo GAhO) are used to indicate the status of the endpoints: 
{{vla|ga'o}} means that the endpoint is included, 
{{vla|ke'i}} that it is excluded:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGTc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGTc}}
{{judri|c14e16d5}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ga'o bi'i ga'o la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [inclusive] [interval] [inclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt, inclusive of both.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGtv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGtv}}
{{judri|c14e16d6}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ga'o bi'i ke'i la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [inclusive] [interval] [exclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden (inclusive) and Frankfurt (exclusive).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgUo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgUo}}
{{judri|c14e16d7}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ke'i bi'i ga'o la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [exclusive] [interval] [inclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden (exclusive) and Frankfurt (inclusive).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGvB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGvB}}
{{judri|c14e16d8}}
{{ind|example|between Dresden and Frankfurt|example}}
:'''mi ca sanli la drezdn. ke'i bi'i ke'i la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand Dresden [exclusive] [interval] [exclusive] Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden and Frankfurt, exclusive of both.''

{{ind|general-imported|GAhO selma'o|grammar of}} As these examples should make clear, the GAhO cmavo that applies to a given endpoint is the one that stands physically adjacent to it: the left-hand endpoint is referred to by the first GAhO, and the right-hand endpoint by the second GAhO. It is ungrammatical to have just one GAhO.

{{ind|general-imported|ke'i|etymology of}}  {{ind|general-imported|ga'o|etymology of}} (Etymologically, 
{{vla|ga'o}} is derived from 
{{vla|ganlo}}, which means 
“closed”, and 
{{vla|ke'i}} from 
{{vla|kalri}}, which means 
“open”. In mathematics, inclusive intervals are referred to as closed intervals, and exclusive intervals as open ones.)

{{ind|general-imported|BIhI selma'o|grammar of}} BIhI joiks are grammatical anywhere that other joiks are, including in tanru connection and (as ijoiks) between sentences. No meanings have been found for these uses.

{{ind|general-imported|intervals|effect of nai on}}  {{ind|general-imported|nai|effect on intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|negated intervals|meaning of}} Negated intervals, marked with a 
:{{jbo|-nai}} following the BIhI cmavo, indicate an interval that includes everything but what is between the endpoints (with respect to some understood scale):

{{dsp|example-random-id-39EI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-39EI}}
{{judri|c14e16d9}}
{{ind|example|except from 10 to 12|example}}
:'''do dicra .e'a mi ca la daucac. bi'onai la gaicac.'''
:<code>You disturb (allowed) me at 10 not-from ... to 12</code>
:''You can contact me except from 10 to 12.''

The complete syntax of joiks is:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GAhO selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|general-imported|joiks|syntax of}}

*{{grammar|[se] JOI  [nai]}}
*{{grammar|[se] BIhI [nai]}}
*{{grammar|GAhO [se] BIhI [nai] GAhO}}

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|joigik|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|intervals|forethought}} Notice that the colloquial English translations of 
{{vla|bi'i}} and 
{{vla|bi'o}} have forethought form: 
“between ... and” for 
{{vla|bi'i}}, and 
“from ... to” for 
{{vla|bi'o}}. In Lojban too, non-logical connectives can be expressed in forethought. Rather than using a separate selma'o, the forethought logical connectives are constructed from the afterthought ones by suffixing {{vla|gi}}. Such a compound cmavo is not unnaturally called a “joigik”; the syntax of joigiks is any of:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GAhO selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|BIhI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|nai}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|se}}  {{ind|general-imported|joigiks|syntax of}}
*{{grammar|[se] JOI  [nai] GI}}
*{{grammar|[se] BIhI [nai] GI}}
*{{grammar|GAhO [se] BIhI [nai] GAhO GI}}

{{ind|general-imported|joigiks|connection types}} Joigiks may be used to non-logically connect bridi, sumti, and bridi-tails; and also in termsets.

{{linker|example-random-id-pC5x}} in forethought becomes:

{{dsp|example-random-id-iBpP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-iBpP}}
{{judri|c14e16d10}}
{{ind|example|carry the piano|example}}
:'''joigi la djan. gi la .alis. bevri le pipno'''
:<code>[Together] John and Alice carry the piano.</code>

The first 
{{vla|gi}} is part of the joigik; the second {{vla|gi}} is the regular gik that separates the two things being connected in all forethought forms.

{{linker|example-random-id-qGtv}} can be expressed in forethought as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-u51K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-u51K}}
{{judri|c14e16d11}}
{{ind|example|between Dresden and Frankfurt|example}}
:'''mi ca sanli ke'i bi'i ga'o gi la drezdn. gi la frankfurt.'''
:<code>I [present] stand [exclusive] between [inclusive] Dresden and Frankfurt.</code>
:''I am standing between Dresden (exclusive) and Frankfurt (inclusive).''

{{ind|general-imported|GAhO position in forethought intervals}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought intervals|GAhO position}} In forethought, unfortunately, the GAhOs become physically separated from the endpoints, but the same rule applies: the first GAhO refers to the first endpoint.

{{judri|section-mekso-connections}}
==Logical and non-logical connectives within mekso==
{{ind|general-imported|mathematical expressions|connectives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|in mathematical expressions}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in mathematical expressions}} Lojban has a separate grammar embedded within the main grammar for representing mathematical expressions (or mekso in Lojban) such as “2 + 2”. Mathematical expressions are explained fully in [[#chapter-mekso|this chapter]]. The basic components of mekso are operands, like 
“2”, and operators, like “+”. Both of these may be either logically or non-logically connected.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GUhA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|GA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operators|with bo in connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|in joiks for operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|in jeks for operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|guheks|connecting operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|jeks|connecting operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|operators|connecting}}  {{ind|general-imported|operands|connecting}}  {{ind|general-imported|geks|connecting operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|eks|connecting operands}} Operands are connected in afterthought with eks and in forethought with geks, just like sumti. Operators, on the other hand, are connected in afterthought with jeks and in forethought with guheks, just like tanru components. (However, jeks and joiks with 

{{vla|bo}} are not allowed for operators.) This parallelism is no accident.

{{ind|general-imported|operators|analogue of tanru in}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operators|with ke in connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operands|with ke in connective}}  {{ind|general-imported|connecting operands|with bo in connective}} In addition, eks with 
{{vla|bo}} and with 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} are allowed for grouping logically connected operands, and 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} is allowed for grouping logically connected operators, although there is no analogue of tanru among the operators.

Only a few examples of each kind of mekso connection will be given. Despite the large number of rules required to support this feature, it is of relatively minor importance in either the mekso or the logical-connective scheme of things. These examples are drawn from 
[[#section-connectives-within-mekso|this section]], and contain many mekso features not explained in this chapter.

{{linker|example-random-id-gMU4}} exhibits afterthought logical connection between operands:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gMU4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gMU4}}
{{judri|c14e17d1}}
{{ind|example|three of four people|example}}
:'''vei ci .a vo [ve'o] prenu cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>( Three or four ) people go-to the market.</code>

{{linker|example-random-id-ftNY}} is equivalent in meaning, but uses forethought connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ftNY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ftNY}}
{{judri|c14e17d2}}
:'''vei ga ci gi vo [ve'o] prenu cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>( Either 3 or 4 ) people go-to the market.</code>

Note that the mekso in 
{{linker|example-random-id-gMU4}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-ftNY}} are being used as quantifiers. Lojban requires that any mekso other than a simple number be enclosed in 
{{vla|vei}} and 
{{vla|ve'o}} parentheses when used as a quantifier. The right parenthesis mark, 
{{vla|ve'o}}, is an elidable terminator.

Simple examples of logical connection between operators are hard to come by. A contrived example is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-dCxf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-dCxf}}
{{judri|c14e17d3}}
:'''li re su'i je pi'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number 2 plus and times 2 equals the-number 4.</code>
:''{{math|2 + 2 = 4}} and {{math|2 x 2 = 4}}.''

The forethought form of 
{{linker|example-random-id-dCxf}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YBD6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YBD6}}
{{judri|c14e17d4}}
:'''li re ge su'i gi pi'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number two both plus and times two equals the-number four.</code>
:''Both {{math|2 + 2 = 4}} and {{math|2 x 2 = 4}}.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|ke'i}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|ga'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|mathematical intervals}} Non-logical connection with joiks or joigiks is also permitted between operands and between operators. One use for this construct is to connect operands with 

{{vla|bi'i}} to create mathematical intervals:

{{dsp|example-random-id-z2oF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-z2oF}}
{{judri|c14e17d5}}
{{ind|example|zero to one|example}}
:'''li no ga'o bi'i ke'i pa'''
:<code>the-number zero (inclusive) from-to (exclusive) one</code>
{{math|[0,1)}}
:''the numbers from zero to one, including zero but not including one''

{{ind|general-imported|compound subscript}} You can also combine two operands with 
{{vla|ce'o}}, the sequence connective of selma'o JOI, to make a compound subscript:

{{dsp|example-random-id-8rEL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8rEL}}
{{judri|c14e17d6}}
{{ind|example|x sub b,d|example}} 
:'''xy. boi xi vei by. ce'o dy. [ve'o]'''
:<code>“x” sub ( “b” sequence “d”)</code>
:{{math|x<subscript>b,d</subscript>}}

Note that the 
{{vla|boi}} in 
{{linker|example-random-id-8rEL}} is not elidable, because the 
{{vla|xi}} subscript needs something to attach to.

{{judri|section-sumtcita}}
==Tenses, modals, and logical connection==
The tense and modal systems of Lojban interact with the logical connective system. No one chapter can explain all of these simultaneously, so each chapter must present its own view of the area of interaction with emphasis on its own concepts and terminology. In the examples of this chapter, the many tenses of various selma'o as well as the modals of selma'o BAI are represented by the simple time cmavo 
{{vla|pu}}, {{vla|ca}}, and {{vla|ba}} (of selma'o PU) representing the past, the present, and the future respectively. Preceding a selbri, these cmavo state the time when the bridi was, is, or will be true (analogous to English verb tenses); preceding a sumti, they state that the event of the main bridi is before, simultaneous with, or after the event given by the sumti (which is generally a {{jbo|le nu}} abstraction; See [[#section-events|this section]]).

{{ind|general-imported|logically connected tenses|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|interaction with tenses}} The two types of interaction between tenses and logical connectives are logically connected tenses and tensed logical connections. The former are fairly simple. Jeks may be used between tense cmavo to specify two connected bridi that differ only in tense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-g6iT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-g6iT}}
{{judri|c14e18d1}}
{{ind|example|once and future king|example}}
:'''la .artr. pu nolraitru .ije la .artr. ba nolraitru'''
:<code>Arthur [past] is-a-noblest-governor. And Arthur [future] is-a-noblest-governor.</code>
:''Arthur was a king, and Arthur will be a king.''

can be reduced to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PLgw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PLgw}}
{{judri|c14e18d2}}
{{ind|example|once and future king|example}}
:'''la .artr. pu je ba nolraitru'''
:<code>Arthur [past] and [future] is-a-noblest-governor.</code>
:''Arthur was and will be king.''

{{linker|example-random-id-g6iT}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-PLgw}} are equivalent in meaning; neither says anything about whether Arthur is king now.

{{ind|general-imported|non-logically connected tenses}} Non-logical connection with joiks is also possible between tenses:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Mcsi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Mcsi}}
{{judri|c14e18d3}}
{{ind|example|breathe|example}}
:'''mi pu bi'o ba vasxu'''
:<code>I [past] from ... to [future] breathe.</code>
:''I breathe from a past time until a future time.''

The full tense system makes more interesting tense intervals expressible, such as “from a medium time ago until a long time from now”.

{{ind|general-imported|tenses|grouping of connectives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|grouping|of connection in tenses}}  {{ind|general-imported|tenses|forethought connection in}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|in tenses}} No forethought connections between tenses are permitted by the grammar, nor is there any way to override the default left-grouping rule; these limitations are imposed to keep the tense grammar simpler. Whatever can be said with tenses or modals can be said with subordinate bridi stating the time, place, or mode explicitly, so it is reasonable to try to remove at least some complications.

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connection}} Tensed logical connections are both more complex and more important than logical connections between tenses. Consider the English sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-efav}}
{{judri|c14e18d4}}
{{ind|example|went and bought|example}}
I went to the market, and I bought food.

The verbatim translation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-efav}}, namely:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PMTu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PMTu}}
{{judri|c14e18d5}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci .ije mi pu tervecnu lo cidja'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the market. And I [past] buy items-of food.</code>

fails to fully represent a feature of the English, namely that the buying came after the going. (It also fails to represent that the buying was a consequence of the going, which can be expressed by a modal that is discussed in 
[[#chapter-sumti-tcita|this chapter]].) However, the tense information &ndash; that the event of my going to the market preceded the event of my buying food &ndash; can be added to the logical connective as follows. The 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}} is replaced by 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}}{{vla|bo}}, and the tense cmavo 
{{vla|ba}} is inserted between 
{{vla|.i}}{{vla|je}} and 
{{vla|bo}}:

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|.ijebabo}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-BPG1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BPG1}}
{{judri|c14e18d6}}
:'''mi pu klama le zarci .ijebabo mi pu tervecnu lo cidja'''
:<code>I [past] go-to the market. And [later] I [past] buy items-of food.</code>

Here the 
{{vla|pu}} cmavo in the two bridi-tails express the time of both actions with respect to the speaker: in the past. The 
{{vla|ba}} relates the two items to one another: the second item is later than the first item. The grammar does not permit omitting the 
{{vla|bo}}; if it were omitted, the 
{{vla|ba}} and the second 
{{vla|pu}} would run together to form a compound tense 

{{vla|bapu}} applying to the second bridi-tail only.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ek…bo}} Adding tense or modal information to a logical connective is permitted only in the following situations:

Between an ek (or joik) and 
{{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-129L}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-129L}}
{{judri|c14e18d7}}
{{ind|example|simultaneously|example}}
:'''la .djan .ecabo la .alis. klama le zarci'''
:<code>John and [simultaneous] Alice go-to the market.</code>
:''John and Alice go to the market simultaneously.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in joik…ke}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ek…ke}} Between an ek (or joik) and 
{{vla|ke}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nydK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nydK}}
{{judri|c14e18d8}}
{{ind|example|and earlier|example}}
:'''mi dzukla le zarci .epuke le zdani .a le ckule [ke'e]'''
:<code>I walk-to the market and [earlier] ( the house or the school ).</code>
:''I walk to the market and, before that, to the house or the school.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GIhA selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in gihek…bo}} Between a gihek and 
{{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-APPE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-APPE}}
{{ind|example|and then}}  
{{judri|c14e18d9}}
:'''mi dunda le cukta gi'ebabo lebna lo rupnu vau do'''
:<code>I give the book and [later] take some currency-units from/to you.</code>
:''I give you the book and then take some dollars (pounds, yen) from you.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GIhA selma'o}}  
{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in gihek…ke}} Between a gihek and 
{{vla|ke}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-A0yC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-A0yC}}
{{judri|c14e18d10}}
{{ind|example|and simultaneously|example}}
:'''mi dzukla le zarci gi'ecake cusku zo'e la djan. [ke'e]'''
:<code>I walk-to the market and [simultaneous] express something to-John.</code>
:''I walk to the market and at the same time talk to John.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|I selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijoik…bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijek…bo}} Between an ijek (or ijoik) and {{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-AhnP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AhnP}}
{{judri|c14e18d11}}
{{ind|example|and then|example}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu .ijebabo mi viska pa ninmu'''
:<code>I see a man. And [later] I see a woman.</code>
:''I see a man, and then I see a woman.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|I selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  

{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijoik…tu'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in ijek…tu'e}} Between an ijek (or ijoik) and {{vla|tu'e}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-GBgP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GBgP}}
{{judri|c14e18d12}}
{{ind|example|and then|example}}
:'''mi viska pa nanmu .ijebatu'e mi viska pa ninmu [tu'u]'''
:<code>I see a man. And [later] I see a woman.</code>
:''I see a man, and then I see a woman.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  

{{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in joik…bo}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|in jek…bo}} And finally, between a jek (or joik) and 
{{vla|bo}}, as in:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ce09}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ce09}}
{{judri|c14e18d13}}
{{ind|example|doctor and then rich|example}}
:'''mi mikce jebabo ricfu'''
:<code>I-am-a doctor and [later] rich</code>
:''I am a doctor and future rich person.''

{{ind|general-imported|tu'e|contrasted with bo for tensed logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|contrasted with tu'e for tensed logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|ke|contrasted with bo for tensed logical connection}}  {{ind|general-imported|bo|contrasted with ke for tensed logical connection}} As can be seen from 
{{linker|example-random-id-AhnP}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-GBgP}}, the choice between 
{{vla|bo}} and {{vla|ke}} (or {{vla|tu'e}}) is arbitrary when there are only two things to be connected. If there were no tense information to include, of course neither would be required; it is only the rule that tense information must always be sandwiched between the logical connective and a following {{vla|bo}}, 
{{vla|ke}}, or {{vla|tu'e}} that requires the use of one of these grouping cmavo in {{linker|example-random-id-129L}} and {{linker|example-random-id-APPE}} through 
{{linker|example-random-id-Ce09}}.

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical expressions|tensed connection in}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed connectives|in mathematical expressions}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed non-logical connectives|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed logical connectives|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connectives|with tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tensed non-logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|including tense}} Non-logical connectives with 
{{vla|bo}} and 
{{vla|ke}} can include tense information in exactly the same way as logical connectives. Forethought connectives, however (except as noted below) are unable to do so, as are termsets or tense connectives. Mathematical operands and operators can also include tense information in their logical connectives as a result of their close parallelism with sumti and tanru components respectively:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sgUo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-sgUo}}
{{judri|c14e18d14}}
:'''vei ci .ebabo vo [ve'o] tadni cu zvati le kumfa'''
:<code>( 3 and [future] 4 ) students are-at the room.</code>
:''Three and, later, four students were in the room.''

{{ind|general-imported|forethought bridi-tail connection|special rule for tense}}  {{ind|general-imported|tense|in forethought bridi-tail connection|special rule}} is a simple example. There is a special grammatical rule for use when a tense applies to both of the selbri in a forethought bridi-tail connection: the entire forethought construction can just be preceded by a tense. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DxuA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DxuA}}
{{judri|c14e18d15}}
{{ind|example|went and bought|example}}
:'''mi pu ge klama le zarci gi tervecnu lo cidja'''
:<code>I [past] both go-to the market and buy some food</code>
:''I went to the market and bought some food.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|pu ge}}  

{{linker|example-random-id-DxuA}} is similar to 
{{linker|example-random-id-PMTu}}. There is no time relationship specified between the going and the buying; both are simply set in the past.

{{judri|section-abstractors}}
==Abstractor connection and connection within abstractions==
{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|NU selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|jeks|connecting abstractors}}  {{ind|general-imported|abstractions|logical connection of}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection of abstractors}} Last and (as a matter of fact) least: a logical connective is allowed between abstraction markers of selma'o NU. As usual, the connection can be expanded to a bridi connection between two bridi which differ only in abstraction marker. Jeks are the appropriate connective. 

{{linker|example-random-id-qGVP}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qgVR}} are equivalent in meaning:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGVP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qGVP}}
{{judri|c14e19d1}}
{{ind|example|quality and quantity|example}}
:'''le ka la frank. ciska cu xlali .ije le ni la frank. ciska cu xlali'''
:<code>The quality-of Frank's writing is bad, and the quantity of Frank's writing is bad.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgVR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgVR}}
{{judri|c14e19d2}}
{{ind|example|quality and quantity|example}}
:'''le ka je ni la frank. ciska cu xlali'''
:''The quality and quantity of Frank's writing is bad.''

{{ind|general-imported|abstractions|grouping of connectives in}}  {{ind|general-imported|grouping|of connection in abstractions}}  {{ind|general-imported|abstractions|forethought connection in}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|in abstractions}} As with tenses and modals, there is no forethought and no way to override the left-grouping rule.

{{ind|general-imported|logical connection|inside abstractions|contrasted with outside}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|in abstractions|inner bridi contrasted with outer bridi}} Logical connectives and abstraction are related in another way as well, though. Since an abstraction contains a bridi, the bridi may have a logical connection inside it. Is it legitimate to split the outer bridi into two, joined by the logical connection? Absolutely not. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-f1uT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-f1uT}}
{{judri|c14e19d3}}
{{ind|example|Jupiter life|example}}
:'''mi jinvi le du'u loi jmive cu zvati gi'onai na zvati vau la .iupiter.'''
:<code>I opine the fact-that a-mass-of living-things (is-at or-else isn't-at) Jupiter.</code>
:''I believe there either is or isn't life on Jupiter.''

is true, since the embedded sentence is a tautology, but:

{{dsp|example-random-id-X69J}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-X69J}}
{{judri|c14e19d4}}
:'''mi jinvi le du'u loi jmive cu zvati la .iupiter. .ijonai mi jinvi le du'u loi jmive cu zvati la .iupiter.'''
:<code>I opine the fact-that a-mass-of living-things is-at Jupiter or-else I opine the fact-that a-mass-of living-things isn't-at Jupiter</code>

is false, since I have no evidence one way or the other ( 
{{vla|jinvi}} requires some sort of evidence, real or fancied, unlike 
{{vla|krici}}).

{{judri|section-construction-summary}}
==Rules for making logical and non-logical connectives==
{{ind|general-imported|non-logical connectives|syntax rules summary}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|syntax rules summary}} The full set of rules for inserting 
{{vla|na}}, 
{{vla|se}}, and 
{{vla|nai}} into any connective is:

Afterthought logical connectives (eks, jeks, giheks, ijeks):
*Negate first construct: Place {{vla|na}} before the connective cmavo (but after the {{vla|i}} of an ijek).
*Negate second construct: Place {{vla|nai}} after the connective cmavo.
*Exchange constructs: Place {{vla|se}} before the connective cmavo (after {{vla|na}} if any).

Forethought logical connectives (geks, guheks):
*Negate first construct: Place 
{{vla|nai}} after the connective cmavo.
*Negate second construct: Place 
{{vla|nai}} after the 
{{vla|gi}}.
*Exchange constructs: Place 
{{vla|se}} before the connective cmavo.

Non-logical connectives (joiks, joigiks):
*Negate connection: Place 
{{vla|nai}} after the connective cmavo (but before the 
{{vla|gi}} of a joigik).
*Exchange constructs: Place 
{{vla|se}} before the connective cmavo.

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{judri|chapter-negation}}
= “No” Problems: On Lojban Negation=
{{image|xml:id="chapter-negation-picture"|The picture for chapter 15|media/chapter-negation.gif}}
{{judri|section-negation-introduction}}
==Introductory==
The grammatical expression of negation is a critical part of Lojban's claim to being logical. The problem of negation, simply put, is to come up with a complete definition of the word 
“not”. For Lojban's unambiguous grammar, this means further that meanings of 
“not” with different grammatical effect must be different words, and even different grammatical structures.

Logical assertions are implicitly required in a logical language; thus, an apparatus for expressing them is built into Lojban's logical connectives and other structures.

In natural languages, especially those of Indo-European grammar, we have sentences composed of two parts which are typically called 
“subject” and 
“predicate”. In the statement

{{dsp|example-random-id-vrXe}}
{{judri|c15e1d1}}
:''John goes to the store.''

“John” is the subject, and “goes to the store” is the predicate. Negating {{linker|example-random-id-vrXe}} to produce

{{dsp|example-random-id-gm3I}}
{{judri|c15e1d2}}
:''John doesn't go to the store.''

has the effect of declaring that the predicate does not hold for the subject. 
{{linker|example-random-id-gm3I}} says nothing about whether John goes somewhere else, or whether someone else besides John goes to the store.

We will call this kind of negation 
“natural language negation”. This kind of negation is difficult to manipulate by the tools of logic, because it doesn't always follow the rules of logic. Logical negation is bi-polar: either a statement is true, or it is false. If a statement is false, then its negation must be true. Such negation is termed contradictory negation.

Let's look at some examples of how natural language negation can violate the rules of contradictory negation.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGWR}}
{{judri|c15e1d3}}
Some animals are not white.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgXI}}
{{judri|c15e1d4}}
Some animals are white.

Both of these statements are true; yet one is apparently the negation of the other. Another example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgxL}}
{{judri|c15e1d5}}
I mustn't go to the dance.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGXL}}
{{judri|c15e1d6}}
I must go to the dance.

At first thought, 
{{linker|example-random-id-qgxL}} negates 
{{linker|example-random-id-qGXL}}. Thinking further, we realize that there is an intermediate state wherein I am permitted to go to the dance, but not obligated to do so. Thus, it is possible that both statements are false.

Sometimes order is significant:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgyb}}
{{judri|c15e1d7}}
The falling rock didn't kill Sam.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qGYX}}
{{judri|c15e1d8}}
Sam wasn't killed by the falling rock.

Our minds play tricks on us with this one. Because 
{{linker|example-random-id-qgyb}} is written in what is called the 
“active voice”, we immediately get confused about whether 
“the falling rock” is a suitable subject for the predicate 
“did kill Sam”. 
“Kill” implies volition to us, and rocks do not have volition. This confusion is employed by opponents of gun control who use the argument 
“Guns don't kill people; people kill people.”

Somehow, we don't have the same problem with 
{{linker|example-random-id-qGYX}}. The subject is Sam, and we determine the truth or falsity of the statement by whether he was or wasn't killed by the falling rock.

{{linker|example-random-id-qGYX}} also helps us focus on the fact that there are at least two questionable facts implicit in this sentence: whether Sam was killed, and if so, whether the falling rock killed him. If Sam wasn't killed, the question of what killed him is moot.

This type of problem becomes more evident when the subject of the sentence turns out not to exist:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgzq}}
{{judri|c15e1d9}}
The King of Mexico didn't come to dinner.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgzv}}
{{judri|c15e1d10}}
The King of Mexico did come to dinner.

In the natural languages, we would be inclined to say that both of these statements are false, since there is no King of Mexico.

The rest of this chapter is designed to explain the Lojban model of negation.

{{judri|section-bridi-negation}}
==bridi negation==
In discussing Lojban negation, we will call the form of logical negation that simply denies the truth of a statement 
“bridi negation”. Using bridi negation, we can say the equivalent of 
“I haven't stopped beating my wife” without implying that I ever started, nor even that I have a wife, meaning simply 
“It isn't true that I have stopped beating my wife.” Since Lojban uses bridi as smaller components of complex sentences, bridi negation is permitted in these components as well at the sentence level.

For the bridi negation of a sentence to be true, the sentence being negated must be false. A major use of bridi negation is in making a negative response to a yes/no question; such responses are usually contradictory, denying the truth of the entire sentence. A negative answer to

{{dsp|example-random-id-sCNE}}
{{judri|c15e2d1}}
Did you go to the store?

is taken as a negation of the entire sentence, equivalent to

{{dsp|example-random-id-vFYC}}
{{judri|c15e2d2}}
No, I didn't go to the store.

The most important rule about bridi negation is that if a bridi is true, its negation is false, and vice versa.

The simplest way to express a bridi negation is to use the cmavo 
{{vla|na}} of selma'o NA before the selbri of the affirmative form of the bridi (but after the 
{{vla|cu}}, if there is one):

{{dsp|example-random-id-7nrv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7nrv}}
{{judri|c15e2d3}}
:'''mi klama le zarci'''
:<code>I go-to the store.</code>

when negated becomes:

{{dsp|example-random-id-bV3b}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-bV3b}}
{{judri|c15e2d4}}
:'''mi na klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [false] go-to the store.</code>

Note that we have used a special convention to show in the English that a bridi negation is present. We would like to use the word 
“not”, because this highlights the naturalness of putting the negation marker just before the selbri, and makes the form easier to learn. But there is a major difference between Lojban's bridi negation with 
{{vla|na}} and natural language negation with 
“not”. In English, the word 
“not” can apply to a single word, to a phrase, to an English predicate, or to the entire sentence. In addition, 
“not” may indicate either contradictory negation or another form of negation, depending on the sentence. Lojban's internal bridi negation, on the other hand, always applies to an entire bridi, and is always a contradictory negation; that is, it contradicts the claim of the whole bridi.

Because of the ambiguity of English 
“not”, we will use 
“[false]” in the translation of Lojban examples to remind the reader that we are expressing a contradictory negation. Here are more examples of bridi negation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qgzz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qgzz}}
{{judri|c15e2d5}}
:'''mi [cu] na ca klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [false] now am-a-go-er to the market.</code>
:''I am not going to the market now.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh10}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh10}}
{{judri|c15e2d6}}
:'''lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu na krecau'''
:<code>The-actual present noblest-governor of the French country [false] is-hair-without.</code>
:''The current king of France isn't bald.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh2i}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh2i}}
{{judri|c15e2d7}}
:'''ti na barda prenu co melbi mi'''
:<code>This [false] is a big-person of-type (beautiful to me).</code>
:''This isn't a big person who is beautiful to me.''

Although there is this fundamental difference between Lojban's internal bridi negation and English negation, we note that in many cases, especially when there are no existential or quantified variables (the cmavo 

{{vla|da}}, 
{{vla|de}}, and 
{{vla|di}} of selma'o KOhA, explained in [[#chapter-quantifiers|this chapter]]) in the bridi, you can indeed translate Lojban {{vla|na}} as “not” (or “isn't” or “doesn't”, as appropriate).

The most important rule about bridi negation is that if a bridi is true, its negation is false, and vice versa.

In Lojban, there are several structures that implicitly contain bridi, so that Lojban sentences may contain more than one occurrence of 
{{vla|na}}. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-WU9u}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-WU9u}}
{{judri|c15e2d8}}
:'''mi na gleki le nu na klama le nu dansu'''
:<code>I [false] am-happy-about the event-of ([false] going-to the event-of dancing).</code>
:<code>It is not the case that I am happy about it not being the case that I am going to the dance.</code>
:''I am not happy about not going to the dance.''

In the previous example, we used internal negations in abstraction bridi; bridi negation may also be found in descriptions within sumti. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-N65f}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-N65f}}
{{judri|c15e2d9}}
:'''mi nelci le na melbi'''
:<code>I am fond of the-one-described-as ([false] beautiful).</code>
:''I am fond of the one who isn't beautiful.''

A more extreme (and more indefinite) example is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eQaI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eQaI}}
{{judri|c15e2d10}}
:'''mi nelci lo na ca nolraitru be le frasygu'e'''
:<code>I am-fond-of one-who-is ([false] the current king of the French-country).</code>
:''I am fond of one who isn't the current king of France.''

The claim of 
{{linker|example-random-id-eQaI}} could apply to anyone except a person who is fond of no one at all, since the relation within the description is false for everyone. You cannot readily express these situations in colloquial English.

Negation with 
{{vla|na}} applies to an entire bridi, and not to just part of a selbri. Therefore, you won't likely have reason to put 
{{vla|na}} inside a tanru. In fact, the grammar currently does not allow you to do so (except in a lujvo and in elaborate constructs involving GUhA, the forethought connector for selbri). Any situation where you might want to do so can be expressed in a less-compressed non-tanru form. This grammatical restriction helps ensure that bridi negation is kept separate from other forms of negation.

The grammar of 
{{vla|na}} allows multiple adjacent negations, which cancel out, as in normal logic:

{{dsp|example-random-id-RJKu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RJKu}}
{{judri|c15e2d11}}
:'''ti na na barda prenu co melbi mi'''
:<code>This [false] [false] is-a-big person that is (beautiful to me).</code>

which is the same as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2UpW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2UpW}}
{{judri|c15e2d12}}
:'''ti barda prenu co melbi mi'''
:<code>This is a big-person that is (beautiful to me).</code>

When a selbri is tagged with a tense or a modal, negation with 
{{vla|na}} is permitted in two positions: before or after the tag. No semantic difference between these forms has yet been defined, but this is not finally determined, since the interactions between tenses/modals and bridi negation have not been fully explored. In particular, it remains to be seen whether sentences using less familiar tenses, such as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-fgmv}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-fgmv}}
{{judri|c15e2d13}}
:'''mi [cu] ta'e klama le zarci'''
:''I habitually go to the market.''

mean the same thing with 
{{vla|na}} before the 
{{vla|ta'e}}, as when the negation occurs afterwards; we'll let future, Lojban-speaking, logicians decide on how they relate to each other.

A final caution on translating English negations into Lojban: if you translate the English literally, you'll get the wrong one. With English causal statements, and other statements with auxiliary clauses, this problem is more likely.

Thus, if you translate the English:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hEa7}}
{{judri|c15e2d14}}
I do not go to the market because the car is broken.

as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-q8su}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-q8su}}
{{judri|c15e2d15}}
:'''mi na klama le zarci ki'u lenu le karce cu spofu'''
:<code>I [false] go-to the market because the car is broken.</code>
:''It is false that: “I go to the market because the car is broken.”''

you end up negating too much.

Such mistranslations result from the ambiguity of English compounded by the messiness of natural language negation. A correct translation of the normal interpretation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-hEa7}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-R3GU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-R3GU}}
{{judri|c15e2d16}}
:'''lenu mi na klama le zarci cu se krinu lenu le karce cu spofu'''
:<code>The event-of (my [false] going-to the market) is justified by the event-of (the car being broken).</code>
:''My not going to the market is because the car is broken.''

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-R3GU}}, the negation is clearly confined to the event abstraction in the x1 sumti, and does not extend to the whole sentence. The English could also have been expressed by two separate sentences joined by a causal connective (which we'll not go into here).

The problem is not confined to obvious causals. In the English:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MGvB}}
{{judri|c15e2d17}}
I was not conscripted into the Army with the help of my uncle the Senator.

we do not intend the uncle's help to be part of the negation. We must thus move the negation into an event clause or use two separate sentences. The event-clause version would look like:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NILi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NILi}}
{{judri|c15e2d18}}
:<code>The event-of (my [false] being-conscripted-into the Army) was aided by my uncle the Senator.</code>

It is possible that someone will want to incorporate bridi negations into lujvo. For this reason, the rafsi 
{{raf|-nar-}} has been reserved for 
{{vla|na}}. However, before using this rafsi, make sure that you intend the contradictory bridi negation, and not the scalar negation described in 
[[#section-scalar-negation|this section]], which will be much more common in tanru and lujvo.

{{judri|section-scalar-negation}}
==Scalar Negation==
Let us now consider some other types of negation. For example, when we say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-GJga}}
{{judri|c15e3d1}}
:''The chair is not brown.''

we make a positive inference &ndash; that the chair is some other color. Thus, it is legitimate to respond:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DDN8}}
{{judri|c15e3d2}}
:''It is green.''

Whether we agree that the chair is brown or not, the fact that the statement refers to color has significant effect on how we interpret some responses. If we hear the following exchange:

{{dsp|example-random-id-muQB}}
{{judri|c15e3d3}}
:''The chair is not brown.''
:''Correct. The chair is wooden.''

we immediately start to wonder about the unusual wood that isn't brown. If we hear the exchange:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MxWM}}
{{judri|c15e3d4}}
:''Is the chair green?''
:''No, it is in the kitchen.''

we are unsettled because the response seems to be a non-sequitur. But since it might be true and it is a statement about the chair, one can't say it is entirely irrelevant!

What is going on in these statements is something called 
“scalar negation”. As the name suggests, scalar negation presumes an implied scale. A negation of this type not only states that one scalar value is false, but implies that another value on the scale must be true. This can easily lead to complications. The following exchange seems reasonably natural (a little suspension of disbelief in such inane conversation will help):

{{dsp|example-random-id-s5DJ}}
{{judri|c15e3d5}}
:''That isn't a blue house.''
:''Right! That is a green house.''

We have acknowledged a scalar negation by providing a correct value which is another color in the set of colors permissible for houses. While a little less likely, the following exchange is also natural:

{{dsp|example-random-id-M472}}
{{judri|c15e3d6}}
:''That isn't a blue house.''
:''Right! That is a blue car.""

Again, we have acknowledged a scalar negation, and substituted a different object in the universe of discourse of things that can be blue.

Now, if the following exchange occurs:

{{dsp|example-random-id-sq36}}
{{judri|c15e3d7}}
:''That isn't a blue house.''
:''Right! That is a green car.''

we find the result unsettling. This is because it seems that two corrections have been applied when there is only one negation. Yet out of context, 
“blue house” and 
“green car” seem to be reasonably equivalent units that should be mutually replaceable in a sentence. It's just that we don't have a clear way in English to say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hd0I}}
{{judri|c15e3d8}}
:''That isn't a “blue-house”.''

aloud so as to clearly imply that the scalar negation is affecting the pair of words as a single unit.

Another even more confusing example of scalar negation is to the sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JTrd}}
{{judri|c15e3d9}}
:''John didn't go to Paris from Rome.''

Might 
{{linker|example-random-id-JTrd}} imply that John went to Paris from somewhere else? Or did he go somewhere else from Rome? Or perhaps he didn't go anywhere at all: maybe someone else did, or maybe there was no event of going whatsoever. One can devise circumstances where any one, two or all three of these statements might be inferred by a listener.

In English, we have a clear way of distinguishing scalar negation from predicate negation that can be used in many situations. We can use the partial word 
“non-” as a prefix. But this is not always considered good usage, even though it would render many statements much clearer. For example, we can clearly distinguish

{{dsp|example-random-id-gN3C}}
{{judri|c15e3d10}}
:''That is a non-blue house.''

from the related sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-GtQC}}
{{judri|c15e3d11}}
:''That is a blue non-house.''

{{linker|example-random-id-gN3C}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-GtQC}} have the advantage that, while they contain a negative indication, they are in fact positive assertions. They say what is true by excluding the false; they do not say what is false.

We can't always use 
“non-” though, because of the peculiarities of English's grammar. It would sound strange to say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-A3yR}}
{{judri|c15e3d12}}
:''John went to non-Paris from Rome.''

or

{{dsp|example-random-id-sn2I}}
{{judri|c15e3d13}}
:''John went to Paris from non-Rome.''

although these would clarify the vague negation. Another circumlocution for English scalar negation is 
“other than”, which works where 
“non-” does not, but is wordier.

Finally, we have natural language negations that are called polar negations, or opposites:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh2s}}
{{judri|c15e3d14}}
:''John is moral.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh3s}}
{{judri|c15e3d15}}
:''John is immoral.''

To be immoral is much more than to just be not moral: it implies the opposite condition. Statements like 
{{linker|example-random-id-qh3s}} are strong negations which not only deny the truth of a statement, but assert its opposite. Since, 
“opposite” implies a scale, polar negations are a special variety of scalar negations.

To examine this concept more closely, let us draw a linear scale, showing two examples of how the scale is used:

<pre>
Affirmations (positive)      Negations (negative)
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
All       Most        Some         Few       None
Excellent Good        Fair         Poor     Awful
</pre>
Some scales are more binary than the examples we diagrammed. Thus we have 
“not necessary” or 
“unnecessary” being the polar opposite of necessary. Another scale, especially relevant to Lojban, is interpreted based on situations modified by one's philosophy: 
“not true” may be equated with 
“false” in a bi-valued truth-functional logic, while in tri-valued logic an intermediate between 
“true” and 
“false” is permitted, and in fuzzy logic a continuous scale exists from true to false. The meaning of “not true” requires a knowledge of which variety of truth scale is being considered.

We will define the most general form of scalar negation as indicating only that the particular point or value in the scale or range is not valid and that some other (unspecified) point on the scale is correct. This is the intent expressed in most contexts by 
“not mild”, for example.

Using this paradigm, contradictory negation is less restrictive than scalar negation &ndash; it says that the point or value stated is incorrect (false), and makes no statement about the truth of any other point or value, whether or not on the scale.

In English, scalar negation semantically includes phrases such as 
“other than”, 
“reverse of”, or 
“opposite from” expressions and their equivalents. More commonly, scalar negation is expressed in English by the prefixes 
“non-”, 
“un-”, 
“il-”, and 
“im-”. Just which form and permissible values are implied by a scalar negation is dependent on the semantics of the word or concept which is being negated, and on the context. Much confusion in English results from the uncontrolled variations in meaning of these phrases and prefixes.

In the examples of 
[[#section-nahe|this section]], we will translate the general case of scalar negation using the general formula 
“other than” when a phrase is scalar-negated, and 
“non-” when a single word is scalar-negated.

{{judri|section-nahe}}
==selbri and tanru negation==
All the scalar negations illustrated in 
[[#section-scalar-negation|this section]] are expressed in Lojban using the cmavo 
{{vla|na'e}} (of selma'o NAhE). The most common use of 
{{vla|na'e}} is as a prefix to the selbri:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh42}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh42}}
{{judri|c15e4d1}}
:'''mi klama le zarci'''
:''I go to the market.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qH4n}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qH4n}}
{{judri|c15e4d2}}
:'''mi na'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I non-go to the market.</code>

Comparing these two, we see that the negation operator being used in 

{{linker|example-random-id-qH4n}} is 
{{vla|na'e}}. But what exactly does 
{{vla|na'e}} negate? Does the negation include only the gismu 
{{vla|klama}}, which is the entire selbri in this case, or does it include the {{jbo|le zarci}} as well? In Lojban, the answer is unambiguously 
“only the gismu”. The cmavo 
{{vla|na'e}} always applies only to what follows it.

{{linker|example-random-id-qH4n}} looks as if it were parallel to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-tqX1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-tqX1}}
{{judri|c15e4d3}}
:'''mi na klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [false] go-to the market.</code>

but in fact there is no real parallelism at all. A negation using 
{{vla|na}} denies the truth of a relationship, but a selbri negation with 
{{vla|na'e}} asserts that a relationship exists other than that stated, one which specifically involves the sumti identified in the statement. The grammar allotted to 
{{vla|na'e}} allows us to unambiguously express scalar negations in terms of scope, scale, and range within the scale. Before we explain the scalar aspects, let us show how the scope of 
{{vla|na'e}} is determined.

In tanru, we may wish to negate an individual element before combining it with another to form the tanru. We in effect need a shorter-than-selbri-scope negation, for which we can use 
{{vla|na'e}} as well. The positive sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-ETuV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ETuV}}
{{judri|c15e4d4}}
:'''mi cadzu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I walking-ly go to the market.</code>

can be subjected to selbri negation in several ways. Two are:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh4w}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh4w}}
{{judri|c15e4d5}}
:'''mi na'e cadzu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I (other-than-walkingly)-go-to the market.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qH6w}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qH6w}}
{{judri|c15e4d6}}
:'''mi cadzu na'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I walkingly-(other-than-go-to) the market.</code>

These negations show the default scope of 
{{vla|na'e}} is close-binding on an individual brivla in a tanru. 

{{linker|example-random-id-qh4w}} says that I am going to the market, but in some kind of a non-walking manner. (As with most tanru, there are a few other possible interpretations, but we'll assume this one &ndash; See [[#chapter-selbri|this chapter]] for a discussion of tanru meaning).

In neither 
{{linker|example-random-id-qh4w}} nor 
{{linker|example-random-id-qH6w}} does the 
{{vla|na'e}} negate the entire selbri. While both sentences contain negations that deny a particular relationship between the sumti, they also have a component which makes a positive claim about such a relationship. This is clearer in 
{{linker|example-random-id-qh4w}}, which says that I am going, but in a non-walking manner. In 
{{linker|example-random-id-qH6w}}, we have claimed that the relationship between me and the market in some way involves walking, but is not one of 
“going to” (perhaps we are walking around the market, or walking-in-place while at the market).

The “scale”, or actually the “set”, implied in Lojban tanru negations is anything which plausibly can be substituted into the tanru. (Plausibility here is interpreted in the same way that answers to a 
{{vla|mo}} question must be plausible &ndash; the result must not only have the right number of places and have sumti values appropriate to the place structure, it must also be appropriate or relevant to the context.) This minimal condition allows a speaker to be intentionally vague, while still communicating meaningful information. The speaker who uses selbri negation is denying one relationship, while minimally asserting a different relationship.

We also need a scalar negation form that has a scope longer than a single brivla. There exists such a longer-scope selbri negation form, as exemplified by (each Lojban sentence in the next several examples is given twice, with parentheses in the second copy showing the scope of the 
{{vla|na'e}}):

{{dsp|example-random-id-t20b}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-t20b}}
{{judri|c15e4d7}}
:'''mi na'eke cadzu klama [ke'e] le zarci'''
:'''mi na'e (ke cadzu klama [ke'e]) le zarci'''
:<code>I other-than-(walkingly-go-to) the market.</code>

This negation uses the same 
{{vla|ke}} and 
{{vla|ke'e}} delimiters (the 
{{vla|ke'e}} is always elidable at the end of a selbri) that are used in tanru. The sentence clearly negates the entire selbri. The 
{{vla|ke'e}}, whether elided or not, reminds us that the negation does not include the trailing sumti. While the trailing-sumti place-structure is defined as that of the final brivla, the trailing sumti themselves are not part of the selbri and are thus not negated by 
{{vla|na'e}}.

Negations of just part of the selbri are also permitted:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PVct}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PVct}}
{{judri|c15e4d8}}
:'''mi na'eke sutra cadzu ke'e klama le zarci'''
:'''mi na'e (ke sutra cadzu ke'e) klama le zarci'''
:<code>I other-than-(quickly-walkingly) go-to the market.</code>

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-PVct}}, only the 
:{{jbo|sutra cadzu}} tanru is negated, so the speaker is indeed going to the market, but not by walking quickly.

Negations made with {{vla|na'e}} or {{jbo|na'eke}} also include within their scope any sumti attached to the brivla or tanru with 
{{vla|be}} or {{vla|bei}}. Such attached sumti are considered part of the brivla or tanru:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MYYa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MYYa}}
{{judri|c15e4d9}}
:'''mi na'e ke sutra cadzu be le mi birka ke'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I other-than-(quickly walking-on-my-arms-ly) go-to the market.</code>

Note that 
{{linker|example-random-id-qh7T}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qH8J}} do not express the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh7T}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh7T}}
{{judri|c15e4d10}}
:'''mi na'eke sutra cadzu [ke'e] lemi birka'''
:'''mi na'e (ke sutra cadzu [ke'e]) lemi birka'''
:<code>I other-than-(quickly-walk-on) my-arms.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qH8J}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qH8J}}
{{judri|c15e4d11}}
:'''mi na'eke sutra cadzu be lemi birka [ke'e]'''
:'''mi na'e (ke sutra cadzu be lemi birka [ke'e])'''
:<code>I other-than-(quickly-walk-on my-arms).</code>

The translations show that the negation in 
{{linker|example-random-id-qh7T}} is more restricted in scope; i.e. less of the sentence is negated with respect to x1 ( 
{{vla|mi}}).

Logical scope being an important factor in Lojban's claims to be unambiguous, let us indicate the relative precedence of 
{{vla|na'e}} as an operator. Grouping with 
{{vla|ke}} and 
{{vla|ke'e}}, of course, has an overt scope, which is its advantage. 
{{vla|na'e}} is very close binding to its brivla. Internal binding of tanru, with 
{{vla|bo}}, is not as tightly bound as 
{{vla|na'e}}. 
{{vla|co}}, the tanru inversion operator has a scope that is longer than all other tanru constructs.

In short, 
{{vla|na'e}} and 
:{{jbo|na'eke}} define a type of negation, which is shorter in scope than bridi negation, and which affects all or part of a selbri. The result of 
{{vla|na'e}} negation remains an assertion of some specific truth and not merely a denial of another claim.

The similarity becomes striking when it is noticed that the rafsi {{raf|-nal-}}, representing {{vla|na'e}} when a tanru is condensed into a lujvo, forms an exact parallel to the English usage of {{jbo|non-}}. Turning a series of related negations into lujvo gives:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2buq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2buq}} <!-- FIXME: this "example" should probably just be a simplelist -->
{{judri|c15e4d12}}
:'''na'e klama becomes nalkla'''
:'''na'e cadzu klama becomes naldzukla'''
:'''na'e sutra cadzu klama becomes nalsu'adzukla'''
:'''nake sutra cadzu ke'e klama becomes nalsu'adzuke'ekla'''

Note: 
{{raf|-kem-}} is the rafsi for 
{{vla|ke}}, but it is omitted in the final lujvo as superfluous &ndash; 
{{vla|ke'e}} is its own rafsi, and its inclusion in the lujvo implies a 

{{vla|ke}} after the 
{{raf|-nal-}}, since it needs to close something; only a 
{{vla|ke}} immediately after the negation would make the 
{{vla|ke'e}} meaningful in the tanru expressed in this lujvo.

In a lujvo, it is probably clearest to translate 
{{raf|-nal-}} as 
“non-”, to match the English combining forms, except when the 
{{vla|na'e}} has single word scope and English uses 
“un-” or 
“im-” to negate that single word. Translation style should determine the use of 
“other than”, 
“non-”, or another negator for 
{{vla|na'e}} in tanru; the translator must render the Lojban into English so it is clear in context. Let's go back to our simplest example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh9c}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh9c}}
{{judri|c15e4d13}}
:'''mi na'e klama le zarci'''
:<code>I am other-than-(going-to) the market.</code>
:<code>I am not going-to the market.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qH9e}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qH9e}}
{{judri|c15e4d14}}
:'''mi nalkla le zarci'''
:<code>I am-a-non-go-er-to the market.</code>

Note that to compare with the English translation form using 
“non-”, we've translated the Lojban as if the selbri were a noun. Since Lojban 
{{vla|klama}} is indifferently a noun, verb, or adjective, the difference is purely a translation change, not a true change in meaning. The English difference seems significant, though, due to the strongly different English grammatical forms and the ambiguity of English negation.

Consider the following highly problematic sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-GFFo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GFFo}}
{{judri|c15e4d15}}
:'''lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu krecau'''
:<code>An-actual currently noblest-governor of the French country is-hair-without.</code>
:''The current King of France is bald.''

The selbri 
{{vla|krecau}} negates with 
{{vla|na'e}} as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2maY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2maY}}
{{judri|c15e4d16}}
:'''lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu na'e krecau'''
:<code>An-actual currently noblest-governor of the French country is-other-than hair-without.</code>
:''The current King of France is other-than-bald.''

or, as a lujvo:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wGXL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wGXL}}
{{judri|c15e4d17}}
:'''lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu nalkrecau'''
:<code>An-actual currently noblest-governor of the French country is-non-hair-without.</code>
:''The current King of France is a non-bald-one.''

{{linker|example-random-id-2maY}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-wGXL}} express the predicate negation forms using a negation word ( 
{{vla|na'e}}) or rafsi ( 
{{raf|-nal-}}); yet they make positive assertions about the current King of France; ie., that he is other-than-bald or non-bald. This follows from the close binding of 
{{vla|na'e}} to the brivla. The lujvo form makes this overt by absorbing the negative marker into the word.

Since there is no current King of France, it is false to say that he is bald, or non-bald, or to make any other affirmative claim about him. Any sentence about the current King of France containing only a selbri negation is as false as the sentence without the negation. No amount of selbri negations have any effect on the truth value of the sentence, which is invariably 
“false”, since no affirmative statement about the current King of France can be true. On the other hand, bridi negation does produce a truth:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Bwdy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Bwdy}}
{{judri|c15e4d18}}
:'''lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu na krecau'''
:<code>An-actual current noblest-governor of the French Country [false] is-hair-without.</code>
:''It is false that the current King of France is bald.''

Note: 
{{vla|lo}} is used in these sentences because negation relates to truth conditions. To meaningfully talk about truth conditions in sentences carrying a description, it must be clear that the description actually applies to the referent. A sentence using 
{{vla|le}} instead of 
{{vla|lo}} can be true even if there is no current king of France, as long as the speaker and the listener agree to describe something as the current king of France. (See the explanations of 
{{vla|le}} in 
[[#section-basic-descriptors|this section]].)

{{judri|section-scales-negation}}
==Expressing scales in selbri negation==
In expressing a scalar negation, we can provide some indication of the scale, range, frame-of-reference, or universe of discourse that is being dealt with in an assertion. As stated in 
[[#section-nahe|this section]], the default is the set of plausible alternatives. Thus if we say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mw3B}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mw3B}}
{{judri|c15e5d1}}
:'''le stizu cu na'e xunre'''
:<code>The chair is a non-(red-thing).</code>

the pragmatic interpretation is that we mean a different color and not

{{dsp|example-random-id-7iMz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7iMz}}
{{judri|c15e5d2}}
:'''le stizu cu dzukla be le zarci'''
:<code>The chair walkingly-goes-to-the-market.</code>

However, if we have reason to be more explicit (an obtuse or contrary listener, or simply an overt logical analysis), we can clarify that we are referring to a color by saying:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yWSC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yWSC}}
{{judri|c15e5d3}}
:'''le stizu cu na'e xunre skari'''
:<code>The chair is of a non-(red)-color (as perceived by something under some conditions).</code>

We might also have reduced the pragmatic ambiguity by making the two trailing sumti values explicit (the 
“as perceived by” and 
“under conditions” places have been added to the place structure of 
{{vla|xunre}}). But assume we have a really stubborn listener (an artificially semi-intelligent computer?) who will find a way to misinterpret 
{{linker|example-random-id-yWSC}} even with three specific sumti provided.

In this case, we use a sumti tagged with the sumti tcita 
{{vla|ci'u}}, which translates roughly as 

“on a scale of X”, where 
X is the sumti. For maximal clarity, the tagged sumti can be bound into the negated selbri with 
{{vla|be}}. To clarify 
{{linker|example-random-id-yWSC}}, we might say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-a8S1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-a8S1}}
{{judri|c15e5d4}}
:'''le stizu cu na'e xunre be ci'u loka skari'''
:<code>The chair is a non-(red on-a-scale-of-colorness)-thing.</code>

We can alternately use the sumti tcita 
{{vla|teci'e}}, based on 
{{vla|ciste}}, which translates roughly as 
“of a system of components X”, for universes of discourse; in this case, we would express 
{{linker|example-random-id-yWSC}} as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-I0eV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-I0eV}}
{{judri|c15e5d5}}
:'''le stizu cu na'e xunre be teci'e le skari'''
:<code>The chair is a non-(red of-a-system-with-components-the-colors)-thing.</code>

Other places of 
{{vla|ciste}} can be brought out using the grammar of selma'o BAI modals, allowing slightly different forms of expression, thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Rj71}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Rj71}}
{{judri|c15e5d6}}
:'''le stizu cu na'e xunre be ci'e lo'i skari'''
:<code>The chair is a non-(red of-a-system-which-is-the-set-of-colors)-thing.</code>

The cmavo 
{{vla|le'a}}, also in selma'o BAI, can be used to specify a category:

{{dsp|example-random-id-5ibb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5ibb}}
{{judri|c15e5d7}}
:'''le stizu cu na'e xunre be le'a lo'i skari'''
:<code>The chair is a non-(red of-a-category-which-is-the-set-of-colors)-thing.</code>

which is minimally different in meaning from 
{{linker|example-random-id-Rj71}}.

The cmavo 
{{vla|na'e}} is not the only member of selma'o NAhE. If we want to express a scalar negation which is a polar opposite, we use the cmavo 
{{vla|to'e}}, which is grammatically equivalent to 
{{vla|na'e}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-RuvP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-RuvP}}
{{judri|c15e5d8}}
:'''le stizu cu to'e xunre be ci'u loka skari'''
:<code>The chair is a (opposite-of red) on-scale a-property-of color-ness.</code>

Likewise, the midpoint of a scale can be expressed with the cmavo 
{{vla|no'e}}, also grammatically equivalent to 
{{vla|na'e}}. Here are some parallel examples of 
{{vla|na'e}}, 
{{vla|no'e}}, and 
{{vla|to'e}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qH9T}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qH9T}}
{{judri|c15e5d9}}
:'''ta melbi'''
:<code>That is-beautiful.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qh9U}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qh9U}}
{{judri|c15e5d10}}
:'''ta na'e melbi'''
:<code>That is-non-beautiful.</code>
:<code>That is other than beautiful.</code>
:''That is ugly [in one sense].''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhAI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhAI}}
{{judri|c15e5d11}}
:'''ta no'e melbi'''
:<code>That is-neutrally beautiful.</code>
:''That is plain/ordinary-looking (neither ugly nor beautiful).''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHAV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHAV}}
{{judri|c15e5d12}}
:'''ta to'e melbi'''
:<code>That is-opposite-of beautiful.</code>
:''That is ugly/very ugly/repulsive.''

The cmavo 
{{vla|to'e}} has the assigned rafsi 
{{raf|-tol-}} and 
:{{jbo|-to'e-}}; the cmavo 
{{vla|no'e}} has the assigned rafsi 
{{raf|-nor-}} and 
{{raf|-no'e-}}. The selbri in 
{{linker|example-random-id-qh9U}} through 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHAV}} could be replaced by the lujvo 
{{vla|nalmle}}, 
{{vla|normle}}, and 
{{vla|tolmle}} respectively.

This large variety of scalar negations is provided because different scales have different properties. Some scales are open-ended in both directions: there is no 
“ultimately ugly” or 
“ultimately beautiful”. Other scales, like temperature, are open at one end and closed at the other: there is a minimum temperature (so-called 
“absolute zero”) but no maximum temperature. Still other scales are closed at both ends.

Correspondingly, some selbri have no obvious 
{{vla|to'e}}- what is the opposite of a dog? &ndash; while others have more than one, and need 
{{vla|ci'u}} to specify which opposite is meant.

{{judri|section-sumti-negation}}
==sumti negation==
There are two ways of negating sumti in Lojban. We have the choice of quantifying the sumti with zero, or of applying the sumti-negator 
:{{jbo|na'ebo}} before the sumti. It turns out that a zero quantification serves for contradictory negation. As the cmavo we use implies, 

:{{jbo|na'ebo}} forms a scalar negation.

Let us show examples of each.

{{dsp|example-random-id-PL1E}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PL1E}}
{{judri|c15e6d1}}
:'''no lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu krecau'''
:<code>Zero of those who are currently noblest-governors of the French country are-hair-without.</code>
:''No current king of France is bald.''

Is 
{{linker|example-random-id-PL1E}} true? Yes, because it merely claims that of the current Kings of France, however many there may be, none are bald, which is plainly true, since there are no such current Kings of France.

Now let us look at the same sentence using 
:{{jbo|na'ebo}} negation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LebJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LebJ}}
{{judri|c15e6d2}}
:'''na'ebo lo ca nolraitru be le fasygu'e cu krecau'''
:<code>[Something] other-than-(the-current-noblest-governor of the French country) is-hair-without.</code>
:''Something other than the current King of France is bald.''

{{linker|example-random-id-LebJ}} is true provided that something reasonably describable as 
“other than a current King of France”, such as the King of Saudi Arabia, or a former King of France, is in fact bald.

In place of {{jbo|na'ebo}}, you may also use {{jbo|no'ebo}} and {{jbo|to'ebo}}, to be more specific about the sumti which would be appropriate in place of the stated sumti. Good examples are hard to come by, but here's a valiant try:

{{dsp|example-random-id-S4AU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-S4AU}}
{{judri|c15e6d3}}
:'''mi klama to'ebo la bastn.'''
:<code>I go to the-opposite-of Boston.</code>
:''I go to Perth.''

(Boston and Perth are nearly, but not quite, antipodal cities. In a purely United States context, San Francisco might be a better 
“opposite”.) Coming up with good examples is difficult, because attaching 
:{{jbo|to'ebo}} to a description sumti is usually the same as attaching 
{{vla|to'e}} to the selbri of the description.

It is not possible to transform sumti negations of either type into bridi negations or scalar selbri negations. Negations of sumti will be used in Lojban conversation. The inability to manipulate these negations logically will, it is hoped, prevent the logical errors that result when natural languages attempt corresponding manipulations.

{{judri|section-other-negation}}
==Negation of minor grammatical constructs==
We have a few other constructs that can be negated, all of them based on negating individual words. For such negation, we use the suffix-combining negator, which is 
{{vla|nai}}. 
{{vla|nai}}, by the way, is almost always written as a compound into the previous word that it is negating, although it is a regular separate-word cmavo and the sole member of selma'o NAI.

Most of these negation forms are straightforward, and should be discussed and interpreted in connection with an analysis of the particular construct being negated. Thus, we will not go into much detail here.

The following are places where 
{{vla|nai}} is used:

When attached to tenses and modals (See [[#section-modal-negation|this section]], [[#section-interval-properties|this section]], [[#section-tense-negation|this section]] and [[#section-connected-tenses|this section]]), the
{{vla|nai}} suffix usually indicates a contradictory negation of the tagged bridi. Thus 
:{{jbo|punai}} as a tense inflection means 
“not-in-the-past”, or 
“not-previously”, without making any implication about any other time period unless explicitly stated. As a result,

{{dsp|example-random-id-PprX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PprX}}
{{judri|c15e7d1}}
:'''mi na pu klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [false] [past] go-to the store.</code>
:''I didn't go to the store.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-0hv2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-0hv2}}
{{judri|c15e7d2}}
:'''mi punai klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [past-not] go-to the store.</code>
:''I didn't go to the store.''

mean exactly the same thing, although there may be a difference of emphasis.

Tenses and modals can be logically connected, with the logical connectives containing contradictory negations; this allows negated tenses and modals to be expressed positively using logical connectives. Thus 
:{{jbo|punai je ca}} means the same thing as 
:{{jbo|pu naje ca}}.

As a special case, a 
:{{jbo|-nai}} attached to the interval modifiers of selma'o TAhE, ROI, or ZAhO (explained in 
[[#chapter-tenses|this chapter]]) signals a scalar negation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4YYQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4YYQ}}
{{judri|c15e7d3}}
:'''mi paroinai dansu le bisli'''
:<code>I [once] [not] dance-on the ice</code>

means that I dance on the ice either zero or else two or more times within the relevant time interval described by the bridi. 
{{linker|example-random-id-4YYQ}} is very different from the English use of 
“not once”, which is an emphatic way of saying 
“never” &ndash; that is, exactly zero times.

In indicators and attitudinals of selma'o UI or CAI, 
{{vla|nai}} denotes a polar negation. As discussed in 
[[#section-intensity-scale|this section]], most indicators have an implicit scale, and 
{{vla|nai}} changes the indicator to refer to the opposite end of the scale. Thus 
{{vla|.uinai}} expresses unhappiness, and 
{{vla|.ienai}} expresses disagreement (not ambivalence, which is expressed with the neutral or undecided intensity as 
:{{jbo|.iecu'i}}).
