Vocative cmavo of selma'o COI are considered a kind of indicator, but one which identifies the listener. Semantically, we could dispense with about half of the COI selma'o words based on the scalar paradigm. For example, {{vla|co'o}} could be expressed as {{jbo|coinai}}. However, this is not generally done.

Most of the COI cmavo are used in what are commonly called protocol situations. These protocols are used, for example, in radio conversations, which often take place in a noisy environment. The negatives of protocol words tend to convey diametrically opposite communications situations (as might be expected). Therefore, only one protocol vocative is dependent on {{vla|nai}}: negative acknowledgement, which is {{vla|je'enai}} ( “I didn't get that”).

Unlike the attitudinal indicators, which tend to be unimportant in noisy situations, the protocol vocatives become more important. So if, in a noisy environment, a protocol listener makes out only 

{{vla|nai}}, he or she can presume it is a negative acknowledgement and repeat transmission or otherwise respond accordingly. 
[[#section-vocative-scales|this section]] provides more detail on this topic.

The abstractors of selma'o NU follow the pattern of the tenses and modals. NU allows negative abstractions, especially in compound abstractions connected by logical connectives: 
:{{jbo|su'ujeninai}}, which corresponds to 
:{{jbo|su'u jenai ni}} just as 
:{{jbo|punai je ca}} corresponds to 
:{{jbo|pu naje ca}}. It is not clear how much use logically connected abstractors will be: See [[#section-abstractor-connection|this section]].

A {{vla|nai}} attached to a non-logical connective (of selma'o JOI or BIhI) is a scalar negation, and says that the bridi is false under the specified mixture, but that another connective is applicable. Non-logical connectives are discussed in 
[[#section-non-logical-connectives|this section]].

{{judri|section-truth-questions}}
==Truth questions==
One application of negation is in answer to truth questions (those which expect the answers 
“Yes” or 
“No”). The truth question cmavo 
{{vla|xu}} is in selma'o UI; placed at the beginning of a sentence, it asks whether the sentence as a whole is true or false.

{{dsp|example-random-id-5y84}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-5y84}}
{{judri|c15e8d1}}
:'''xu la djan. pu klama la paris. .e la rom.'''
:<code>Is it true that: (John previously went-to [both] Paris and Rome.)</code>

You can now use each of the several kinds of negation we've discussed in answer to this (presuming the same question and context for each answer).

The straightforward negative answer is grammatically equivalent to the expanded sentence with the {{vla|na}} immediately after the {{vla|cu}} (and before any tense/modal):

{{dsp|example-random-id-DMAd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DMAd}}
{{judri|c15e8d2}}
:'''na go'i'''
:<code>[false] [repeat previous]</code>
:''No.''

which means

{{dsp|example-random-id-mQSJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mQSJ}}
{{judri|c15e8d3}}
:'''la djan. [cu] na pu klama la paris. .e la rom.'''
:<code>John [false] previously went-to [both] Paris and Rome.</code>
:''It's not true that John went to Paris and Rome.''

The respondent can change the tense, putting the 
{{vla|na}} in either before or after the new tense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-rii2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-rii2}}
{{judri|c15e8d4}}
:'''na ba go'i'''
:<code>[false] [future] [repeat previous]</code>

meaning

{{dsp|example-random-id-Fn2c}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Fn2c}}
{{judri|c15e8d5}}
:'''la djan. [cu] na ba klama la paris. .e la rom.'''
:<code>John [false] later-will-go-to [both] Paris and Rome.</code>
:''It is false that John will go to Paris and Rome.''

or alternatively

{{dsp|example-random-id-acM9}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-acM9}}
{{judri|c15e8d6}}
:'''ba na go'i'''
:<code>[false] [future] [repeat previous]</code>

meaning

{{dsp|example-random-id-2SK0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2SK0}}
{{judri|c15e8d7}}
:'''la djan. [cu] ba na klama la paris. .e la rom.'''
:<code>John later-will [false] go-to [both] Paris and Rome.</code>

We stated in 
[[#section-scalar-negation|this section]] that sentences like 
{{linker|example-random-id-Fn2c}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-2SK0}} appear to be semantically identical, but that subtle semantic distinctions may eventually be found.

You can also use a scalar negation with {{vla|na'e}}, in which case, it is equivalent to putting a {{jbo|na'eke}} immediately after any tense:

{{dsp|example-random-id-q70h}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-q70h}}
{{judri|c15e8d8}}
:'''na'e go'i'''
:<code>other-than [repeat previous]</code>

which means

{{dsp|example-random-id-nQRQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nQRQ}}
{{judri|c15e8d9}}
:'''la djan. [cu] pu na'eke klama [ke'e] la paris. .e la rom.'''
:<code>John previously other-than(went-to) [both] Paris and Rome.</code>

He might have telephoned the two cities instead of going there. The unnecessary 
{{vla|ke}} and 
{{vla|ke'e}} would have been essential if the selbri had been a tanru.

{{judri|section-affirmations}}
==Affirmations==
There is an explicit positive form for both selma'o NA ( 
{{vla|ja'a}}) and selma'o NAhE ( 
{{vla|je'a}}), each of which would supplant the corresponding negator in the grammatical position used, allowing one to assert the positive in response to a negative question or statement without confusion. Assuming the same context as in 
[[#section-truth-questions|this section]]:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KhoH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KhoH}}
{{judri|c15e9d1}}
:'''xu na go'i'''
:<code>Is-it-true-that [false] [repeat previous]?</code>

or equivalently

{{dsp|example-random-id-8VCt}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8VCt}}
{{judri|c15e9d2}}
:'''xu la djan. [cu] na pu klama la paris. .e la rom.'''
:<code>Is it true that: John [false] previously-went-to [both] Paris and Rome.]</code>

The obvious, but incorrect, positive response to this negative question is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-F3LE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-F3LE}}
{{judri|c15e9d3}}
:'''go'i'''
:''[repeat previous]''

A plain {{vla|go'i}} does not mean “Yes it is”; it merely abbreviates repeating the previous statement unmodified, including any negators present; and 
{{linker|example-random-id-F3LE}} actually states that it is false that John went to both Paris and Rome.

When considering:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Pgrw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Pgrw}}
{{judri|c15e9d4}}
:'''na go'i'''
:<code>[false] [repeat previous]</code>

as a response to a negative question like 
{{linker|example-random-id-8VCt}}, Lojban designers had to choose between two equally plausible interpretations with opposite effects. Does 
{{linker|example-random-id-Pgrw}} create a double negative in the sentence by adding a new 
{{vla|na}} to the one already there (forming a double negative and hence a positive statement), or does the 
{{vla|na}} replace the previous one, leaving the sentence unchanged?

It was decided that substitution, the latter alternative, is the preferable choice, since it is then clear whether we intend a positive or a negative sentence without performing any manipulations. This is the way English usually works, but not all languages work this way &ndash; Russian, Japanese, and Navajo all interpret a negative reply to a negative question as positive.

The positive assertion cmavo of selma'o NA, which is "ja'a", can also replace the 
{{vla|na}} in the context, giving:

{{dsp|example-random-id-iUfV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-iUfV}}
{{judri|c15e9d5}}
:'''ja'a go'i'''
:<code>(John truly-(previously went-to) [both] Paris and Rome.)</code>

{{vla|ja'a}} can replace 
{{vla|na}} in a similar manner wherever the latter is used:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mrtu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mrtu}}
{{judri|c15e9d6}}
:'''mi ja'a klama le zarci'''
:''I indeed go to the store.''

{{vla|je'a}} can replace 
{{vla|na'e}} in exactly the same way, stating that scalar negation does not apply, and that the relation indeed holds as stated. In the absence of a negation context, it emphasizes the positive:

{{dsp|example-random-id-toQK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-toQK}}
{{judri|c15e9d7}}
:'''ta je'a melbi'''
:<code>that is-indeed beautiful.</code>

{{judri|section-metalinguistic-negation}}
==Metalinguistic negation forms==
The question of truth or falsity is not entirely synonymous with negation. Consider the English sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-QsJ9}}
{{judri|c15e10d1}}
:''I have not stopped beating my wife.''

If I never started such a heinous activity, then this sentence is neither true nor false. Such a negation simply says that something is wrong with the non-negated statement. Generally, we then use either tone of voice or else a correction to express a preferred true claim: “I never have beaten my wife.”

Negations which follow such a pattern are called 
“metalinguistic negations”. In natural languages, the mark of metalinguistic negation is that an indication of a correct statement always, or almost always, follows the negation. Tone of voice or emphasis may be further used to clarify the error.

Negations of every sort must be expressible in Lojban; errors are inherent to human thought, and are not excluded from the language. When such negations are metalinguistic, we must separate them from logical claims about the truth or falsity of the statement, as well as from scalar negations which may not easily express (or imply) the preferred claim. Because Lojban allows concepts to be so freely combined in tanru, limits on what is plausible or not plausible tend to be harder to determine.

Mimicking the muddled nature of natural language negation would destroy this separation. Since Lojban does not use tone of voice, we need other means to metalinguistically indicate what is wrong with a statement. When the statement is entirely inappropriate, we need to be able to express metalinguistic negation in a more non-specific fashion.

Here is a list of some different kinds of metalinguistic negation with English-language examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhbg}}
{{judri|c15e10d2}}
:''I have not <u>stopped</u> beating my wife.''

(I never started &ndash; failure of presupposition).

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHcI}}
{{judri|c15e10d3}}
:''5 is not blue.''
(color does not apply to abstract concepts &ndash; failure of category).

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHEQ}}
{{judri|c15e10d4}}
:''The current King of France is not bald.''

(there is no current King of France &ndash; existential failure)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhet}}
{{judri|c15e10d5}}
:''I do not have THREE children.''
(I have two &ndash; simple undue quantity)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhEU}}
{{judri|c15e10d6}}
:''I have not held THREE jobs previously, but four.''

(inaccurate quantity; the difference from the previous
example is that someone who has held four jobs has also held
three jobs)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhf5}}
{{judri|c15e10d7}}
:''It is not good, but bad.''

(undue quantity negation indicating that the value on a scale for measuring the predicate is incorrect)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHhA}}
{{judri|c15e10d8}}
:''She is not PRETTY; she is beautiful.''

(undue quantity transferred to a non-numeric scale)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhHI}}
{{judri|c15e10d9}}
:''The house is not blue, but green.''

(the scale/category being used is incorrect, but a related category applies)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHHw}}
{{judri|c15e10d10}}
:''The house is not blue, but is colored.''

(the scale/category being used is incorrect, but a broader category applies)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHI4}}
{{judri|c15e10d11}}
:''The cat is not blue, but long-haired.''

(the scale/category being used is incorrect, but an unrelated category applies)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHja}}
{{judri|c15e10d12}}
:A: He ain't coming today.
:B: “Ain't” ain't a word.
(solecism, or improper grammatical action)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHJi}}
{{judri|c15e10d13}}
:''I haven't STOOPED beating my wife; I've STOPPED.''

(spelling or mispronunciation error)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhJj}}
{{judri|c15e10d14}}
:''Not only was it a sheep, it was a black sheep.''
(non-contradictory correction)

The set of possible metalinguistic errors is open-ended.

Many of these forms have a counterpart in the various examples that we've discussed under logical negation. Metalinguistic negation doesn't claim that the sentence is false or true, though. Rather, it claims that, due to some error in the statement, 
“true” and 
“false” don't really apply.

Because one can metalinguistically negate a true statement intending a non-contradictory correction (say, a spelling error); we need a way (or ways) to metalinguistically negate a statement which is independent of our logical negation schemes using 
{{vla|na}}, 
{{vla|na'e}} and kin. The cmavo 
{{vla|na'i}} is assigned this function. If it is present in a statement, it indicates metalinguistically that something in the statement is incorrect. This metalinguistic negation must override any evaluation of the logic of the statement. It is equally allowed in both positive and negative statements.

Since 
{{vla|na'i}} is not a logical operator, multiple occurrences of 
{{vla|na'i}} need not be assumed to cancel each other. Indeed, we can use the position of 
{{vla|na'i}} to indicate metalinguistically what is incorrect, preparatory to correcting it in a later sentence; for this reason, we give 
{{vla|na'i}} the grammar of UI. The inclusion of 

{{vla|na'i}} anywhere in a sentence makes it a non-assertion, and suggests one or more pitfalls in assigning a truth value.

Let us briefly indicate how the above-mentioned metalinguistic errors can be identified. Other metalinguistic problems can then be marked by devising analogies to these examples:

Existential failure can be marked by attaching {{vla|na'i}} to the descriptor {{vla|lo}} or the {{vla|poi}} in a {{jbo|da poi}}-form sumti. (See
[[#section-basic-descriptors|this section]] and [[#section-restricted-claims|this section]] for details on these constructions.) Remember that if a 
{{vla|le}} sumti seems to refer to a non-existent referent, you may not understand what the speaker has in mind &ndash; the appropriate response is then 
{{vla|ki'a}}, asking for clarification.

Presupposition failure can be marked directly if the presupposition is overt; if not, one can insert a “mock presupposition” to question with the sumti tcita (selma'o BAI) word {{vla|ji'u}}; {{jbo|ji'uku}} thus explicitly refers to an unexpressed assumption, and {{jbo|ji'una'iku}} metalinguistically says that something is wrong with that assumption. (See [[#chapter-sumti-tcita|this chapter]].)

Scale errors and category errors can be similarly expressed with selma'o BAI. 
{{vla|le'a}} has meaning 
“of category/class/type X”, 
{{vla|ci'u}} has meaning 

“on scale X”, and 
{{vla|ci'e}}, based on 
{{vla|ciste}}, can be used to talk about universes of discourse defined either as systems or sets of components, as shown in 
[[#section-truth-questions|this section]]. 
{{vla|kai}} and 
{{vla|la'u}} also exist in BAI for discussing other quality and quantity errors.

We have to make particular note of potential problems in the areas of undue quantity and incorrect scale/category. Assertions about the relationships between gismu are among the basic substance of the language. It is thus invalid to logically require that if something is blue, that it is colored, or if it is not-blue, then it is some other color. In Lojban, 
{{vla|blanu}} ( 
“blue”) is not explicitly defined as a 
{{vla|skari}} ( 
“color”). Similarly, it is not implicit that the opposite of 
“good” is 
“bad”.

This mutual independence of gismu is only an ideal. Pragmatically, people will categorize things based on their world-views. We will write dictionary definitions that will relate gismu, unfortunately including some of these world-view assumptions. Lojbanists should try to minimize these assumptions, but this seems a likely area where logical rules will break down (or where Sapir-Whorf effects will be made evident). In terms of negation, however, it is vital that we clearly preserve the capability of denying a presumably obvious scale or category assumption.

Solecisms, grammatical and spelling errors will be marked by marking the offending word or phrase with 
{{vla|na'i}} (in the manner of any selma'o UI cmavo). In this sense, 
{{vla|na'i}} becomes equivalent to the English metalinguistic marker 
“[sic]”. Purists may choose to use ZOI or LOhU/LEhU quotes or 
{{vla|sa'a}}-marked corrections to avoid repeating a truly unparsable passage, especially if a computer is to analyze the speech/text. See 

[[#section-parentheses|this section]] for explanations of these usages.

In summary, metalinguistic negation will typically take the form of referring to a previous statement and marking it with one or more 
{{vla|na'i}} to indicate what metalinguistic errors have been made, and then repeating the statement with corrections. References to previous statements may be full repetitions, or may use members of selma'o GOhA. 
{{vla|na'i}} at the beginning of a statement merely says that something is inappropriate about the statement, without specificity.

In normal use, metalinguistic negation requires that a corrected statement follow the negated statement. In Lojban, however, it is possible to completely and unambiguously specify metalinguistic errors without correcting them. It will eventually be seen whether an uncorrected metalinguistic negation remains an acceptable form in Lojban. In such a statement, metalinguistic expression would involve an ellipsis not unlike that of tenseless expression.

Note that metalinguistic negation gives us another kind of legitimate negative answer to a 

{{vla|xu}} question (See [[#section-truth-questions|this section]]). 
{{vla|na'i}} will be used when something about the questioned statement is inappropriate, such as in questions like 
“Have you stopped beating your wife?”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-SfSU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-SfSU}}
{{judri|c15e10d15}}
:'''xu do sisti lezu'o do rapydarxi ledo fetspe'''
:<code>Have you ceased the activity of repeat-hitting your female-spouse?</code>

Responses could include:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHJJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHJJ}}
{{judri|c15e10d16}}
:'''na'i go'i'''
:''The bridi as a whole is inappropriate in some way.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHKe}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHKe}}
{{judri|c15e10d17}}
:'''go'i na'i'''
:''The selbri ({{vla|sisti}}) is inappropriate in some way.''

One can also specifically qualify the metalinguistic negation, by explicitly repeating the erroneous portion of the bridi to be metalinguistically negated, or adding on of the selma'o BAI qualifiers mentioned above:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ANpd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ANpd}}
{{judri|c15e10d18}}
:'''go'i ji'una'iku'''
:''Some presupposition is wrong with the previous bridi.''

Finally, one may metalinguistically affirm a bridi with 
{{vla|jo'a}}, another cmavo of selma'o UI. A common use for 

{{vla|jo'a}} might be to affirm that a particular construction, though unusual or counterintuitive, is in fact correct; another usage would be to disagree with &ndash; by overriding &ndash; a respondent's metalinguistic negation.

{{judri|section-are-all-questions-answered}}
==Summary &ndash; Are All Possible Questions About Negation Now Answered?==

{{dsp|example-random-id-MdRP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MdRP}}
{{judri|c15e11d1}}
:'''na go'i .ije na'e go'i .ije na'i go'i'''

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{judri|chapter-quantifiers}}
= “Who Did You Pass On The Road? Nobody”: Lojban And Logic=
{{image|xml:id="chapter-quantifiers-picture"|The picture for chapter 16|media/chapter-quantifiers.gif}}
{{judri|section-quantifiers-introduction}}
==What's wrong with this picture?==
{{ind|general-imported|nobody|interpretation of}} The following brief dialogue is from {{cite|chapter|Chapter 7}} of 
{{cite|book|Through The Looking Glass}} by Lewis Carroll.

<!-- Perhaps these should be combined into one example. -->

{{dsp|example-random-id-KB90}}
{{judri|c16e1d1}}
“Who did you pass on the road?” the King went on, holding out his hand to the Messenger for some more hay.

{{dsp|example-random-id-1UVT}}
{{judri|c16e1d2}}
“Nobody,” said the Messenger.

{{dsp|example-random-id-x9fC}}
{{judri|c16e1d3}}
“Quite right,” said the King: 
“this young lady saw him too. So of course Nobody walks slower than you.”

{{dsp|example-random-id-105i}}
{{judri|c16e1d4}}
“I do my best,” the Messenger said in a sulky tone. 
“I'm sure nobody walks much faster than I do!”

{{dsp|example-random-id-ANLu}}
{{judri|c16e1d5}}
“He can't do that,” said the King, 
“or else he'd have been here first.”

This nonsensical conversation results because the King insists on treating the word 
“nobody” as a name, a name of somebody. However, the essential nature of the English word 
“nobody” is that it doesn't refer to somebody; or to put the matter another way, there isn't anybody to which it refers.

{{ind|general-imported|nobody|ambiguous interpretations of}} The central point of contradiction in the dialogue arises in 
{{linker|example-random-id-x9fC}}, when the King says 
“... Nobody walks slower than you”. This claim would be plausible if 
“Nobody” were really a name, since the Messenger could only pass someone who does walk more slowly than he. But the Messenger interprets the word 
“nobody” in the ordinary English way, and says (in 
{{linker|example-random-id-105i}}) 
“... nobody walks much faster than I do” (i.e., I walk faster, or as fast as, almost everyone), which the King then again misunderstands. Both the King and the Messenger are correct according to their respective understandings of the ambiguous word 
“nobody/Nobody”.

{{ind|general-imported|nobody|Lojban contrasted with English}} There are Lojban words or phrases corresponding to the problematic English words 
“somebody”, 
“nobody”, 
“anybody”, 
“everybody” (and their counterparts 
“some/no/any/everyone” and 
“some/no/any/everything”), but they obey rules which can often be surprising to English-speakers. The dialogue above simply cannot be translated into Lojban without distortion: the name 
“Nobody” would have to be represented by a Lojban name, which would spoil the perfection of the wordplay. As a matter of fact, this is the desired result: a logical language should not allow two conversationalists to affirm 

“Nobody walks slower than the Messenger” and 
“Nobody walks faster than the Messenger” and both be telling the truth. (Unless, of course, nobody but the Messenger walks at all, or everyone walks at exactly the same speed.)

{{ind|general-imported|logic|resolving ambiguities of &quot;nobody&quot;}} This chapter will explore the Lojban mechanisms that allow the correct and consistent construction of sentences like those in the dialogue. There are no new grammatical constructs explained in this chapter; instead, it discusses the way in which existing facilities that allow Lojban-speakers to resolve problems like the above, using the concepts of modern logic. However, we will not approach the matter from the viewpoint of logicians, although readers who know something of logic will discover familiar notions in Lojban guise.

{{ind|general-imported|logic|limits of}} Although Lojban is called a logical language, not every feature of it is 

“logical”. In particular, the use of 
{{vla|le}} is incompatible with logical reasoning based on the description selbri, because that selbri may not truthfully apply: you cannot conclude from my statement that

{{dsp|example-random-id-4J5Y}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4J5Y}}
{{judri|c16e1d6}}
:'''mi viska le nanmu'''
:<code>I see the-one-I-refer-to-as-the man.</code>
:''I see the man/men.''

that there really is a man; the only thing you can conclude is that there is one thing (or more) that I choose to refer to as a man. You cannot even tell which man is meant for sure without asking me (although communication is served if you already know from the context).

{{ind|general-imported|attitudinals|and logic}}  {{ind|general-imported|logic|and attitudinals}} In addition, the use of attitudinals (See [[#chapter-attitudinals|this chapter]]) often reduces or removes the ability to make deductions about the bridi to which those attitudinals are applied. From the fact that I hope George will win the election, you can conclude nothing about George's actual victory or defeat.

{{judri|section-da-and-zohu}}
==Existential claims, prenexes, and variables==
Let us consider, to begin with, a sentence that is not in the dialogue:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Mxj3}}
{{judri|c16e2d1}}
{{ind|example|something sees me|example}}
Something sees me.

There are two plausible Lojban translations of 
{{linker|example-random-id-Mxj3}}. The simpler one is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-b9pV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-b9pV}}
{{judri|c16e2d2}}
:'''[zo'e] viska mi'''
:<code>Something-unspecified sees me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|something|unspecified definite with &quot;zo'e&quot;}}  {{ind|general-imported|zo'e|as a translation for &quot;something&quot;}} The cmavo 
{{vla|zo'e}} indicates that a sumti has been omitted (indeed, even 
{{vla|zo'e}} itself can be omitted in this case, as explained in 
[[#section-zohe-cohe-series|this section]]) and the listener must fill in the correct value from context. In other words, 
{{linker|example-random-id-b9pV}} means 
“"You-know-what" sees me.”

However, 
{{linker|example-random-id-Mxj3}} is just as likely to assert simply that there is someone who sees me, in which case a correct translation is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-jjLd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jjLd}}
{{judri|c16e2d3}}
:'''da zo'u da viska mi'''
:<code>There-is-an-X such-that X sees me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|zo'e|contrasted with da}}  {{ind|general-imported|da|contrasted with zo'e}}  {{ind|general-imported|existential claims|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|da|as a translation for &quot;something&quot;}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-jjLd}} does not presuppose that the listener knows who sees the speaker, but simply tells the listener that there is someone who sees the speaker. Statements of this kind are called 
“existential claims”. (Formally, the one doing the seeing is not restricted to being a person; it could be an animal or &ndash; in principle &ndash; an inanimate object. We will see in 

[[#section-restricted-claims|this section]] how to represent such restrictions.)

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|notation convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|variables|logical}}  {{ind|general-imported|prenex|syntax of}}  {{ind|general-imported|prenex|explanation}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-jjLd}} has a two-part structure: there is the part 
:{{jbo|da zo'u}}, called the prenex, and the part 
:{{jbo|da viska mi}}, the main bridi. Almost any Lojban bridi can be preceded by a prenex, which syntactically is any number of sumti followed by the cmavo 
{{vla|zo'u}} (of selma'o ZOhU). For the moment, the sumti will consist of one or more of the cmavo 
{{vla|da}}, 
{{vla|de}}, and 
{{vla|di}} (of selma'o KOhA), glossed in the literal translations as 
“X”, 
“Y”, and 
“Z” respectively. By analogy to the terminology of symbolic logic, these cmavo are called 
“variables”.

Here is an example of a prenex with two variables:

{{dsp|example-random-id-t4qI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-t4qI}}
{{judri|c16e2d4}}
{{ind|example|somebody loves somebody|example}}
:'''da de zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>There-is-an-X there-is-a-Y such that X loves Y.</code>
:''Somebody loves somebody.''

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|effect of using multiple different}}  {{ind|general-imported|somebody|contrasted with somebody else}} In 
{{linker|example-random-id-t4qI}}, the literal interpretation of the two variables 
{{vla|da}} and 
{{vla|de}} as 
“there-is-an-X” and 
“there-is-a-Y” tells us that there are two things which stand in the relationship that one loves the other. It might be the case that the supposed two things are really just a single thing that loves itself; nothing in the Lojban version of 
{{linker|example-random-id-t4qI}} rules out that interpretation, which is why the colloquial translation does not say 
“Somebody loves somebody else.” The things referred to by different variables may be different or the same. (We use 
“somebody” here rather than 
“something” for naturalness; lovers and beloveds are usually persons, though the Lojban does not say so.)

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|with multiple appearances in bridi}} It is perfectly all right for the variables to appear more than once in the main bridi:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wBYE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wBYE}}
{{judri|c16e2d5}}
{{ind|example|somebody loves self|example}}
:'''da zo'u da prami da'''
:<code>There-is-an-X such that X loves X</code>
:''Somebody loves himself/herself.''

{{ind|general-imported|da prami de|contrasted with da prami da}}  {{ind|general-imported|da prami da|contrasted with da prami de}} What 
{{linker|example-random-id-wBYE}} claims is fundamentally different from what 
{{linker|example-random-id-t4qI}} claims, because 
:{{jbo|da prami da}} is not structurally the same as 

:{{jbo|da prami de}}. However,

{{dsp|example-random-id-3QV5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3QV5}}
{{judri|c16e2d6}}
:'''de zo'u de prami de'''
:<code>There-is-a-Y such that Y loves Y</code>

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|effect of global substitution}} means exactly the same thing as 
{{linker|example-random-id-wBYE}}; it does not matter which variable is used as long as they are used consistently.

It is not necessary for a variable to be a sumti of the main bridi directly:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ArXX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ArXX}}
{{judri|c16e2d7}}
{{ind|example|somebody's dog|example}}
:'''da zo'u le da gerku cu viska mi'''
:<code>There-is-an-X such-that the of-X dog sees me</code>
:''Somebody's dog sees me''

is perfectly correct even though the 
{{vla|da}} is used only in a possessive construction. (Possessives are explained in 
[[#section-possessive-sumti|this section]].)

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|when not in main bridi}} It is very peculiar, however, even if technically grammatical, for the variable not to appear in the main bridi at all:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mE4m}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mE4m}}
{{judri|c16e2d8}}
{{ind|example|Ralph|example}}
:'''da zo'u la ralf. gerku'''
:''There is something such that Ralph is a dog.''

has a variable bound in a prenex whose relevance to the claim of the following bridi is completely unspecified.

{{judri|section-universal-claims}}
==Universal claims==
What happens if we substitute 
“everything” for 
“something” in 
{{linker|example-random-id-Mxj3}}? We get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-UwYG}}
{{judri|c16e3d1}}
{{ind|example|everything sees me|example}}
Everything sees me.

{{ind|general-imported|universal claims|explanation}} Of course, this example is false, because there are many things which do not see the speaker. It is not easy to find simple truthful examples of so-called universal claims (those which are about everything), so bear with us for a while. (Indeed, some Lojbanists tend to avoid universal claims even in other languages, since they are so rarely true in Lojban.)

The Lojban translation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-UwYG}} is

{{dsp|example-random-id-nraD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nraD}}
{{judri|c16e3d2}}
:'''ro da zo'u da viska mi'''
:<code>For-every X : X sees me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|everything|expressing with &quot;ro da&quot;}} When the variable cmavo 
{{vla|da}} is preceded by 
{{vla|ro}}, the combination means 
“For every X” rather than 
“There is an X”. Superficially, these English formulations look totally unrelated: 
[[#section-quantified-variables|this section]] will bring them within a common viewpoint. For the moment, accept the use of 
:{{jbo|ro da}} for 
“everything” on faith.

Here is a universal claim with two variables:

{{dsp|example-random-id-jSrU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jSrU}}
{{judri|c16e3d3}}
{{ind|example|everything loves everything|example}}
:'''ro da ro de zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>For-every X, for-every Y : X loves Y.</code>
:''Everything loves everything.''

Again, X and Y can represent the same thing, so 
{{linker|example-random-id-jSrU}} does not mean 
“Everything loves everything else.” Furthermore, because the claim is universal, it is about every thing, not merely every person, so we cannot use 
“everyone” or 
“everybody” in the translation.

{{ind|general-imported|universal|mixed claim with existential}}  {{ind|general-imported|existential|mixed claim with universal}}  {{ind|general-imported|mixed claim|definition}} Note that 
{{vla|ro}} appears before both 
{{vla|da}} and 
{{vla|de}}. If 
{{vla|ro}} is omitted before either variable, we get a mixed claim, partly existential like those of 

[[#section-da-and-zohu|this section]], partly universal.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHKm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHKm}}
{{judri|c16e3d4}}
{{ind|example|everything sees something|example}}  
:'''ro da de zo'u da viska de'''
:<code>For-every X, there-is-a-Y : X sees Y.</code>
:''Everything sees something.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHKo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHKo}}
{{judri|c16e3d5}}
{{ind|example|something sees everything|example}}
:'''da ro de zo'u da viska de'''
:<code>There-is-an-X such-that-for-every-Y : X sees Y.</code>
:''Something sees everything.''

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|effect of order in prenex}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHKm}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHKo}} mean completely different things. 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHKm}} says that for everything, there is something which it sees, not necessarily the same thing seen for every seer. 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHKo}}, on the other hand, says that there is a particular thing which can see everything that there is (including itself). Both of these are fairly silly, but they are different kinds of silliness.

There are various possible translations of universal claims in English: sometimes we use 

“anybody/anything” rather than 
“everybody/everything”. Often it makes no difference which of these is used: when it does make a difference, it is a rather subtle one which is explained in 
[[#section-any|this section]].

{{judri|section-restricted-claims}}
==Restricted claims: {{jbo|da poi}}==
{{ind|general-imported|restricted claims|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|universal claims|restricting}} The universal claims of 

[[#section-universal-claims|this section]] are not only false but absurd: there is really very little to be said that is both true and non-trivial about every object whatsoever. Furthermore, we have been glossing over the distinction between 
“everything” and 
“everybody” and the other pairs ending in 
“-thing” and 
“-body”. It is time to bring up the most useful feature of Lojban variables: the ability to restrict their ranges.

{{ind|general-imported|existential claims|restricting}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|use in restricting existential claims}} In Lojban, a variable 
{{vla|da}}, 
{{vla|de}}, or 
{{vla|di}} may be followed by a 
{{vla|poi}} relative clause in order to restrict the range of things that the variable describes. Relative clauses are described in detail in 
[[#chapter-relative-clauses|this chapter]], but the kind we will need at present consist of 
{{vla|poi}} followed by a bridi (often just a selbri) terminated with 
{{vla|ku'o}} or 
{{vla|vau}} (which can usually be elided). Consider the difference between

{{dsp|example-random-id-NPX7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NPX7}}
{{judri|c16e4d1}}
:'''da zo'u da viska la djim.'''
:<code>There-is-an-X : X sees Jim.</code>
:''Something sees Jim.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-I8AF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-I8AF}}
{{judri|c16e4d2}}
:'''da poi prenu zo'u da viska la djim.'''
:<code>There-is-an-X which is-a-person : X sees Jim.</code>
:''Someone sees Jim.''

{{ind|general-imported|something|contrasted with someone}} In 
{{linker|example-random-id-NPX7}}, the variable 
{{vla|da}} can refer to any object whatever; there are no restrictions on it. In 
{{linker|example-random-id-I8AF}}, 
{{vla|da}} is restricted by the 
:{{jbo|poi prenu}} relative clause to persons only, and so 
:{{jbo|da poi prenu}} translates as 
“someone.” (The difference between 
“someone” and 
“somebody” is a matter of English style, with no real counterpart in Lojban.) If 
{{linker|example-random-id-I8AF}} is true, then 
{{linker|example-random-id-NPX7}} must be true, but not necessarily vice versa.

{{ind|general-imported|universal claims|restricting}}  {{ind|general-imported|relative clauses|use in restricting universal claims}} Universal claims benefit even more from the existence of relative clauses. Consider

{{dsp|example-random-id-DFen}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DFen}}
{{judri|c16e4d3}}
{{ind|example|everything breathes|example}}
:'''ro da zo'u da vasxu'''
:<code>For-every X : X breathes</code>
:''Everything breathes''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-njh0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-njh0}}
{{judri|c16e4d4}}
:'''ro da poi gerku zo'u da vasxu'''
:<code>For-every X which is-a-dog : X breathes.</code>
:<code>Every dog breathes.</code>
:<code>Each dog breathes.</code>
:''All dogs breathe.''

{{ind|general-imported|dog breathes}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-DFen}} is a silly falsehood, but 
{{linker|example-random-id-njh0}} is an important truth (at least if applied in a timeless or potential sense: See [[#section-caha|this section]]). Note the various colloquial translations 
“every dog”, 
“each dog”, and 
“all dogs”. They all come to the same thing in Lojban, since what is true of every dog is true of all dogs. 
“All dogs” is treated as an English plural and the others as singular, but Lojban makes no distinction.

If we make an existential claim about dogs rather than a universal one, we get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4BTd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4BTd}}
{{judri|c16e4d5}}
:'''da poi gerku zo'u da vasxu'''
:<code>There-is-an-X which is-a-dog : X breathes.</code>
:''Some dog breathes.''

{{judri|section-prenex-elision}}
==Dropping the prenex==
{{ind|general-imported|prenex|considerations for dropping}} It isn't really necessary for every Lojban bridi involving variables to have a prenex on the front. In fact, none of the examples we've seen so far required prenexes at all! The rule for dropping the prenex is simple: if the variables appear in the same order within the bridi as they did in the prenex, then the prenex is superfluous. However, any 
{{vla|ro}} or 
{{vla|poi}} appearing in the prenex must be transferred to the first occurrence of the variable in the main part of the bridi. Thus, 
{{linker|example-random-id-jjLd}} becomes just:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9zAo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9zAo}}
{{judri|c16e5d1}}
:'''da viska mi'''
:<code>There-is-an-X-which sees me.</code>
:''Something sees me.''

and 
{{linker|example-random-id-njh0}} becomes:

{{dsp|example-random-id-na9C}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-na9C}}
{{judri|c16e5d2}}
:'''ro da poi gerku cu vasxu'''
:<code>For-every X which is-a-dog, it-breathes.</code>
:''Every dog breathes.''

{{ind|general-imported|prenex|effect of order of variables in}}  {{ind|general-imported|prenex|purpose of}} You might well suppose, then, that the purpose of the prenex is to allow the variables in it to appear in a different order than the bridi order, and that would be correct. Consider

{{ind|general-imported|everyone bitten by dog}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-Cfnb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Cfnb}}
{{judri|c16e5d3}}
:'''ro da poi prenu ku'o de poi gerku ku'o zo'u de batci da'''
:<code>For-every X which is-a-person, there-is-a-Y which is-a-dog: Y bites X.</code>

The prenex of 
{{linker|example-random-id-Cfnb}} is like that of 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHKm}} (but with relative clauses): it notes that the following bridi is true of every person with respect to some dog, not necessarily the same dog for each. But in the main bridi part, the 
{{vla|de}} appears before the 
{{vla|da}}. Therefore, the true translation is

{{dsp|example-random-id-KLAr}}
{{judri|c16e5d4}}
Every person is bitten by some dog (or other).

If we tried to omit the prenex and move the 
{{vla|ro}} and the relative clauses into the main bridi, we would get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-c9bq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-c9bq}}
{{judri|c16e5d5}}
{{ind|example|dog bites|example}}
{{ind|example|Fido|example}} 
:'''de poi gerku cu batci ro da poi prenu'''
:<code>There-is-a-Y which is-a-dog which-bites every X which is-a-person</code>
:''Some dog bites everyone.''

which has the structure of 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHKo}}: it says that there is a dog (call him Fido) who bites, has bitten, or will bite every person that has ever existed! We can safely rule out Fido's existence, and say that 
{{linker|example-random-id-c9bq}} is false, while agreeing to 
{{linker|example-random-id-Cfnb}}.

{{ind|general-imported|universal claims|dangers of using}} Even so, 
{{linker|example-random-id-Cfnb}} is most probably false, since some people never experience dogbite. Examples like 5.3 and 4.4 (might there be some dogs which never have breathed, because they died as embryos?) indicate the danger in Lojban of universal claims even when restricted. In English we are prone to say that 

“Everyone says” or that 
“Everybody does” or that 
“Everything is” when in fact there are obvious counterexamples which we are ignoring for the sake of making a rhetorical point. Such statements are plain falsehoods in Lojban, unless saved by a context (such as tense) which implicitly restricts them.

{{ind|general-imported|re-ordering logical variables with se}}  {{ind|general-imported|se|using to re-order logical variables}} How can we express 
{{linker|example-random-id-Cfnb}} in Lojban without a prenex? Since it is the order in which variables appear that matters, we can say:

{{dsp|example-random-id-y90e}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-y90e}}
{{judri|c16e5d6}}
:'''ro da poi prenu cu se batci de poi gerku'''
:<code>Every-X which is-a-person is-bitten-by some-Y which is-a-dog.</code>

using the conversion operator 
{{vla|se}} (explained in 
[[#section-place-conversion|this section]]) to change the selbri 
{{vla|batci}} ( 
“bites”) into 
:{{jbo|se batci}} ( 
“is bitten by”). The translation given in 
{{linker|example-random-id-KLAr}} uses the corresponding strategy in English, since English does not have prenexes (except in strained 
“logician's English”). This implies that a sentence with both a universal and an existential variable can't be freely converted with 

{{vla|se}}; one must be careful to preserve the order of the variables.

{{ind|general-imported|poi|dropping from multiple appearances on logical variables}}  {{ind|general-imported|ro|dropping from multiple appearances on logical variables}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical variables|with poi|in multiple appearances}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical variables|with ro|in multiple appearances}} If a variable occurs more than once, then any 
{{vla|ro}} or 
{{vla|poi}} decorations are moved only to the first occurrence of the variable when the prenex is dropped. For example,

{{dsp|example-random-id-4nqt}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4nqt}}
{{judri|c16e5d7}}
{{ind|example|weapon against self|example}}
:'''di poi prenu zo'u ti xarci di di'''
:<code>There-is-a-Z which is-a-person : this-thing is-a-weapon for-use-against-Z by-Z</code>
:''This is a weapon for someone to use against himself/herself.''

(in which 
{{vla|di}} is used rather than 
{{vla|da}} just for variety) loses its prenex as follows:

{{dsp|example-random-id-CseH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-CseH}}
{{judri|c16e5d8}}
:'''ti xarci di poi prenu ku'o di'''
:<code>This-thing is-a-weapon-for-use-against some-Z which is-a-person by-Z.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|prenex|dropping for terseness}} As the examples in this section show, dropping the prenex makes for terseness of expression often even greater than that of English (Lojban is meant to be an unambiguous language, not necessarily a terse or verbose one), provided the rules are observed.

{{judri|section-quantified-variables}}
==Variables with generalized quantifiers==
{{ind|general-imported|quantifiers|with logical variables}} So far, we have seen variables with either nothing in front, or with the cmavo 
{{vla|ro}} in front. Now 
{{vla|ro}} is a Lojban number, and means 
“all”; thus 
:{{jbo|ro prenu}} means 

“all persons”, just as 

:{{jbo|re prenu}} means 
“two persons”. In fact, unadorned 
{{vla|da}} is also taken to have an implicit number in front of it, namely 
{{vla|su'o}}, which means 
“at least one”. Why is this? Consider 
{{linker|example-random-id-jjLd}} again, this time with an explicit 
{{vla|su'o}}:

{{ind|general-imported|something|expressing using &quot;su'o&quot;}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-TI8K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TI8K}}
{{judri|c16e6d1}}
{{ind|example|something sees me|example}}
:'''su'o da zo'u da viska mi'''
:<code>For-at-least-one X : X sees me.</code>
:''Something sees me.''

From this version of 
{{linker|example-random-id-jjLd}}, we understand the speaker's claim to be that of all the things that there are, at least one of them sees him or her. The corresponding universal claim, 
{{linker|example-random-id-nraD}}, says that of all the things that exist, every one of them can see the speaker.

{{ind|general-imported|numbers|on logical variables}} Any other number can be used instead of 
{{vla|ro}} or 
{{vla|su'o}} to precede a variable. Then we get claims like:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3C69}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3C69}}
{{judri|c16e6d2}}
:'''re da zo'u da viska mi'''
:<code>For-two-Xes : X sees me.</code>
:''Two things see me.''

{{ind|general-imported|numbers|English contrasted with Lojban on exactness}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|Lojban contrasted with English on exactness}} This means that exactly two things, no more or less, saw the speaker on the relevant occasion. In English, we might take 
“Two things see me” to mean that at least two things see the speaker, but there might be more; in Lojban, though, that claim would have to be made as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-mSzo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-mSzo}}
{{judri|c16e6d3}}
:'''su'ore da zo'u da viska mi'''
:<code>For-at-least-two Xes : X sees me.</code>

which would be false if nothing, or only one thing, saw the speaker, but not otherwise. We note the 
{{vla|su'o}} here meaning 
“at least”; 
{{vla|su'o}} by itself is short for 
:{{jbo|su'opa}} where 
{{vla|pa}} means 
“one”, as is explained in 
[[#section-approximation|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|prenex|removing when numeric quantifiers present}} The prenex may be removed from 
{{linker|example-random-id-3C69}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-mSzo}} as from the others, leading to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2r5v}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2r5v}}
{{judri|c16e6d4}}
:'''re da viska mi'''
:''Two Xes see me.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-GWoD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GWoD}}
{{judri|c16e6d5}}
:'''su'ore da viska mi'''
:<code>At-least-two Xes see me.</code>

respectively, subject to the rules prescribed in 
[[#section-prenex-elision|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|restricted variable|compared with indefinite description}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite description|compared with restricted variable}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite description|definition}} Now we can explain the constructions 
:{{jbo|ro prenu}} for “all persons” and :{{jbo|re prenu}} for “two persons” which were casually mentioned at the beginning of this Section. In fact, 
:{{jbo|ro prenu}}, a so-called “indefinite description”, is shorthand for {{jbo|ro DA poi prenu}}, where “DA” represents a fictitious variable that hasn't been used yet and will not be used in future. (Even if all three of 
{{vla|da}}, {{vla|de}}, and {{vla|di}} have been used up, it does not matter, for there are ways of getting more variables, discussed in 
[[#section-notes-on-variables|this section]].) So in fact

{{dsp|example-random-id-Kr4S}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Kr4S}}
{{judri|c16e6d6}}
:'''re prenu cu viska mi'''
:''Two persons see me.''

is short for

{{dsp|example-random-id-E6wI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-E6wI}}
{{judri|c16e6d7}}
:'''re da poi prenu cu viska mi'''
:<code>Two Xes which are-persons see me.</code>

which in turn is short for:

{{dsp|example-random-id-u1sb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-u1sb}}
{{judri|c16e6d8}}
:'''re da poi prenu zo'u da viska mi'''
:<code>For-two Xes which are-persons : X sees me.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|order of variables|in moving to prenex}} Note that when we move more than one variable to the prenex (along with its attached relative clause), we must make sure that the variables are in the same order in the prenex as in the bridi proper.

{{judri|section-quantifier-grouping}}
==Grouping of quantifiers==
{{ind|general-imported|distribution of quantified sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite sumti|multiple in sentence}} Let us consider a sentence containing two quantifier expressions neither of which is 
{{vla|ro}} or 
{{vla|su'o}} (remembering that 
{{vla|su'o}} is implicit where no explicit quantifier is given):

{{dsp|example-random-id-Uovr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Uovr}}
{{judri|c16e7d1}}
{{ind|example|dogs bite|example}}
{{ind|example|three dogs bite two men|example}}  
:'''ci gerku cu batci re nanmu'''
:''Three dogs bite two men.''

{{ind|general-imported|multiple indefinite sumti|meaning}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite sumti|meaning when multiple in sentence}} The question raised by 
{{linker|example-random-id-Uovr}} is, does each of the dogs bite the same two men, or is it possible that there are two different men per dog, for six men altogether? If the former interpretation is taken, the number of men involved is fixed at two; but if the latter, then the speaker has to be taken as saying that there might be any number of men between two and six inclusive. Let us transform 
{{linker|example-random-id-Uovr}} step by step as we did with 
{{linker|example-random-id-Kr4S}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-neNT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-neNT}}
{{judri|c16e7d2}}
:'''ci da poi gerku cu batci re de poi nanmu'''
:<code>Three Xes which are-dogs bite two Ys which are-men.</code>

(Note that we need separate variables 
{{vla|da}} and 
{{vla|de}}, because of the rule that says each indefinite description gets a variable never used before or since.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-Iuj2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Iuj2}}
{{judri|c16e7d3}}
:'''ci da poi gerku ku'o re de poi nanmu zo'u da batci de'''
:<code>For-three Xes which are-dogs, for-two Ys which are-men : X bites Y.</code>

Here we see that indeed each of the dogs is said to bite two men, and it might be different men each time; a total of six biting events altogether.

{{ind|general-imported|multiple indefinite sumti|effect of re-ordering in sentence}} How then are we to express the other interpretation, in which just two men are involved? We cannot just reverse the order of variables in the prenex to

{{dsp|example-random-id-4Qxe}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4Qxe}}
{{judri|c16e7d4}}
:'''re de poi nanmu ku'o ci da poi gerku zo'u da batci de'''
:<code>For-two Ys which are-men, for-three Xes which are-dogs, X bites Y</code>

for although we have now limited the number of men to exactly two, we end up with an indeterminate number of dogs, from three to six. The distinction is called a 
“scope distinction”: in {{linker|example-random-id-neNT}}, {{jbo|ci gerku}} is said to have wider scope than {{jbo|re nanmu}}, and therefore precedes it in the prenex. In {{linker|example-random-id-4Qxe}} the reverse is true.

{{ind|general-imported|termset|effect on scope of multiple indefinite sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple indefinite sumti scope|in termset}}  {{ind|general-imported|multiple indefinite sumti|expressing with equal scope}} The solution is to use a termset, which is a group of terms either joined by 
{{vla|ce'e}} (of selma'o CEhE) between each term, or else surrounded by 
{{vla|nu'i}} (of selma'o NUhI) on the front and 
{{vla|nu'u}} (of selma'o NUhU) on the rear. Terms (which are either sumti or sumti prefixed by tense or modal tags) that are grouped into a termset are understood to have equal scope:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JbVH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JbVH}}
{{judri|c16e7d5}}
:'''ci gerku ce'e re nanmu cu batci'''
:'''nu'i ci gerku re nanmu [nu'u] cu batci'''
:<code>Three dogs [plus] two men, bite.</code>

which picks out two groups, one of three dogs and the other of two men, and says that every one of the dogs bites each of the men. The second Lojban version uses forethought; note that 
{{vla|nu'u}} is an elidable terminator, and in this case can be freely elided.

{{ind|general-imported|ro|effect of order when multiple in sentence}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite sumti|compared to sumti with lo}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti with lo|compared to indefinite sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantified sumti|different types contrasted for scope for distribution}} What about descriptors, like 
:{{jbo|ci lo gerku}}, 
:{{jbo|le nanmu}} or 
:{{jbo|re le ci mlatu}}? They too can be grouped in termsets, but usually need not be, except for the 
{{vla|lo}} case which functions like the case without a descriptor. Unless an actual quantifier precedes it, 
:{{jbo|le nanmu}} means 
:{{jbo|ro le nanmu}}, as is explained in 
[[#section-quantified-descriptions|this section]]. Two sumti with 
{{vla|ro}} quantifiers are independent of order, so:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MADY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MADY}}
{{judri|c16e7d6}}
:'''[ro] le ci gerku cu batci [ro] le re nanmu'''
:<code>[All of] the three dogs bite [all of] the two men.</code>

means that each of the dogs specified bites each of the men specified, for six acts of biting altogether. However, if there is an explicit quantifier before 
{{vla|le}} other than 
{{vla|ro}}, the problems of this section reappear.

{{judri|section-any}}
==The problem of “any”==
Consider the English sentence
{{ind|general-imported|any|as a translation problem}} 

{{dsp|example-random-id-R4mX}}
{{judri|c16e8d1}}
{{ind|example|anyone who goes|walks|example}} 
Anyone who goes to the store, walks across the field.

Using the facilities already discussed, a plausible translation might be

{{dsp|example-random-id-7Kn8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7Kn8}}
{{judri|c16e8d2}}
:'''ro da poi klama le zarci cu cadzu le foldi'''
:<code>All X such-that-it goes-to the store walks-on the field.</code>
:''Everyone who goes to the store walks across the field.''

{{ind|general-imported|everyone|contrasted with anyone in assumption of existence}}  {{ind|general-imported|anyone|contrasted with everyone in assumption of existence}}  {{ind|general-imported|any|as a restricted universal claim}} But there is a subtle difference between 
{{linker|example-random-id-R4mX}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-7Kn8}}. 
{{linker|example-random-id-7Kn8}} tells us that, in fact, there are people who go to the store, and that they walk across the field. A sumti of the type 
:{{jbo|ro da poi klama}} requires that there are things which 
{{vla|klama}}: Lojban universal claims always imply the corresponding existential claims as well. 

{{linker|example-random-id-R4mX}}, on the other hand, does not require that there are any people who go to the store: it simply states, conditionally, that if there is anyone who goes to the store, he or she walks across the field as well. This conditional form mirrors the true Lojban translation of 

{{linker|example-random-id-R4mX}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-BwU7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BwU7}}
{{judri|c16e8d3}}
:'''ro da zo'u da go klama le zarci gi cadzu le foldi'''
:<code>For-every X: X is-a-goer-to the store if-and-only-if is-a-walker-on the field.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|any|as a universal claim|later restricted}} Although 
{{linker|example-random-id-BwU7}} is a universal claim as well, its universality only implies that there are objects of some sort or another in the universe of discourse. Because the claim is conditional, nothing is implied about the existence of goers-to-the-store or of walkers-on-the-field, merely that any entity which is one is also the other.

{{ind|general-imported|any|as an existential claim}} There is another use of 
“any” in English that is not universal but existential. Consider

{{dsp|example-random-id-7Eu9}}
{{judri|c16e8d4}}
:''I need any box that is bigger than this one.''

{{ind|general-imported|any box}}  {{ind|general-imported|need any box}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-7Eu9}} does not at all mean that I need every box bigger than this one, for indeed I do not; I require only one box. But the naive translation

{{dsp|example-random-id-KHya}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KHya}}
{{judri|c16e8d5}}
:'''mi nitcu da poi tanxe gi'e bramau ti'''
:<code>I need some-X which is-a-box and is-bigger-than this-one</code>

does not work either, because it asserts that there really is such a box, as the prenex paraphrase demonstrates:

{{dsp|example-random-id-fAo5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-fAo5}}
{{judri|c16e8d6}}
:'''da poi tanxe gi'e bramau ti zo'u mi nitcu da'''
:<code>There-is-an-X which is-a-box and is-bigger-than this : I need X.</code>

What to do? Well, the x2 place of 
{{vla|nitcu}} can be filled with an event as well as an object, and in fact 
{{linker|example-random-id-KHya}} can also be paraphrased as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-e7ta}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-e7ta}}
{{judri|c16e8d7}}
:'''mi nitcu lo nu mi ponse lo tanxe poi bramau ti'''
:<code>I need an event-of I possess some box(es) which-are bigger-than this-one.</code>

Rewritten using variables, {{linker|example-random-id-e7ta}} becomes

{{dsp|example-random-id-4Pz8}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4Pz8}}
{{judri|c16e8d8}}
:'''mi nitcu lo nu da zo'u da se ponse mi gi'e tanxe gi'e bramau ti'''
:<code>I need an event-of there-being an-X such-that : X is-possessed-by me and is-a-box and is-bigger-than this-thing.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|logical variables|explicitly placing in outer prenex}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical variables|implicit placement in smallest enclosing bridi prenex}}  {{ind|general-imported|prenex|internal to a bridi}} So we see that a prenex can be attached to a bridi that is within a sentence. By default, a variable always behaves as if it is bound in the prenex which (notionally) is attached to the smallest enclosing bridi, and its scope does not extend beyond that bridi. However, the variable may be placed in an outer prenex explicitly:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7KKM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7KKM}}
{{judri|c16e8d9}}
:'''da poi tanxe gi'e bramau ti zo'u mi nitcu le nu mi ponse da'''
:<code>There-is-an-X which is-a-box and is-bigger-than this-one such-that : I need the event-of my possessing X.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|existential variable|in main bridi contrasted with in abstraction}}  {{ind|general-imported|existential variable|in abstraction contrasted with in main bridi}} But what are the implications of 
{{linker|example-random-id-e7ta}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-7KKM}}? The main difference is that in 
{{linker|example-random-id-7KKM}}, the 
{{vla|da}} is said to exist in the real world of the outer bridi; but in 

{{linker|example-random-id-e7ta}}, the existence is only within the inner bridi, which is a mere event that need not necessarily come to pass. So 
{{linker|example-random-id-7KKM}} means

{{dsp|example-random-id-xC32}}
{{judri|c16e8d10}}
There's a box, bigger than this one, that I need

{{ind|general-imported|any|expressing as existential by variable in subordinate bridi}} which is what 
{{linker|example-random-id-fAo5}} says, whereas 
{{linker|example-random-id-e7ta}} turns out to be an effective translation of our original 
{{linker|example-random-id-R4mX}}. So uses of 
“any” that aren't universal end up being reflected by variables bound in the prenex of a subordinate bridi.

{{judri|section-negation-boundaries}}
==Negation boundaries==
{{ind|general-imported|&quot;there is a Y&quot;|expression|notation convention}} This section, as well as 
[[#section-connectives|this section]] through 
[[#section-demorgans-law|this section]], are in effect a continuation of 
[[#chapter-negation|this chapter]], introducing features of Lojban negation that require an understanding of prenexes and variables. In the examples below, 
“there is a Y” and the like must be understood as “there is at least one Y, possibly more”.

{{ind|general-imported|bridi negation|two forms of}} As explained in 
[[#section-bridi-negation|this section]], the negation of a bridi is usually accomplished by inserting 
{{vla|na}} at the beginning of the selbri:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hBRH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hBRH}}
{{judri|c16e9d1}}
:'''mi na klama le zarci'''
:<code>I [false] go-to the store.</code>
:<code>It is false that I go to the store.</code>
:''I don't go to the store.''

The other form of bridi negation is expressed by using the compound cmavo {{jbo|naku}} in the prenex, which is identified and compounded by the lexer before looking at the sentence grammar. In Lojban grammar, {{jbo|naku}} is then treated like a sumti. In a prenex, {{jbo|naku}} means precisely the same thing as the logician's “it is not the case that” in a similar English context. (Outside of a prenex, {{jbo|naku}} is also grammatically treated as a single entity &ndash; the equivalent of a sumti &ndash; but does not have this exact meaning; we'll discuss these other situations in [[#section-na-outside-prenex|this section]].)

{{ind|general-imported|external bridi negation|compared to internal bridi negation}}  {{ind|general-imported|internal bridi negation|compared to external bridi negation}}  {{ind|general-imported|internal bridi negation|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|external bridi negation|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi negation|na before selbri compared to naku in prenex}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi negation|naku in prenex compared to na before selbri}} To represent a bridi negation using a prenex, remove the 
{{vla|na}} from before the selbri and place 
:{{jbo|naku}} at the left end of the prenex. This form is called “external bridi negation”, as opposed to “internal bridi negation” using {{vla|na}}. The prenex version of {{linker|example-random-id-hBRH}} is

{{dsp|example-random-id-IH8J}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-IH8J}}
{{judri|c16e9d2}}
:'''naku zo'u la djan. klama'''
:<code>It is not the case that: John comes.</code>
:''It is false that: John comes.''

{{ind|general-imported|negation in prenex|effects of position}} However, {{jbo|naku}} can appear at other points in the prenex as well. Compare

{{dsp|example-random-id-cy6j}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cy6j}}
{{judri|c16e9d3}}
{{ind|example|nothing sits|example}}
:'''naku de zo'u de zutse'''
:<code>It is not the case that: for some Y, Y sits.</code>
:<code>It is false that: for at least one Y, Y sits.</code>
:<code>It is false that something sits.</code>
:''Nothing sits.''

with

{{dsp|example-random-id-2Fw3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2Fw3}}
{{judri|c16e9d4}}
:'''su'ode naku zo'u de zutse'''
:<code>For at least one Y, it is false that: Y sits.</code>
:''There is something that doesn't sit.''

The relative position of negation and quantification terms within a prenex has a drastic effect on meaning. Starting without a negation, we can have:

{{dsp|example-random-id-21Y5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-21Y5}}
{{judri|c16e9d5}}
{{ind|example|everybody loves something|example}}
:'''roda su'ode zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>For every X, there is a Y, such that X loves Y.</code>
:''Everybody loves at least one thing (each, not necessarily the same thing).''

or:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Tj99}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Tj99}}
{{judri|c16e9d6}}
{{ind|example|something is loved by everybody|example}}
:'''su'ode roda zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>There is a Y, such that for each X, X loves Y.</code>
:''There is at least one particular thing that is loved by everybody.''

The simplest form of bridi negation to interpret is one where the negation term is at the beginning of the prenex:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1LqV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1LqV}}
{{judri|c16e9d7}}
:'''naku roda su'ode zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>It is false that: for every X, there is a Y, such that: X loves Y.</code>
:<code>It is false that: everybody loves at least one thing.</code>
:''(At least) someone doesn't love anything.''

the negation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-21Y5}}, and

{{dsp|example-random-id-u1jY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-u1jY}}
{{judri|c16e9d8}}
:'''naku su'ode roda zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>It is false that: there is a Y such that for each X, X loves Y.</code>
:<code>It is false that: there is at least one thing that is loved by everybody.</code>
:''There isn't any one thing that everybody loves.''

the negation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-Tj99}}.

{{ind|general-imported|inversion of quantifiers|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|inversion of quantifiers|in moving negation boundary}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation boundary|effect of moving}} The rules of formal logic require that, to move a negation boundary within a prenex, you must 
“invert any quantifier” that the negation boundary passes across. Inverting a quantifier means that any 
{{vla|ro}} (all) is changed to 
{{vla|su'o}} (at least one) and vice versa. Thus, 
{{linker|example-random-id-1LqV}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-u1jY}} can be restated as, respectively:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cJLQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cJLQ}}
{{judri|c16e9d9}}
:'''su'oda naku su'ode zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>For some X, it is false that: there is a Y such that: X loves Y.</code>
:''There is somebody who doesn't love anything.''

and:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hBXT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hBXT}}
{{judri|c16e9d10}}
:'''rode naku roda zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>For every Y, it is false that: for every X, X loves Y.</code>
:''For each thing, it is not true that everybody loves it.''

Another movement of the negation boundary produces:

{{dsp|example-random-id-w6XF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-w6XF}}
{{judri|c16e9d11}}
:'''su'oda rode naku zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>There is an X such that, for every Y, it is false that X loves Y.</code>
:''There is someone who, for each thing, doesn't love that thing.''

and

{{dsp|example-random-id-JY08}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JY08}}
{{judri|c16e9d12}}
:'''rode su'oda naku zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>For every Y, there is an X, such that it is false that: X loves Y.</code>
:''For each thing there is someone who doesn't love it.''

{{ind|general-imported|inversion of quantifiers on passing negation boundary|rationale for}} Investigation will show that, indeed, each transformation preserves the meanings of 
{{linker|example-random-id-1LqV}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-u1jY}}.

{{ind|general-imported|negation boundary|and zero}}  {{ind|general-imported|zero|relation to negation boundary}} The quantifier 
{{vla|no}} (meaning 
“zero of”) also involves a negation boundary. To transform a bridi containing a variable quantified with 
{{vla|no}}, we must first expand it. Consider

{{dsp|example-random-id-qCph}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qCph}}
{{judri|c16e9d13}}
:'''noda rode zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>There is no X, for every Y, such that X loves Y.</code>
:''Nobody loves everything.''

which is negated by:

{{dsp|example-random-id-fpeW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-fpeW}}
{{judri|c16e9d14}}
:'''naku noda rode zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>It is false that: there is no X that, for every Y, X loves Y.</code>
:''It is false that there is nobody who loves everything.''

{{ind|general-imported|naku su'oda|as expansion of noda}}  {{ind|general-imported|noda|expanding to naku su'oda}}  {{ind|general-imported|&quot;no&quot; quantifier|expanding}}  {{ind|general-imported|expanding &quot;no&quot; quantifier}} We can simplify {{linker|example-random-id-fpeW}} by transforming the prenex. To move the negation phrase within the prenex, we must first expand the {{vla|no}} quantifier. Thus “for no x” means the same thing as “it is false for some x”, and the corresponding Lojban {{vla|noda}} can be replaced by {{jbo|naku su'oda}}. Making this substitution, we get:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xTie}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xTie}}
{{judri|c16e9d15}}
:'''naku naku su'oda rode zo'u da prami de'''

:''It is false that it is false that: for an X, for every Y: X loves Y.''

Adjacent pairs of negation boundaries in the prenex can be dropped, so this means the same as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-y7NU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-y7NU}}
{{judri|c16e9d16}}
:'''su'oda rode zo'u da prami de'''
:<code>There is an X such that, for every Y, X loves Y.</code>
:''At least one person loves everything.''

which is clearly the desired contradiction of 
{{linker|example-random-id-qCph}}.

{{ind|general-imported|double negatives|effect of interactions between quantifiers and negation on}}  {{ind|general-imported|interactions between quantifiers and negation|effect}} The interactions between quantifiers and negation mean that you cannot eliminate double negatives that are not adjacent. You must first move the negation phrases so that they are adjacent, inverting any quantifiers they cross, and then the double negative can be eliminated.

{{judri|section-connectives}}
==bridi negation and logical connectives==

{{ind|general-imported|logical connectives and bridi negation}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi negation and logical connectives}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives and negation|caveat for logic chapter discussions}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation and logical connectives|caveat for logic chapter discussions}} A complete discussion of logical connectives appears in 
[[#chapter-connectives|this chapter]]. What is said here is intentionally quite incomplete and makes several oversimplifications.

A logical connective is a cmavo or compound cmavo. In this chapter, we will make use of the logical connectives 
“and” and 
“or” (where 
“or” really means 
“and/or”, 
“either or both”). The following simplified recipes explain how to make some logical connectives:
* {{ind|general-imported|logical connectives|recipes|simplified for logic chapter discussion}} To logically connect two Lojban sumti with “and”, put them both in the bridi and separate them with the cmavo {{vla|e}}.
*To logically connect two Lojban bridi with “and”, replace the regular separator cmavo {{vla|i}} with the compound cmavo {{vla|.ije}}.
*To logically connect two Lojban sumti with “or”, put them both in the bridi and separate them with the cmavo {{vla|a}}.
*To logically connect two Lojban bridi with “or”, replace the regular separator cmavo {{vla|i}} with the compound cmavo {{vla|.ija}}.

More complex logical connectives also exist; in particular, one may place 

{{vla|na}} before 
{{vla|e}} or 
{{vla|a}}, or between 
{{vla|i}} and 
{{vla|je}} or 
{{vla|ja}}; likewise, one may place 
{{vla|nai}} at the end of a connective. Both 
{{vla|na}} and 
{{vla|nai}} have negative effects on the sumti or bridi being connected. Specifically, 
{{vla|na}} negates the first or left-hand sumti or bridi, and 
{{vla|nai}} negates the second or right-hand one.

Whenever a logical connective occurs in a sentence, that sentence can be expanded into two sentences by repeating the common terms and joining the sentences by a logical connective beginning with 
{{vla|i}}. Thus the following sentence:

{{dsp|example-random-id-jmDS}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-jmDS}}
{{judri|c16e10d1}}
:'''mi .e do klama ti'''
:''I and you come here.''

can be expanded to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-KTQH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-KTQH}}
{{judri|c16e10d2}}
:'''mi klama ti .ije do klama ti'''
:''I come here, and, you come here.''

The same type of expansion can be performed for any logical connective, with any valid combination of 
{{vla|na}} or 
{{vla|nai}} attached. No change in meaning occurs under such a transformation.

Clearly, if we know what negation means in the expanded sentence forms, then we know what it means in all of the other forms. But what does negation mean between sentences?

{{ind|general-imported|negation between sentences|meaning of}}  {{ind|general-imported|bridi negation|compared with negation between sentences}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation between sentences|compared with bridi negation}} The mystery is easily solved. A negation in a logical expression is identical to the corresponding bridi negation, with the negator placed at the beginning of the prenex. Thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pLiB}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pLiB}}
{{judri|c16e10d3}}
:'''mi .enai do prami roda'''
:''I, and not you, love everything.''

expands to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-h6Wz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-h6Wz}}
{{judri|c16e10d4}}
:'''mi prami roda .ijenai do prami roda'''
:<code>I love everything, and-not, you love everything.</code>

and then into prenex form as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-JxDJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-JxDJ}}
{{judri|c16e10d5}}
:'''roda zo'u mi prami da .ije naku zo'u do prami da'''
:''For each thing: I love it, and it is false that you love (the same) it.''

{{ind|general-imported|quantifier scope|in multiple connected sentences}} By the rules of predicate logic, the 
{{vla|ro}} quantifier on 
{{vla|da}} has scope over both sentences. That is, once you've picked a value for 
{{vla|da}} for the first sentence, it stays the same for both sentences. (The 
{{vla|da}} continues with the same fixed value until a new paragraph or a new prenex resets the meaning.)

Thus the following example has the indicated translation:

{{dsp|example-random-id-yCA1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-yCA1}}
{{judri|c16e10d6}}
:'''su'oda zo'u mi prami da .ije naku zo'u do prami da'''
:<code>For at least one thing: I love that thing. And it is false that: you love that (same) thing.</code>
:''There is something that I love that you don't.''

{{ind|general-imported|prenex manipulation|rules}} If you remember only two rules for prenex manipulation of negations, you won't go wrong:
* {{ind|general-imported|prenex manipulation|moving naku past bound variable}} Within a prenex, whenever you move {{jbo|naku}} past a bound variable (da, de, di, etc.), you must invert the quantifier.
* {{ind|general-imported|prenex manipulation|exporting na from left of prenex}}  {{ind|general-imported|prenex manipulation|importing na from selbri}} A {{vla|na}} before the selbri is always transformed into a {{jbo|naku}} at the left-hand end of the prenex, and vice versa.

{{judri|section-na-outside-prenex}}
==Using {{jbo|naku}} outside a prenex==
Let us consider the English sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-hp0j}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hp0j}}
{{judri|c16e11d1}}
{{ind|example|some do not go to school|example}}
:'''Some children do not go to school.'''

We cannot express this directly with {{vla|na}}; the apparently obvious translation

{{dsp|example-random-id-6mHh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6mHh}}
{{judri|c16e11d2}}
:'''su'oda poi verba na klama su'ode poi ckule'''
:<code>At-least-one X which-are child(ren) [false] go-to at-least-one Y which-are school(s).</code>

when converted to the external negation form produces:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nGTc}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nGTc}}
{{judri|c16e11d3}}
:'''naku zo'u su'oda poi verba cu klama su'ode poi ckule'''
:<code>It is false that some which are children go-to some which are schools.</code>
:''All children don't go to some school (not just some children).''

{{ind|general-imported|contradictory negation|using naku before selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|naku|outside of prenex}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation|form for emulating natural language negation}} Lojban provides a negation form which more closely emulates natural language negation. This involves putting {{jbo|naku}} before the selbri, instead of a {{vla|na}}. {{jbo|naku}} is clearly a contradictory negation, given its parallel with prenex bridi negation. Using {{jbo|naku}}, {{linker|example-random-id-hp0j}} can be expressed as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nvtf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nvtf}}
{{judri|c16e11d4}}
:'''su'oda poi verba naku klama su'ode poi ckule'''
:<code>Some which-are children don't go-to some which-are schools.</code>
:''Some children don't go to a school.''

{{ind|general-imported|naku|compared with sumti in grammar}} Although it is not technically a sumti, {{jbo|naku}} can be used in most of the places where a sumti may appear. We'll see what this means in a moment.

{{ind|general-imported|inverting quantifiers|with movement relative to naku}}  {{ind|general-imported|quantifiers|effect of moving naku}}  {{ind|general-imported|naku|effect on moving quantifiers}}  {{ind|general-imported|naku|as creating a negation boundary}} When you use {{jbo|naku}} within a bridi, you are explicitly creating a negation boundary. As explained in 
[[#section-negation-boundaries|this section]], when a prenex negation boundary expressed by {{jbo|naku}} moves past a quantifier, the quantifier has to be inverted. The same is true for {{jbo|naku}} in the bridi proper. We can move {{jbo|naku}} to any place in the sentence where a sumti can go, inverting any quantifiers that the negation boundary crosses. Thus, the following are equivalent to {{linker|example-random-id-nvtf}} (no good English translations exist):
