{{judri|section-proposed-lerfu-words}}
==Proposed lerfu words &ndash; introduction==
{{ind|general-imported|lerfu words|list of proposed|notation convention}} The following sections contain tables of proposed lerfu words for some of the standard alphabets supported by the Lojban lerfu system. The first column of each list is the lerfu (actually, a Latin-alphabet name sufficient to identify it). The second column is the proposed name-based lerfu word, and the third column is the proposed lerfu word in the system based on using the cmavo of selma'o BY with a shift word.

{{ind|general-imported|proposed lerfu words|as working basis}} These tables are not meant to be authoritative (several authorities within the Lojban community have niggled over them extensively, disagreeing with each other and sometimes with themselves). They provide a working basis until actual usage is available, rather than a final resolution of lerfu word problems. Probably the system presented here will evolve somewhat before settling down into a final, conventional form.

For Latin-alphabet lerfu words, See [[#section-lerfu-liste|this section]] (for Lojban) and 
[[#section-alien-alphabets|this section]] (for non-Lojban Latin-alphabet lerfu).

{{ind|general-imported|Phonetic Alphabet|proposed lerfu words for}}  {{ind|general-imported|ICAO Phonetic Alphabet|proposed lerfu words for}}  {{ind|general-imported|noisy environments|proposed lerfu words for}}  {{ind|general-imported|radio communication|proposed lerfu words for}}  {{ind|general-imported|lerfu words|proposed for radio communication}}  {{ind|general-imported|lerfu words|proposed for noisy environments}} There is a set of English words which are used, by international agreement, as lerfu words (for the English alphabet) over the radio, or in noisy situations where the utmost clarity is required. Formally they are known as the 
“ICAO Phonetic Alphabet”, and are used even in non-English-speaking countries.

This table presents the standard English spellings and proposed Lojban versions. The Lojbanizations are not straightforward renderings of the English sounds, but make some concessions both to the English spellings of the words and to the Lojban pronunciations of the lerfu (thus 
:{{jbo|carlis. bu}}, not 
:{{jbo|tcarlis. bu}}).

{{startchapter|{{#var:uni}}}}{{judri|chapter-mekso}}
=lojbau mekso: Mathematical Expressions in Lojban=
{{image|xml:id="chapter-mekso-picture"|The picture for chapter 18|media/chapter-mekso.gif}}
{{judri|section-mekso-introduction}}
==Introductory==
lojbau mekso ( 
“Lojbanic mathematical-expression”) is the part of the Lojban language that is tailored for expressing statements of a mathematical character, or for adding numerical information to non-mathematical statements. Its formal design goals include:
* {{ind|general-imported|mekso goal|for mathematical writing}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso|design goals}} representing all the different forms of expression used by mathematicians in their normal modes of writing, so that a reader can unambiguously read off mathematical text as written with minimal effort and expect a listener to understand it;
* {{ind|general-imported|mekso goal|for common use}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso goal|expandable}} providing a vocabulary of commonly used mathematical terms which can readily be expanded to include newly coined words using the full resources of Lojban;
* {{ind|general-imported|mekso goal|unambiguous}} permitting the formulation, both in writing and in speech, of unambiguous mathematical text;
* {{ind|general-imported|mekso goal|precision}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso goal|coverage}} encompassing all forms of quantified expression found in natural languages, as well as encouraging greater precision in ordinary language situations than natural languages allow.

{{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|and mekso goals}}  {{ind|general-imported|Polish notation|and mekso goals}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso goals|mathematical notation form}} Goal 1 requires that mekso not be constrained to a single notation such as Polish notation or reverse Polish notation, but make provision for all forms, with the most commonly used forms the most easily used.

{{ind|general-imported|mekso goals|and non-mathematical expression}} Goal 2 requires the provision of several conversion mechanisms, so that the boundary between mekso and full Lojban can be crossed from either side at many points.

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical notation|international uniqueness of}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso goals|and ambiguity}} Goal 3 is the most subtle. Written mathematical expression is culturally unambiguous, in the sense that mathematicians in all parts of the world understand the same written texts to have the same meanings. However, international mathematical notation does not prescribe unique forms. For example, the expression

{{dsp|example-random-id-dGcT}}
{{judri|c18e1d1}}
{{math|3x + 2y}}

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical notation|and omitted operators}} contains omitted multiplication operators, but there are other possible interpretations for the strings 

“3x” and 
“2y” than as mathematical multiplication. Therefore, the Lojban verbal (spoken and written) form of 

{{linker|example-random-id-dGcT}} must not omit the multiplication operators.

{{ind|general-imported|mekso chapter|completeness}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso chapter|table notation convention}} The remainder of this chapter explains (in as much detail as is currently possible) the mekso system. This chapter is by intention complete as regards mekso components, but only suggestive about uses of those components &ndash; as of now, there has been no really comprehensive use made of mekso facilities, and many matters must await the test of usage to be fully clarified.

{{judri|section-mekso-numbers}}
==Lojban numbers==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|pa}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|re}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ci}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|vo}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|mu}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|xa}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ze}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|bi}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|so}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|no}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|hundred|expressing as number}}  {{ind|general-imported|ten|expressing as number}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|as compound cmavo}}  {{ind|general-imported|digits|cmavo for}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|expressing simple}} The simplest kind of mekso are numbers, which are cmavo or compound cmavo. There are cmavo for each of the 10 decimal digits, and numbers greater than 9 are made by stringing together the cmavo. Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LmPr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LmPr}}
{{judri|c18e2d1}}
{{ind|example|123|example}}
:'''pa re ci'''
:<code>one two three</code>
{{math|123}}
:''one hundred and twenty three''

{{dsp|example-random-id-TNjj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TNjj}}
{{judri|c18e2d2}}
:'''pa no'''
:<code>one zero</code>
{{math|10}}
:''ten''

{{dsp|example-random-id-gjzw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gjzw}}
{{judri|c18e2d3}}
:'''pa re ci vo mu xa ze bi so no'''
:<code>one two three four five six seven eight nine zero</code>
{{math|1234567890}}
:''one billion, two hundred and thirty-four million, five hundred and sixty-seven thousand, eight hundred and ninety.''

{{ind|general-imported|numbers|greater than 9}} Therefore, there are no separate cmavo for 
“ten”, 
“hundred”, etc.

{{ind|general-imported|number words|pattern in}} There is a pattern to the digit cmavo (except for 
{{vla|no}}, 0) which is worth explaining. The cmavo from 1 to 5 end in the vowels 
{{lerfu|a}}, 
{{lerfu|e}}, 
{{lerfu|i}}, 
{{lerfu|o}}, 
{{lerfu|u}} respectively; and the cmavo from 6 to 9 likewise end in the vowels 
{{lerfu|a}}, 
{{lerfu|e}}, 
{{lerfu|i}}, and 
{{lerfu|o}} respectively. None of the digit cmavo begin with the same consonant, to make them easy to tell apart in noisy environments.

{{judri|section-signs-punctuation}}
==Signs and numerical punctuation==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ma'u}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ni'u}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|pi}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|fi'u}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ra'e}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ce'i}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ki'o}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|negative numbers|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|positive numbers|explicit expression}}  {{ind|general-imported|signed numbers|expressing}} A number can be given an explicit sign by the use of 
{{vla|ma'u}} and 
{{vla|ni'u}}, which are the positive and negative signs as distinct from the addition, subtraction, and negation operators. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-6A5H}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-6A5H}}
{{judri|c18e3d1}}
{{ind|example|-1|example}}
:'''ni'u pa'''
:<code>negative-sign 1</code>
{{math|-1}}

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|pa}}  

{{ind|general-imported|signs on numbers|grammar}} Grammatically, the signs are part of the number to which they are attached. It is also possible to use 
{{vla|ma'u}} and 
{{vla|ni'u}} by themselves as numbers; the meaning of these numbers is explained in 
[[#section-indefinite-numbers|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|decimal point|as numerical punctuation}}  {{ind|general-imported|punctuation|in numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|numerical punctuation}} Various numerical punctuation marks are likewise expressed by cmavo, as illustrated in the following examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Ust4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Ust4}}
{{judri|c18e3d2}}
{{ind|example|3.1415|example}}
:'''ci pi pa vo pa mu'''
:<code>three point one four one five</code>
{{math|3.1415}}

{{ind|general-imported|decimal point|effect of different notations}} (In some cultures, a comma is used instead of a period in the symbolic version of 
{{linker|example-random-id-Ust4}}; 
{{vla|pi}} is still the Lojban representation for the decimal point.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-AeRL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-AeRL}}
{{judri|c18e3d3}}
{{ind|example|2/7|example}}
:'''re fi'u ze'''
:<code>two fraction seven</code>
{{math|2/7}}

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|fi'u}}  

{{ind|general-imported|reciprocal|expression of mathematical}}  {{ind|general-imported|fractions|numerator default}}  {{ind|general-imported|fractions|expressing with numerical punctuation}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-AeRL}} is the name of the number two-sevenths; it is not the same as 
“the result of 2 divided by 7” in Lojban, although numerically these two are equal. If the denominator of the fraction is present but the numerator is not, the numerator is taken to be 1, thus expressing the reciprocal of the following number:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhvj}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhvj}}
{{judri|c18e3d4}}
:'''fi'u ze'''
:<code>fraction seven</code>
{{math|1/7}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhVs}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhVs}}
{{judri|c18e3d5}}
:'''pi ci mu ra'e pa vo re bi mu ze'''
:<code>point three five repeating one four two eight five seven</code>
{{math|.35142857142857...}}

{{ind|general-imported|repeating decimals|marking start of repeating portion}}  {{ind|general-imported|repeating decimals|expressing with numerical punctuation}} Note that the 
{{vla|ra'e}} marks unambiguously where the repeating portion 

“142857” begins.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhWd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhWd}}
{{judri|c18e3d6}}
:'''ci mu ce'i'''
:<code>three five percent</code>

{{math|35%}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhwM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhwM}}
{{judri|c18e3d7}}
:'''pa ki'o re ci vo ki'o mu xa ze'''
:<code>one comma two three four comma five six seven</code>
{{math|1,234,567}}

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|ce'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|commas in numbers|effect of other notation conventions}}  {{ind|general-imported|commas in numbers|as numerical punctuation}}  {{ind|general-imported|percent|as numerical punctuation}} (In some cultures, spaces are used in the symbolic representation of 
{{linker|example-random-id-qhwM}}; 
{{vla|ki'o}} is still the Lojban representation.)

{{ind|general-imported|commas in numbers|with elided digits}} It is also possible to have less than three digits between successive 
{{vla|ki'o}} s, in which case zeros are assumed to have been elided:

{{dsp|example-random-id-TTBx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TTBx}}
{{judri|c18e3d8}}
:'''pa ki'o re ci ki'o vo'''
:<code>one comma two three comma four</code>
{{math|1,023,004}}

In the same way, 
{{vla|ki'o}} can be used after 

{{vla|pi}} to divide fractions into groups of three:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHwu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHwu}}
{{judri|c18e3d9}}
:'''pi ki'o re re'''
:<code>point comma two two</code>
{{math|.022}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhxp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhxp}}
{{judri|c18e3d10}}
:'''pi pa ki'o pa re ki'o pa'''
:<code>point one comma one two comma one</code>
{{math|.001012001}}

{{judri|section-constants}}
==Special numbers==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ci'i}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ka'o}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|pai}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|te'o}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|fi'u}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|fraction|meaning with elided numerator and denominator}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|special}} The last cmavo is the same as the fraction sign cmavo: a fraction sign with neither numerator nor denominator represents the golden ratio.

Numbers can have any of these digit, punctuation, and special-number cmavo of Sections 2, 3, and 4 in any combination:

{{dsp|example-random-id-k2U4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k2U4}}
{{judri|c18e4d1}}
{{ind|example|infinity|example}}
:'''ma'u ci'i'''
{{math|+∞}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-k2VC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k2VC}}
{{judri|c18e4d2}}
:'''ci ka'o re'''
:''3i2 (a complex number equivalent to {{math|3 + 2i}}) ''

{{ind|general-imported|ka'o|as special number compared with as numerical punctuation}}  {{ind|general-imported|complex numbers|expressing}} Note that 
{{vla|ka'o}} is both a special number (meaning 

“i”) and a number punctuation mark (separating the real and the imaginary parts of a complex number).

{{dsp|example-random-id-k32m}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k32m}}
{{judri|c18e4d3}}
{{ind|example|aleph null|example}}
{{ind|example|transfinite cardinal|example}}
:'''ci'i no'''
:''infinity zero''
:''{{math|&#x2135;<subscript>0</subscript>}} (a transfinite cardinal) ''

The special numbers 
{{vla|pai}} and 
{{vla|te'o}} are mathematically important, which is why they are given their own cmavo:

{{dsp|example-random-id-k356}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k356}}
{{judri|c18e4d4}}
:'''pai'''
:''pi, {{math|π}} ''

{{dsp|example-random-id-k36i}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k36i}}
{{judri|c18e4d5}}
:'''te'o'''
:''{{math|e}}''

{{ind|general-imported|numerical punctuation|undefined}} However, many combinations are as yet undefined:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHXr}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHXr}}
{{judri|c18e4d6}}
:'''pa pi re pi ci'''
:''{{math|1.2.3}}''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qHya}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qHya}}
{{judri|c18e4d7}}
:'''pa ni'u re'''
:<code>1 negative-sign 2</code>

{{ind|general-imported|subtraction operator|contrasted with negative sign}}  {{ind|general-imported|negative sign|contrasted with subtraction operator}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-qHya}} is not 
“1 minus 2”, which is represented by a different cmavo sequence altogether. It is a single number which has not been assigned a meaning. There are many such numbers which have no well-defined meaning; they may be used for experimental purposes or for future expansion of the Lojban number system.

It is possible, of course, that some of these 
“oddities” do have a meaningful use in some restricted area of mathematics. A mathematician appropriating these structures for specialized use needs to consider whether some other branch of mathematics would use the structure differently.

More information on numbers may be found in 
[[#section-indefinite-numbers|this section]] to 
[[#section-number-questions|this section]].

{{judri|section-simple-infix}}
==Simple infix expressions and equations==

The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|du}}
:{{s|GOhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|su'i}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|vu'u}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|pi'i}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|te'a}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|ny.}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

“n”
:{{c|vei}}
:{{s|VEI}}
:''description''

:{{c|ve'o}}
:{{s|VEhO}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical notation|infix}} Let us begin at the beginning: one plus one equals two. In Lojban, that sentence translates to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-CUeK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-CUeK}}
{{judri|c18e5d1}}
{{ind|example|1 + 1 = 2|example}}
:'''li pa su'i pa du li re'''
:<code>The-number one plus one equals the-number two.</code>
{{math|1 + 1 = 2}}

{{ind|general-imported|du|grammar of}}  {{ind|general-imported|mathematical equality|expressing}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-CUeK}}, a mekso sentence, is a regular Lojban bridi that exploits mekso features. 
{{vla|du}} is the predicate meaning 
“x1 is mathematically equal to x2”. It is a cmavo for conciseness, but it has the same grammatical uses as any brivla. Outside mathematical contexts, 
{{vla|du}} means 
“x1 is identical with x2” or 
“x1 is the same object as x2”.

{{ind|general-imported|numbers|using for quantification contrasted with talking about}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|talking about contrasted with using for quantification}}  {{ind|general-imported|number article|explanation of use}}  {{ind|general-imported|the|for talking about numbers themselves}}  {{ind|general-imported|article|number}} The cmavo 
{{vla|li}} is the number article. It is required whenever a sentence talks about numbers as numbers, as opposed to using numbers to quantify things. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-nSU9}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-nSU9}}
{{judri|c18e5d2}}
:'''le ci prenu'''
:''the three persons''

requires no 
{{vla|li}} article, because the 

{{vla|ci}} is being used to specify the number of 
{{vla|prenu}}. However, the sentence

{{dsp|example-random-id-BNFi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BNFi}}
{{judri|c18e5d3}}
{{ind|example|3 grams|example}}
:'''levi sfani cu grake li ci'''
:<code>This fly masses-in-grams the-number three.</code>
:''This fly has a mass of 3 grams.''

{{ind|general-imported|units of measurement|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|measurements|expressing}} requires 
{{vla|li}} because 
{{vla|ci}} is being used as a sumti. Note that this is the way in which measurements are stated in Lojban: all the predicates for units of length, mass, temperature, and so on have the measured object as the first place and a number as the second place. Using 

{{vla|li}} for 
{{vla|le}} in 
{{linker|example-random-id-nSU9}} would produce

{{dsp|example-random-id-gJe1}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gJe1}}
{{judri|c18e5d4}}
:'''li ci prenu'''
:<code>The-number 3 is-a-person.</code>

which is grammatical but nonsensical: numbers are not persons.

{{ind|general-imported|addition operator|contrasted with positive sign}}  {{ind|general-imported|positive sign|contrasted with addition operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|addition|a mathematical operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|mathematical operators}} The cmavo 
{{vla|su'i}} belongs to selma'o VUhU, which is composed of mathematical operators, and means 

“addition”. As mentioned before, it is distinct from 
{{vla|ma'u}} which means the positive sign as an indication of a positive number:

{{dsp|example-random-id-4gsp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-4gsp}}
{{judri|c18e5d5}}
{{ind|example|+1 + -1 = 0|example}}
:'''li ma'u pa su'i ni'u pa du li no'''
:<code>The-number positive-sign one plus negative-sign one equals the-number zero.</code>
{{math|+1 + -1 = 0}}

Of course, it is legal to have complex mekso on both sides of 
{{vla|du}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-d6bM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-d6bM}}
{{judri|c18e5d6}}
:'''li mu su'i pa du li ci su'i ci'''
:<code>The-number five plus one equals the-number three plus three.</code>
{{math|5 + 1 = 3 + 3}}

{{ind|general-imported|conversion into sumti from mekso}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of mekso into sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|li|as converter of mekso into sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|general sumti|contrasted with operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|operands|contrasted with general sumti}}  {{ind|general-imported|VUhU operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|operators of VUhU|grammar of operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|du|with complex mekso on both sides}} Why don't we say 
:{{jbo|li mu su'i li pa}} rather than just 
:{{jbo|li mu su'i pa}}? The answer is that VUhU operators connect mekso operands (numbers, in 
{{linker|example-random-id-d6bM}}), not general sumti. 

{{vla|li}} is used to make the entire mekso into a sumti, which then plays the roles applicable to other sumti: in 
{{linker|example-random-id-d6bM}}, filling the places of a bridi

{{ind|general-imported|precedence|mathematical default}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator left-right grouping|as Lojban default}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|in Lojban default}}  {{ind|general-imported|calculator mathematics|as default in Lojban}} By default, Lojban mathematics is like simple calculator mathematics: there is no notion of 

“operator precedence”. Consider the following example, where 

{{vla|pi'i}} means 
“times”, the multiplication operator:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7a2Q}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7a2Q}}
{{judri|c18e5d7}}
:'''li ci su'i vo pi'i mu du li reci'''
:<code>The-number three plus four times five equals the-number two-three.</code>
{{math|3 + 4 × 5 = 23}}

Is the Lojban version of 
{{linker|example-random-id-7a2Q}} true? No! 
“3 + 4 × 5” is indeed 23, because the usual conventions of mathematics state that multiplication takes precedence over addition; that is, the multiplication 

“4 × 5” is done first, giving 20, and only then the addition 
“3 + 20”. But VUhU operators by default are done left to right, like other Lojban grouping, and so a truthful bridi would be:

{{dsp|example-random-id-XUQh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-XUQh}}
{{judri|c18e5d8}}
:'''li ci su'i vo pi'i mu du li cimu'''
:<code>The-number three plus four times five equals the-number three-five.</code>
{{math|3 + 4 × 5 = 35}}

{{ind|general-imported|default operator precedence|contrasted with mekso goal}} Here we calculate 3 + 4 first, giving 7, and then calculate 7 × 5 second, leading to the result 35. While possessing the advantage of simplicity, this result violates the design goal of matching the standards of mathematics. What can be done?

{{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|effect of pragmatic convention}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|and mathematical notation}}  {{ind|general-imported|mathematical notation|and operator precedence}} There are three solutions, all of which will probably be used to some degree. The first solution is to ignore the problem. People will say 
:{{jbo|li ci su'i vo pi'i mu}} and mean 23 by it, because the notion that multiplication takes precedence over addition is too deeply ingrained to be eradicated by Lojban parsing, which totally ignores semantics. This convention essentially allows semantics to dominate syntax in this one area.

{{ind|general-imported|operator precedence in other languages}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|rationale for default left-grouping}} (Why not hard-wire the precedences into the grammar, as is done in computer programming languages? Essentially because there are too many operators, known and unknown, with levels of precedence that vary according to usage. The programming language 'C' has 13 levels of precedence, and its list of operators is not even extensible. For Lojban this approach is just not practical. In addition, hard-wired precedence could not be overridden in mathematical systems such as spreadsheets where the conventions are different.)

{{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|generalized explicit specification}} The second solution is to use explicit means to specify the precedence of operators. This approach is fully general, but clumsy, and will be explained in 
[[#section-explicit-operator-precedence|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|bi'e|effect on following operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|scope modification with bi'e}} The third solution is simple but not very general. When an operator is prefixed with the cmavo 
{{vla|bi'e}} (of selma'o BIhE), it becomes automatically of higher precedence than other operators not so prefixed. Thus,

{{dsp|example-random-id-LIUa}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LIUa}}
{{judri|c18e5d9}}
:'''li ci su'i vo bi'e pi'i mu du li reci'''
:<code>The-number three plus four-times-five equals the-number two-three.</code>
{{math|3 + 4 × 5 = 23}}

is a truthful Lojban bridi. If more than one operator has a 
{{vla|bi'e}} prefix, grouping is from the right; multiple 

{{vla|bi'e}} prefixes on a single operator are not allowed.

{{ind|general-imported|parenthesis|mathematical}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|specifying by parenthesis}} In addition, of course, Lojban has the mathematical parentheses 
{{vla|vei}} and 
{{vla|ve'o}}, which can be used just like their written equivalents 
“(” and 
“)” to group expressions in any way desired:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wfFV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wfFV}}
{{judri|c18e5d10}}
{{ind|example|(n + 1)(n + 1) = n^2 + 2n + 1|example}}
:'''li vei ny. su'i pa ve'o pi'i vei ny. su'i pa [ve'o] du li ny. [bi'e] te'a re su'i re bi'e pi'i ny. su'i pa'''

:<code>The-number (n plus one) times (n plus one) equals the-number n-power-two plus two-times- n plus 1.</code>
<!-- FIXME: broken math, not the only one -->
{{math|(n + 1)(n + 1) = n}}

{{ind|general-imported|lerfu strings|interpretation of contrasted with normal mathematical interpretation}}  {{ind|general-imported|lerfu strings|in mathematical expressions}} There are several new usages in 
{{linker|example-random-id-wfFV}}: 
{{vla|te'a}} means 

“raised to the power”, and we also see the use of the lerfu word 
{{vla|ny}}, representing the letter 
“n”. In mekso, letters stand for just what they do in ordinary mathematics: variables. The parser will accept a string of lerfu words (called a 
“lerfu string”) as the equivalent of a single lerfu word, in agreement with computer-science conventions; 
“abc” is a single variable, not the equivalent of 
“a × b × c”. (Of course, a local convention could state that the value of a variable like 
“abc”, with a multi-lerfu name, was equal to the values of the variables 
“a”, 
“b”, and 
“c” multiplied together.)

The explicit operator 
{{vla|pi'i}} is required in the Lojban verbal form whereas multiplication is implicit in the symbolic form. Note that 

{{vla|ve'o}} (the right parenthesis) is an elidable terminator: the first use of it in 
{{linker|example-random-id-wfFV}} is required, but the second use (marked by square brackets) could be elided. Additionally, the first 

{{vla|bi'e}} (also marked by square brackets) is not necessary to get the proper grouping, but it is included here for symmetry with the other one.

{{judri|section-forethought}}
==Forethought operators (Polish notation, functions)==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|boi}}
:{{s|BOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|va'a}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|pe'o}}
:{{s|PEhO}}
:''description''

:{{c|ku'e}}
:{{s|KUhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|py.}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

:{{c|xy.}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

:{{c|zy.}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

:{{c|ma'o}}
:{{s|MAhO}}
:''description''

:{{c|fy.}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

The infix form explained so far is reasonable for many purposes, but it is limited and rigid. It works smoothly only where all operators have exactly two operands, and where precedences can either be assumed from context or are limited to just two levels, with some help from parentheses.

But there are many operators which do not have two operands, or which have a variable number of operands. The preferred form of expression in such cases is the use of 
“forethought operators”, also known as Polish notation. In this style of writing mathematics, the operator comes first and the operands afterwards:

{{dsp|example-random-id-I0Bm}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-I0Bm}}
{{judri|c18e6d1}}
:'''li su'i paboi reboi ci[boi] du li xa'''
:<code>The-number the-sum-of one two three equals the-number six.</code>
{{math|sum(1,2,3) = 6}}

Note that the normally elidable number terminator 
{{vla|boi}} is required after 
{{vla|pa}} and 
{{vla|re}} because otherwise the reading would be 
:{{jbo|pareci}}= 123. It is not required after 
{{vla|ci}} but is inserted here in brackets for the sake of symmetry. The only time 
{{vla|boi}} is required is, as in 
{{linker|example-random-id-I0Bm}}, when there are two consecutive numbers or lerfu strings.

Forethought mekso can use any number of operands, in 
{{linker|example-random-id-I0Bm}}, three. How do we know how many operands there are in ambiguous circumstances? The usual Lojban solution is employed: an elidable terminator, namely 
{{vla|ku'e}}. Here is an example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-IxMG}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-IxMG}}
{{judri|c18e6d2}}
:'''li py. su'i va'a ny. ku'e su'i zy du li xy.'''
<code>The-number 
“p” plus negative-of( 
“n”) plus 
“z” equals the-number 
“x”.</code>
{{math|p + -n + z = x}}

where we know that 
{{vla|va'a}} is a forethought operator because there is no operand preceding it.

{{vla|va'a}} is the numerical negation operator, of selma'o VUhU. In contrast, 

{{vla|vu'u}} is not used for numerical negation, but only for subtraction, as it always has two or more operands. Do not confuse 
{{vla|va'a}} and 
{{vla|vu'u}}, which are operators, with 
{{vla|ni'u}}, which is part of a number.

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-IxMG}}, the operator 
{{vla|va'a}} and the terminator 
{{vla|ku'e}} serve in effect as parentheses. (The regular parentheses 
{{vla|vei}} and 
{{vla|ve'o}} are NOT used for this purpose.) If the 
{{vla|ku'e}} were omitted, the 
:{{jbo|su'i zy}} would be swallowed up by the 
{{vla|va'a}} forethought operator, which would then appear to have two operands, 
{{vla|ny}} and 
:{{jbo|su'i zy.}}, where the latter is also a forethought expression.

Forethought mekso is also useful for matching standard functional notation. How do we represent 

“z = f(x)”? The answer is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-VybU}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-VybU}}
{{judri|c18e6d3}}
:'''li zy du li ma'o fy.boi xy.'''
:<code>The-number z equals the-number the-operator f x.</code>
{{math|z = f(x)}}

Again, no parentheses are used. The construct 
:{{jbo|ma'o fy.boi}} is the equivalent of an operator, and appears in forethought here (although it could also be used as a regular infix operator). In mathematics, letters sometimes mean functions and sometimes mean variables, with only the context to tell which. Lojban chooses to accept the variable interpretation as the default, and uses the special flag 
{{vla|ma'o}} to mark a lerfu string as an operator. The cmavo 
{{vla|xy.}} and 
{{vla|zy.}} are variables, but 
{{vla|fy.}} is an operator (a function) because 
{{vla|ma'o}} marks it as such. The 
{{vla|boi}} is required because otherwise the 
{{vla|xy.}} would look like part of the operator name. (The use of 
{{vla|ma'o}} can be generalized from lerfu strings to any mekso operand: See [[#section-miscellany|this section]].)

When using forethought mekso, the optional marker 
{{vla|pe'o}} may be placed in front of the operator. This usage can help avoid confusion by providing clearly marked 

{{vla|pe'o}} and 

{{vla|ku'e}} pairs to delimit the operand list. 
{{linker|example-random-id-I0Bm}} to 
{{linker|example-random-id-VybU}}, respectively, with explicit 
{{vla|pe'o}} and 

{{vla|ku'e}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhz5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhz5}}
{{judri|c18e6d4}}
:'''li pe'o su'i paboi reboi ciboi ku'e du li xa'''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qhzu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qhzu}}
{{judri|c18e6d5}}
:'''li py. su'i pe'o va'a ny. ku'e su'i zy du li xy.'''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi0g}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi0g}}
{{judri|c18e6d6}}
:'''li zy du li pe'o ma'o fy.boi xy. ku'e'''

Note: When using forethought mekso, be sure that the operands really are operands: they cannot contain regular infix expressions unless parenthesized with 

{{vla|vei}} and 
{{vla|ve'o}}. An earlier version of the complex 
{{linker|example-random-id-k36J}} came to grief because I forgot this rule.

{{judri|section-useful-selbri}}
==Other useful selbri for mekso bridi==
So far our examples have been isolated mekso (it is legal to have a bare mekso as a sentence in Lojban) and equation bridi involving 
{{vla|du}}. What about inequalities such as 
“x &lt; 5”? The answer is to use a bridi with an appropriate selbri, thus:

{{dsp|example-random-id-s4TW}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-s4TW}}
{{judri|c18e7d1}}
:'''li xy. mleca li mu'''
:<code>The-number x is-less-than the-number 5.</code>

Here is a partial list of selbri useful in mathematical bridi:



;{{vla|du}}
<listitem>:''x1 is identical to x2, x3, x4, ...''

;{{vla|dunli}}
<listitem>:''x1 is equal/congruent to x2 in/on property/quality/dimension/quantity x3''

;{{vla|mleca}}
<listitem>:''x1 is less than x2''

;{{vla|zmadu}}
<listitem>:''x1 is greater than x2''

;{{vla|dubjavme'a}}
<listitem>:''x1 is less than or equal to x2 [{{vla|du}} {{vla|ja}} {{vla|mleca}}, equal or less]''

;{{vla|dubjavmau}}
<listitem>:''x1 is greater than or equal to x2 [{{vla|du}} {{vla|ja}} {{vla|zmadu}}, equal or greater]''

;{{vla|tamdu'i}}
<listitem>:''x1 is similar to x2 [{{vla|tarmi}} {{vla|dunli}}, shape-equal]''

;{{vla|turdu'i}}
<listitem>:''x1 is isomorphic to x2 [{{vla|stura}} {{vla|dunli}}, structure-equal]''

;{{vla|cmima}}
<listitem>:''x1 is a member of set x2''

;{{vla|gripau}}
<listitem>:''x1 is a subset of set x2 [{{vla|girzu}} {{vla|pagbu}}, set-part]''

;{{vla|na'ujbi}}
<listitem>:''x1 is approximately equal to x2 [{{vla|namcu}} {{vla|jibni}}, number-near]''

;{{vla|terci'e}}
<listitem>:''x1 is a component with function x2 of system x3''

Note the difference between 
{{vla|dunli}} and 

{{vla|du}}; 
{{vla|dunli}} has a third place that specifies the kind of equality that is meant. 

{{vla|du}} refers to actual identity, and can have any number of places:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PTmF}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PTmF}}
{{judri|c18e7d2}}
:'''py. du xy.boi zy.'''
<code>
“p” is-identical-to 
“x”
“z”</code>
{{math|p = x = z}}

Lojban bridi can have only one predicate, so the 
{{vla|du}} is not repeated.

Any of these selbri may usefully be prefixed with 
{{vla|na}}, the contradictory negation cmavo, to indicate that the relation is false:

{{dsp|example-random-id-WuRn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-WuRn}}
{{judri|c18e7d3}}
:'''li re su'i re na du li mu'''
:<code>the-number 2 + 2 is-not equal-to the-number 5.</code>
{{math|2 + 2 ≠ 5}}

As usual in Lojban, negated bridi say what is false, and do not say anything about what might be true.

{{judri|section-indefinite-numbers}}
==Indefinite numbers==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ro}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|so'a}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|so'e}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|so'i}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|so'o}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|so'u}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|no'o}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|da'a}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|rau}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|du'e}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|mo'a}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

Not all the cmavo of PA represent numbers in the usual mathematical sense. For example, the cmavo 
{{vla|ro}} means 
“all” or 
“each”. This number does not have a definite value in the abstract: 
:{{jbo|li ro}} is undefined. But when used to count or quantify something, the parallel between 
{{vla|ro}} and 
{{vla|pa}} is clearer:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qI27}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qI27}}
{{judri|c18e8d1}}
:'''mi catlu pa prenu'''
:<code>I look-at one person</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qI3P}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qI3P}}
{{judri|c18e8d2}}
:'''mi catlu ro prenu'''
:<code>I look-at all persons</code>

{{linker|example-random-id-qI27}} might be true, whereas 
{{linker|example-random-id-qI3P}} is almost certainly false.

The cmavo 
{{vla|so'a}}, 

{{vla|so'e}}, 

{{vla|so'i}}, 

{{vla|so'o}}, and 

{{vla|so'u}} represent a set of indefinite numbers less than 

{{vla|ro}}. As you go down an alphabetical list, the magnitude decreases:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi4a}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi4a}}
{{judri|c18e8d3}}
:'''mi catlu so'a prenu'''
:<code>I look-at almost-all persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi55}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi55}}
{{judri|c18e8d4}}
:'''mi catlu so'e prenu'''
:<code>I look-at most persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi5m}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi5m}}
{{judri|c18e8d5}}
:'''mi catlu so'i prenu'''
:<code>I look-at many persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi5U}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi5U}}
{{judri|c18e8d6}}
:'''mi catlu so'o prenu'''
:<code>I look-at several persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qI6B}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qI6B}}
{{judri|c18e8d7}}
:'''mi catlu so'u prenu'''
:<code>I look-at a-few persons</code>

The English equivalents are only rough: the cmavo provide space for up to five indefinite numbers between 

{{vla|ro}} and 
{{vla|no}}, with a built-in ordering. In particular, 
{{vla|so'e}} does not mean 

“most” in the sense of 
“a majority” or 
“more than half”.

Each of these numbers, plus 
{{vla|ro}}, may be prefixed with 
{{vla|pi}} (the decimal point) in order to make a fractional form which represents part of a whole rather than some elements of a totality. 

{{vla|piro}} therefore means 
“the whole of”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-dwJI}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-dwJI}}
{{judri|c18e8d8}}
:'''mi citka piro lei nanba'''
:<code>I eat the-whole-of the-mass-of bread</code>

Similarly, 
{{vla|piso'a}} means 
“almost the whole of”; and so on down to 
{{vla|piso'u}}, 
“a tiny part of”. These numbers are particularly appropriate with masses, which are usually measured rather than counted, as 
{{linker|example-random-id-dwJI}} shows.

In addition to these cmavo, there is 
{{vla|no'o}}, meaning 

“the typical value”, and 

:{{jbo|pino'o}}, meaning 
“the typical portion”: Sometimes 
{{vla|no'o}} can be translated 

“the average value”, but the average in question is not, in general, a mathematical mean, median, or mode; these would be more appropriately represented by operators.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi7Q}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi7Q}}
{{judri|c18e8d9}}
:'''mi catlu no'o prenu'''
:<code>I look-at a-typical-number-of persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qI8K}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qI8K}}
{{judri|c18e8d10}}
:'''mi citka pino'o lei nanba'''
:<code>I eat a-typical-amount-of the-mass-of bread.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|times|implicit expression of}}  {{ind|general-imported|times|explicit expression of}} 
{{vla|da'a}} is a related cmavo meaning 
“all but”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qi94}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qi94}}
{{judri|c18e8d11}}
:'''mi catlu da'a re prenu'''
:<code>I look-at all-but two persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qia0}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qia0}}
{{judri|c18e8d12}}
:'''mi catlu da'a so'u prenu'''
:<code>I look-at all-but a-few persons</code>

{{linker|example-random-id-qia0}} is similar in meaning to 
{{linker|example-random-id-qi4a}}.

{{ind|general-imported|da'a|default number for}} If no number follows 
{{vla|da'a}}, then 
{{vla|pa}} is assumed; 
{{vla|da'a}} by itself means 
“all but one”, or in ordinal contexts 
“all but the last”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3z2U}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3z2U}}
{{judri|c18e8d13}}
{{ind|example|eat themselves|example}}
:'''ro ratcu ka'e citka da'a ratcu'''
:<code>All rats can eat all-but-one rats.</code>
:''All rats can eat all other rats.''

(The use of 
{{vla|da'a}} means that 
{{linker|example-random-id-3z2U}} does not require that all rats can eat themselves, but does allow it. Each rat has one rat it cannot eat, but that one might be some rat other than itself. Context often dictates that 

“itself” is, indeed, the 
“other” rat.)

{{ind|general-imported|ni'u|with elided number}}  {{ind|general-imported|ma'u|with elided number}} As mentioned in 
[[#section-signs-punctuation|this section]], 
{{vla|ma'u}} and 
{{vla|ni'u}} are also legal numbers, and they mean 
“some positive number” and 
“some negative number” respectively.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiaK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiaK}}
{{judri|c18e8d14}}
:'''li ci vu'u re du li ma'u'''
:<code>the-number 3 − 2 = some-positive-number</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiAq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiAq}}
{{judri|c18e8d15}}
:'''li ci vu'u vo du li ni'u'''
:<code>the-number 3 − 4 = some-negative-number</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiAR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiAR}}
{{judri|c18e8d16}}
:'''mi ponse ma'u rupnu'''
:<code>I possess a-positive-number-of currency-units.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|indefinite values|subjective}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective amounts|expressing}} All of the numbers discussed so far are objective, even if indefinite. If there are exactly six superpowers ( 
{{vla|rairgugde}}, 
“superlative-states”) in the world, then 
:{{jbo|ro rairgugde}} means the same as 
:{{jbo|xa rairgugde}}. It is often useful, however, to express subjective indefinite values. The cmavo 

{{vla|rau}} (enough), 

{{vla|du'e}} (too many), and 

{{vla|mo'a}} (too few) are then appropriate:

{{dsp|example-random-id-TIiE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-TIiE}}
{{judri|c18e8d17}}
{{ind|example|enough currency|example}}
:'''mi ponse rau rupnu'''
:<code>I possess enough currency-units.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|indefinite portions|subjective}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective portions|expressing}} Like the 
{{vla|so'a}}-series, 

{{vla|rau}}, 

{{vla|du'e}}, and 

{{vla|mo'a}} can be preceded by 

{{vla|pi}}; for example, 
:{{jbo|pirau}} means 
“a sufficient part of.”

{{ind|general-imported|definite numbers|combined with indefinite}}  {{ind|general-imported|indefinite numbers|combined with definite}} Another possibility is that of combining definite and indefinite numbers into a single number. This usage implies that the two kinds of numbers have the same value in the given context:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qibb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qibb}}
{{judri|c18e8d18}}
{{ind|example|both dogs|example}}
:'''mi viska le rore gerku'''
:<code>I saw the all-of/two dogs.</code>
:''I saw both dogs.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIBi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIBi}}
{{judri|c18e8d19}}
:'''mi speni so'ici prenu'''
:<code>I am-married-to many/three persons.</code>
:''I am married to three persons (which is “many” in the circumstances).''

{{linker|example-random-id-qIBi}} assumes a mostly monogamous culture by stating that three is 
“many”.

{{judri|section-approximation}}
==Approximation and inexact numbers==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ji'i}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|su'e}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|su'o}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|me'i}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|za'u}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|ji'i|effect of placement}}  {{ind|general-imported|approximate numbers|expressing}} The cmavo 
{{vla|ji'i}} (of selma'o PA) is used in several ways to indicate approximate or rounded numbers. If it appears at the beginning of a number, the whole number is approximate:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YLcy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YLcy}}
{{judri|c18e9d1}}
{{ind|example|approximately 40|example}}
:'''ji'i vo no'''
:<code>approximation four zero</code>
:''approximately 40''

{{ind|general-imported|approximate numbers|expressing some exactness of}} If 
{{vla|ji'i}} appears in the middle of a number, all the digits following it are approximate:

{{dsp|example-random-id-BANC}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-BANC}}
{{judri|c18e9d2}}
:'''vo no ji'i mu no'''
:<code>four zero approximation five zero</code>
<natlang>roughly 4050 (where the 
“four thousand” is exact, but the 
“fifty” is approximate)</natlang>

{{ind|general-imported|rounded numbers|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|truncation of number|expressing}} If 
{{vla|ji'i}} appears at the end of a number, it indicates that the number has been rounded. In addition, it can then be followed by a sign cmavo ( 
{{vla|ma'u}} or 
{{vla|ni'u}}), which indicate truncation towards positive or negative infinity respectively.

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIc5}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIc5}}
{{judri|c18e9d3}}
:'''re pi ze re ji'i'''
:<code>two point seven two approximation</code>
:''2.72 (rounded)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qicz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qicz}}
{{judri|c18e9d4}}
{{ind|example|rounded up|example}}  
:'''re pi ze re ji'i ma'u'''
:<code>two point seven two approximation positive-sign</code>
:''2.72 (rounded up)''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiDE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiDE}}
{{judri|c18e9d5}}
{{ind|example|rounded down|example}}
:'''re pi ze pa ji'i ni'u'''
:<code>two point seven one approximation negative-sign</code>
:''2.71 (rounded down)''

{{ind|general-imported|ji'i|with elided number}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-qIc5}} through 
{{linker|example-random-id-qiDE}} are all approximations to 
{{vla|te'o}} (exponential e). 
{{vla|ji'i}} can also appear by itself, in which case it means 
“approximately the typical value in this context”.

{{ind|general-imported|inexact numbers with bounds}} The four cmavo 
{{vla|su'e}}, 

{{vla|su'o}}, 
{{vla|me'i}}, and 

{{vla|za'u}}, also of selma'o PA, express inexact numbers with upper or lower bounds:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qidi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qidi}}
{{judri|c18e9d6}}
{{ind|example|at most two|example}}
{{ind|example|at most|example}}  
:'''mi catlu su'e re prenu'''
:<code>I look-at at-most two persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiE3}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiE3}}
{{judri|c18e9d7}}
{{ind|example|at least two|example}}
{{ind|example|at least|example}}  
:'''mi catlu su'o re prenu'''
:<code>I look-at at-least two persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIe7}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIe7}}
{{judri|c18e9d8}}
{{ind|example|less than two|example}}
{{ind|example|less than|example}}  
:'''mi catlu me'i re prenu'''
:<code>I look-at less-than two persons</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIfM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIfM}}
{{judri|c18e9d9}}
{{ind|example|more than two|example}}
{{ind|example|more than|example}}  
:'''mi catlu za'u re prenu'''
:<code>I look-at more-than two persons</code>

{{ind|general-imported|plural|Lojban equivalent of}}  
{{ind|general-imported|exact number|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|at most|contrasted with more than|at least, less than}}  {{ind|general-imported|at least|contrasted with more than|less than, at most}}  {{ind|general-imported|more than|contrasted with less than|at least, at most}}  {{ind|general-imported|less than|contrasted with more than|at least, at most}} Each of these is a subtly different claim: 
{{linker|example-random-id-qiE3}} is true of two or any greater number, whereas 
{{linker|example-random-id-qIfM}} requires three persons or more. Likewise, 
{{linker|example-random-id-qidi}} refers to zero, one, or two; 
{{linker|example-random-id-qIe7}} to zero or one. (Of course, when the context allows numbers other than non-negative integers, 
:{{jbo|me'i re}} can be any number less than 2, and likewise with the other cases.) The exact quantifier, 

“exactly 2, neither more nor less” is just 
{{vla|re}}. Note that 
:{{jbo|su'ore}} is the exact Lojban equivalent of English plurals.

{{ind|general-imported|za'u|with elided number}}  {{ind|general-imported|me'i|with elided number}}  {{ind|general-imported|su'o|with elided number}}  {{ind|general-imported|su'e|with elided number}} If no number follows one of these cmavo, 
{{vla|pa}} is understood: therefore,

{{dsp|example-random-id-brir}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-brir}}
{{judri|c18e9d10}}
:'''mi catlu su'o prenu'''
:<code>I look-at at-least [one] person</code>

is a meaningful claim.

{{ind|general-imported|inexact portions with bounds}} Like the numbers in 
[[#section-indefinite-numbers|this section]], all of these cmavo may be preceded by 
{{vla|pi}} to make the corresponding quantifiers for part of a whole. For example, 
{{vla|pisu'o}} means 

“at least some part of”. The quantifiers 
{{vla|ro}}, 
{{vla|su'o}}, 
{{vla|piro}}, and 
{{vla|pisu'o}} are particularly important in Lojban, as they are implicitly used in the descriptions introduced by the cmavo of selma'o LA and LE, as explained in 

[[#section-quantified-descriptions|this section]]. Descriptions in general are outside the scope of this chapter.

{{judri|section-radixen}}
==Non-decimal and compound bases==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|ju'u}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|dau}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|fei}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|gai}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|jau}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|rei}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|vai}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|pi'e}}
:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|radix|decimal (see also base)}} In normal contexts, Lojban assumes that all numbers are expressed in the decimal (base 10) system. However, other bases are possible, and may be appropriate in particular circumstances.

{{ind|general-imported|octal system|specifying numbers in (see also base)}}  {{ind|general-imported|binary system|specifying numbers in (see also base)}}  {{ind|general-imported|base|specifying}} To specify a number in a particular base, the VUhU operator 
{{vla|ju'u}} is suitable:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Iw8u}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Iw8u}}
{{judri|c18e10d1}}
:'''li pa no pa no ju'u re du li pa no'''
:<code>The-number 1010 base 2 equals the-number 10.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|base|changing permanently}}  {{ind|general-imported|base|assumed}} Here, the final 
:{{jbo|pa no}} is assumed to be base 10, as usual; so is the base specification. (The base may also be changed permanently by a metalinguistic specification; no standard way of doing so has as yet been worked out.)

{{ind|general-imported|hexadecimal system|specifying numbers in (see also base)}}  {{ind|general-imported|digits|rationale for having 16}} Lojban has digits for representing bases up to 16, because 16 is a base often used in computer applications. In English, it is customary to use the letters A-F as the base 16 digits equivalent to the numbers ten through fifteen. In Lojban, this ambiguity is avoided:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIgb}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIgb}}
{{judri|c18e10d2}}
{{ind|example|ABC base 16|example}}
:'''li daufeigai ju'u paxa du li rezevobi'''
:<code>The-number ABC base 16 equals the-number 2748.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIha}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIha}}
{{judri|c18e10d3}}
:'''li jaureivai ju'u paxa du li cimuxaze'''
:<code>The-number DEF base 16 equals the-number 3567.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|digits beyond 9|word pattern}} Note the pattern in the cmavo: the diphthongs 
{{vla|au}}, 
{{vla|ei}}, 
{{vla|ai}} are used twice in the same order. The digits for A to D use consonants different from those used in the decimal digit cmavo; E and F unfortunately overlap 2 and 4 &ndash; there was simply not enough available cmavo space to make a full differentiation possible. The cmavo are also in alphabetical order.

{{ind|general-imported|decimal point|in bases other than 10}}  {{ind|general-imported|base point|in bases other than 10}} The base point 

{{vla|pi}} is used in non-decimal bases just as in base 10:

{{dsp|example-random-id-gCo4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-gCo4}}
{{judri|c18e10d4}}
{{ind|example|F.8 base 16|example}}
:'''li vai pi bi ju'u paxa du li pamu pi mu'''
:<code>The-number F.8 base 16 equals the-number 15.5.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|base|non-constant}}  {{ind|general-imported|ju'u|grammar of}} Since 
{{vla|ju'u}} is an operator of selma'o VUhU, it is grammatical to use any operand as the left argument. Semantically, however, it is undefined to use anything but a numeral string on the left. The reason for making 
{{vla|ju'u}} an operator is to allow reference to a base which is not a constant.

{{ind|general-imported|compound base|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound base|separator for}}  {{ind|general-imported|base varying for each digit|separator for}} There are some numerical values that require a 
“base” that varies from digit to digit. For example, times represented in hours, minutes, and seconds have, in effect, three 

“digits”: the first is base 24, the second and third are base 60. To express such numbers, the compound base separator 

{{vla|pi'e}} is used:

{{dsp|example-random-id-17HR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-17HR}}
{{judri|c18e10d5}}
{{ind|example|hours|minutes|seconds: example}}  
:'''ci pi'e rere pi'e vono'''
{{math|3:22:40}}

{{ind|general-imported|compound base|expressing digits in}} Each digit sequence separated by instances of 
{{vla|pi'e}} is expressed in decimal notation, but the number as a whole is not decimal and can only be added and subtracted by special rules:

{{dsp|example-random-id-iUYu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-iUYu}}
{{judri|c18e10d6}}
:'''li ci pi'e rere pi'e vono su'i pi'e ci pi'e cici du li ci pi'e rexa pi'e paci'''
:<code>The-number 3:22:40 plus :3:33 equals the-number 3:26:13.</code>
{{math|3:22:40 + 0:3:33 = 3:26:13}}

Of course, only context tells you that the first part of the numbers in 
{{linker|example-random-id-17HR}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-iUYu}} is hours, the second minutes, and the third seconds.

{{ind|general-imported|base greater than 16|expressing numbers in}}  {{ind|general-imported|Mayan mathematics|as a system with base larger than 16}} The same mechanism using 
{{vla|pi'e}} can be used to express numbers which have a base larger than 16. For example, base-20 Mayan mathematics might use digits from 

{{vla|no}} to 
{{vla|paso}}, each separated by 
{{vla|pi'e}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Nx5T}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Nx5T}}
{{judri|c18e10d7}}
:'''li pa pi'e re pi'e ci ju'u reno du li vovoci'''
:<code>the-number 1;2;3 base 20 equals the-number 443</code>

{{ind|general-imported|base greater than 16|two digits contrasted with compound single-digits}}  {{ind|general-imported|base greater than 16|compound single-digits contrasted with two digits}} Carefully note the difference between:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ydwP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ydwP}}
{{judri|c18e10d8}}
:'''pano ju'u reno'''
:<code>the-digit-10 base 20</code>

which is equal to ten, and:

{{dsp|example-random-id-QBQx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-QBQx}}
{{judri|c18e10d9}}
:'''pa pi'e no ju'u reno'''
:<code>1;0 base 20</code>

which is equal to twenty.

{{ind|general-imported|large-base decimal fraction|expressing}} Both 
{{vla|pi}} and 
{{vla|pi'e}} can be used to express large-base fractions:

{{dsp|example-random-id-26Li}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-26Li}}
{{judri|c18e10d10}}
:'''li pa pi'e vo pi ze ju'u reno du li re vo pi ci mu'''
:<code>The-number 1;4.7 base 20 equals the-number 24.35.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|base|vague}} 
{{vla|pi'e}} is also used where the base of each digit is vague, as in the numbering of the examples in this chapter:

{{dsp|example-random-id-U161}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-U161}}
{{judri|c18e10d11}}
:'''dei jufra panopi'epapamoi'''
:<code>This-utterance is-a-sentence-type-of 10;11th-thing.</code>
:''This is Sentence 10.11.''

{{judri|section-mekso-selbri}}
==Special mekso selbri==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|mei}}
:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|moi}}
:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|si'e}}

:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|cu'o}}

:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|va'e}}

:{{s|MOI}}
:''description''

:{{c|me}}
:{{s|ME}}
:''description''

:{{c|me'u}}
:{{s|MEhU}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|special}} Lojban possesses a special category of selbri which are based on mekso. The simplest kind of such selbri are made by suffixing a member of selma'o MOI to a number. There are five members of MOI, each of which serves to create number-based selbri with specific place structures.

{{ind|general-imported|cardinal selbri|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|cardinal selbri|place structure}} The cmavo 
{{vla|mei}} creates cardinal selbri. The basic place structure is:

:''x1 is a mass formed from the set x2 of n members, one or more of which is/are x3''
{{ind|general-imported|mass|expressing relation with individuals forming}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass|expressing relation with set forming}}  {{ind|general-imported|individuals|expressing relation with mass formed}}  {{ind|general-imported|individuals|expressing relation with set formed}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|expressing relation with individuals forming set}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|expressing relation with mass formed from set}} A cardinal selbri interrelates a set with a given number of members, the mass formed from that set, and the individuals which make the set up. The mass argument is placed first as a matter of convenience, not logical necessity.

Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ujSA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ujSA}}
{{judri|c18e11d1}}
{{ind|example|three rats|example}}
:'''lei mi ratcu cu cimei'''
:<code>Those-I-describe-as-the-mass-of my rats are-a-threesome.</code>
:<code>My rats are three.</code>
:''I have three rats.''

Here, the mass of my rats is said to have three components; that is, I have three rats.

Another example, with one element this time:

{{dsp|example-random-id-1Pen}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-1Pen}}
{{judri|c18e11d2}}
{{ind|example|singular me|example}}
{{ind|example|individual|example}} 
:'''mi poi pamei cu cusku dei'''
:<code>I who am-an-individual express this-sentence.</code>

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-1Pen}}, 
{{vla|mi}} refers to a mass, 
“the mass consisting of me”. Personal pronouns are vague between masses, sets, and individuals.

However, when the number expressed before 
{{raf|-mei}} is an objective indefinite number of the kind explained in 
[[#section-indefinite-numbers|this section]], a slightly different place structure is required:

{{ind|general-imported|individuals of set|expressing measurement standard for indefinites}}  {{ind|general-imported|set|expressing measurement standard for indefinites}}  {{ind|general-imported|mass|expressing measurement standard for indefinites}}  {{ind|general-imported|mei|place structure formed for objective indefinites}}
:''x1 is a mass formed from a set x2 of n members, one or more of which is/are x3, measured relative to the set x4.''
An example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-GJsg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-GJsg}}
{{judri|c18e11d3}}
{{ind|example|rats in park|example}}  
{{ind|example|fewsome|example}}  
{{ind|example|set of all rats|example}}
:'''lei ratcu poi zvati le panka cu so'umei lo'i ratcu'''
:<code>The-mass-of rats which are-in the park are a-fewsome with-respect-to the-set-of rats.</code>
:''The rats in the park are a small number of all the rats there are.''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|lo'i}}  

{{ind|general-imported|lo'i|with elided quantifiers}} In 
{{linker|example-random-id-GJsg}}, the x2 and x3 places are vacant, and the x4 place is filled by 
:{{jbo|lo'i ratcu}}, which (because no quantifiers are explicitly given) means 
“the whole of the set of all those things which are rats”, or simply 
“the set of all rats.”

{{dsp|example-random-id-n52D}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-n52D}}
{{judri|c18e11d4}}
{{ind|example|manysome|example}}
:'''le'i ratcu poi zvati le panka cu se so'imei'''
:<code>The-set-of rats which-are in the park is-a manysome.</code>
:''There are many rats in the park.''

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-n52D}}, the conversion cmavo 
{{vla|se}} swaps the x1 and the x2 places, so that the new x1 is the set. The x4 set is unspecified, so the implication is that the rats are 
“many” with respect to some unspecified comparison set.

More explanations about the interrelationship of sets, masses, and individuals can be found in 
[[#section-masses|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|ordinal selbri|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|ordinal selbri|place structure}} The cmavo 
{{vla|moi}} creates ordinal selbri. The place structure is:

:''x1 is the (n)th member of set x2 when ordered by rule x3''
Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiHw}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiHw}}
{{judri|c18e11d5}}
{{ind|example|first rat|example}} 
:'''ti pamoi le'i mi ratcu'''
:<code>This-one is the first-of the rats associated-with me.</code>
:''This is my first rat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qii2}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qii2}}
{{judri|c18e11d6}}
{{ind|example|all-th|example}}  
:'''ta romoi le'i mi ratcu'''
:<code>That is-the-allth-of the rats associated-with me.</code>
:''That is my last rat.''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIiA}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIiA}}
{{judri|c18e11d7}}
{{ind|example|enough-th|example}}
:'''mi raumoi le velskina porsi'''
:<code>I am-enough-th-in the movie-audience sequence</code>
:<code>I am enough-th in the movie line.</code>

{{linker|example-random-id-qIiA}} means, in the appropriate context, that my position in line is sufficiently far to the front that I will get a seat for the movie.

{{ind|general-imported|portion selbri|place structure}}  {{ind|general-imported|portion selbri|definition}} The cmavo 
{{vla|si'e}} creates portion selbri. The place structure is:

:''x1 is an (n)th portion of mass x2''
Some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-i8r4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-i8r4}}
{{judri|c18e11d8}}
:'''levi sanmi cu fi'ucisi'e lei mi djedi cidja'''
:<code>This-here meal is-a-slash-three-portion-of my day-food.</code>
:''This meal is one-third of my daily food.''

{{ind|general-imported|probability selbri|place structure}}  {{ind|general-imported|probability selbri|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|one-third of food}} The cmavo 
{{vla|cu'o}} creates probability selbri. The place structure is:

:''event x1 has probability (n) of occurring under conditions x2''
{{ind|general-imported|probability selbri|values}} The number must be between 0 and 1 inclusive. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9sf6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9sf6}}
{{judri|c18e11d9}}
{{ind|example|coin heads|example}}
{{ind|example|probability .5|example}}  
:'''le nu lo sicni cu sedja'o cu pimucu'o'''
:<code>The event of a coin being a head-displayer has probability .5.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|scale selbri|place structure}}  {{ind|general-imported|scale selbri|definition}} The cmavo 
{{vla|va'e}} creates a scale selbri. The place structure is:

:''x1 is at scale position (n) on the scale x2''
{{ind|general-imported|unreduced fractions|use in granular scales}}  {{ind|general-imported|scale|granular contrasted with continuous}} If the scale is granular rather than continuous, a form like 

:{{jbo|cifi'uxa}} (3/6) may be used; in this case, 3/6 is not the same as 1/2, because the third position on a scale of six positions is not the same as the first position on a scale of two positions. Here is an example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-XiTd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-XiTd}}
{{judri|c18e11d10}}
{{ind|example|scale of redness|example}}
{{ind|example|9 out of ten|example}}  
:'''le vi rozgu cu sofi'upanova'e xunre'''
:<code>This rose is 9/10-scale red.</code>
:<code>This rose is 9 out of 10 on the scale of redness.</code>
:''This rose is very red.''

{{ind|general-imported|scale selbri|place structure effect from subjective numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|probability selbri|place structure effect from subjective numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|portion selbri|place structure effect from subjective numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|ordinal selbri|place structure effect from subjective numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|cardinal selbri|place structure effect from subjective numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|effect on place structure for scale selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|effect on place structure for probability selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|effect on place structure for portion selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|effect on place structure for ordinal selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|effect on place structure for cardinal selbri}} When the quantifier preceding any MOI cmavo includes the subjective numbers 
{{vla|rau}}, 

{{vla|du'e}}, or 

{{vla|mo'a}} (enough, too many, too few) then an additional place is added for 

“by standard”. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-aGLh}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-aGLh}}
{{judri|c18e11d11}}
:'''lei ratcu poi zvati le panka cu du'emei fo mi'''
:<code>The-mass-of rats which-are in the park are too-many by-standard me.</code>
:''There are too many rats in the park for me.''

{{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|rationale for effect on place structure}}  {{ind|general-imported|too many rats|example}} The extra place (which for 
:{{jbo|-mei}} is the x4 place labeled by 
{{vla|fo}}) is provided rather than using a BAI tag such as 
{{vla|ma'i}} because a specification of the standard for judgment is essential to the meaning of subjective words like 

“enough”.

{{ind|general-imported|subjective numbers|specifying standard for}}  {{ind|general-imported|standard for subjective numbers|specifying}} This place is not normally explicit when using one of the subjective numbers directly as a number. Therefore, 
:{{jbo|du'e ratcu}} means 

“too many rats” without specifying any standard.

{{ind|general-imported|lerfu strings|with numerical selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|special|with lerfu strings}} It is also grammatical to substitute a lerfu string for a number:

{{dsp|example-random-id-cyLo}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-cyLo}}
{{judri|c18e11d12}}
{{ind|example|nth rat|example}}
:'''ta ny.moi le'i mi ratcu'''
:<code>That is-nth-of the-set-of my rats.</code>
:''That is my nth rat.''

{{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|restriction on numbers used for}}  {{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|grammar}} More complex mekso cannot be placed directly in front of MOI, due to the resulting grammatical ambiguities. Instead, a somewhat artificial form of expression is required.

{{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|alternative to compensate for restriction on numbers}}  {{ind|general-imported|&quot;me&quot;|effect of MOI on}}  {{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|complex}}  {{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|use of &quot;me&quot; with}} The cmavo 
{{vla|me}} (of selma'o ME) has the function of making a sumti into a selbri. A whole 
{{vla|me}} construction can have a member of MOI added to the end to create a complex mekso selbri:

{{dsp|example-random-id-xaYd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-xaYd}}
{{judri|c18e11d13}}
{{ind|example|(n+1)-th rat|example}}
:'''ta me li ny. su'i pa me'u moi le'i mi ratcu'''
:<code>That is the-number n plus one-th-of the-set-of my rats.</code>
:<code>That is my (n+1)-th rat.</code>

Here the mekso 
:{{jbo|ny. su'i pa}} is made into a sumti (with 
{{vla|li}}) and then changed into a mekso selbri with 
{{vla|me}} and 
:{{jbo|me'u moi}}. The elidable terminator 
{{vla|me'u}} is required here in order to keep the 
{{vla|pa}} and the 
{{vla|moi}} separate; otherwise, the parser will combine them into the compound 
{{vla|pamoi}} and reject the sentence as ungrammatical.

{{ind|general-imported|numerical selbri|based on non-numerical sumti}} It is perfectly possible to use non-numerical sumti after 
{{vla|me}} and before a member of MOI, producing strange results indeed:

{{dsp|example-random-id-enCe}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-enCe}}
{{judri|c18e11d14}}
{{ind|example|snowball's chance|example}}
:'''le nu mi nolraitru cu me le'e snime bolci be vi la xel. cu'o'''
:<code>The event-of me being-a-nobly-superlative-ruler has-the-stereotypical snow type-of-ball at Hell probability.</code>
:''I have a snowball's chance in Hell of being king.''

{{ind|general-imported|boi|effect on elidability of me'u}}  {{ind|general-imported|MOI selma'o|use of boi before}}  {{ind|general-imported|PA selma'o|exception on use of boi with MOI}}  {{ind|general-imported|boi|exception before MOI}} Note: the elidable terminator 
{{vla|boi}} is not used between a number and a member of MOI. As a result, the 
{{vla|me'u}} in 
{{linker|example-random-id-xaYd}} could also be replaced by a 
{{vla|boi}}, which would serve the same function of preventing the 
{{vla|pa}} and 
{{vla|moi}} from joining into a compound.

{{judri|section-number-questions}}
==Number questions==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|xo}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|number questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|questions|number}} The cmavo 
{{vla|xo}}, a member of selma'o PA, is used to ask questions whose answers are numbers. Like most Lojban question words, it fills the blank where the answer should go. (See 

[[#section-questions-and-answers|this section]] for more on Lojban questions.)

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIiE}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIiE}}
{{judri|c18e12d1}}
:'''li re su'i re du li xo'''
:<code>The-number 2 plus 2 equals the-number what?</code>
:''What is 2 + 2?''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiIQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiIQ}}
{{judri|c18e12d2}}
:'''le xomoi prenu cu darxi do'''
:<code>The what-number-th person hit you?</code>
:<code>Which person [as in a police lineup] hit you?</code>

{{ind|general-imported|questions|digit}}  {{ind|general-imported|digit questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|police lineup}} 
{{vla|xo}} can also be combined with other digits to ask questions whose answers are already partly specified. This ability could be very useful in writing tests of elementary arithmetical knowledge:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hSee}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hSee}}
{{judri|c18e12d3}}
:'''li remu pi'i xa du li paxono'''
:<code>The-number 25 times 6 equals the-number 1?0</code>

{{ind|general-imported|number questions|answers to}}  {{ind|general-imported|numbers|as grammatically complete utterances}} to which the correct reply would be 
{{vla|mu}}, or 5. The ability to utter bare numbers as grammatical Lojban sentences is primarily intended for giving answers to 
{{vla|xo}} questions. (Another use, obviously, is for counting off physical objects one by one.)

{{judri|section-subscripts-math}}
==Subscripts==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|xi}}
:{{s|XI}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|subscripts|external grammar of}} Subscripting is a general Lojban feature, not used only in mekso; there are many things that can logically be subscripted, and grammatically a subscript is a free modifier, usable almost anywhere. In particular, of course, mekso variables (lerfu strings) can be subscripted:

{{dsp|example-random-id-MT0a}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-MT0a}}
{{judri|c18e13d1}}
{{ind|example|x-sub-3|example}}
:'''li xy.boixici du li xy.boixipa su'i xy.boixire'''
:<code>The-number x-sub-3 equals the-number x-sub-1 plus x-sub-2.</code>

{{math|x<subscript>3</subscript> = x<subscript>1</subscript> + x<subscript>2</subscript>}}

{{ind|general-imported|subscripts|internal grammar of}} Subscripts always begin with the flag 
{{vla|xi}} (of selma'o XI). 
{{vla|xi}} may be followed by a number, a lerfu string, or a general mekso expression in parentheses:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiIs}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiIs}}
{{judri|c18e13d2}}
:'''xy.boixino'''
{{math|x<subscript>0</subscript>}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIJ6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIJ6}}
{{judri|c18e13d3}}
:'''xy.boixiny.'''
{{math|x<subscript>n</subscript>}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIjf}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIjf}}
{{judri|c18e13d4}}
:'''xy.boixi vei ny. su'i pa [ve'o]'''
{{math|x<subscript>(n+1)</subscript>}}

{{ind|general-imported|free modifiers|effects on elidability of terminators}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts|effects on elidability of terminators}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts on lerfu words|effect on elidability of boi}} Note that subscripts attached directly to lerfu words (variables) generally need a 
{{vla|boi}} terminating the variable. Free modifiers, of which subscripts are one variety, generally require the explicit presence of an otherwise elidable terminator.

{{ind|general-imported|superscripts}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts|before main expression}} There is no standard way of handling superscripts (other than those used as exponents) or for subscripts or superscripts that come before the main expression. If necessary, further cmavo could be assigned to selma'o XI for these purposes.

{{ind|general-imported|sub-subscripts}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts|multiple as sub-subscript}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts|terminator for}} The elidable terminator for a subscript is that for a general number or lerfu string, namely 
{{vla|boi}}. By convention, a subscript following another subscript is taken to be a sub-subscript:

{{dsp|example-random-id-FddL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-FddL}}
{{judri|c18e13d5}}
:'''xy.boi xi by.boi xi vo'''
{{math|x<subscript>b<subscript>4</subscript></subscript>}}

See {{linker|example-random-id-eMsd}} for the standard method of specifying multiple subscripts on a single object.

More information on the uses of subscripts may be found in 
[[#section-subscripts-general|this section]].

{{judri|section-infix-again}}
==Infix operators revisited==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|tu'o}}

:{{s|PA}}
:''description''

:{{c|ge'a}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|gei}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

The infix operators presented so far have always had exactly two operands, and for more or fewer operands forethought notation has been required. However, it is possible to use an operator in infix style even though it has more or fewer than two operands, through the use of a pair of tricks: the null operand 

{{vla|tu'o}} and the null operator 

{{vla|ge'a}}. The first is suitable when there are too few operands, the second when there are too many. For example, suppose we wanted to express the numerical negation operator 

{{vla|va'a}} in infix form. We would use:

{{dsp|example-random-id-8Uh9}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-8Uh9}}
{{judri|c18e14d1}}
:'''li tu'o va'a ny. du li no vu'u ny.'''
:<code>The-number (null) additive-inverse n equals the-number zero minus n.</code>
{{math|-n = 0 − n}}

{{ind|general-imported|operands|too few for infix operation}}  {{ind|general-imported|null operand|for infix operations with too few operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|tu'o|for infix operations with too few operands}} The 
{{vla|tu'o}} fulfills the grammatical requirement for a left operand for the infix use of 

{{vla|va'a}}, even though semantically none is needed or wanted.

{{ind|general-imported|exponential notation|with gei}}  {{ind|general-imported|scientific notation|with gei}}  {{ind|general-imported|gei|as a binary operator}} Finding a suitable example of 
{{vla|ge'a}} requires exhibiting a ternary operator, and ternary operators are not common. The operator 
{{vla|gei}}, however, has both a binary and a ternary use. As a binary operator, it provides a terse representation of scientific (also called 
“exponential”) notation. The first operand of 
{{vla|gei}} is the exponent, and the second operand is the mantissa or fraction:

{{dsp|example-random-id-VjtV}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-VjtV}}
{{judri|c18e14d2}}
{{ind|example|3 * 10^8|example}}
:'''li cinonoki'oki'o du li bi gei ci'''
:<code>The-number three-zero-zero-comma-comma equals the-number eight scientific three.</code>
{{math|300,000,000 = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup>}}

{{ind|general-imported|gei|rationale for order of places}}  {{ind|general-imported|scientific notation|rationale for order of places}} Why are the arguments to 
{{vla|gei}} in reverse order from the conventional symbolic notation? So that 
{{vla|gei}} can be used in forethought to allow easy specification of a large (or small) imprecise number:

{{dsp|example-random-id-zmqy}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-zmqy}}
{{judri|c18e14d3}}
{{ind|example|10^20|example}}
:'''gei reno'''
:<code>(scientific) two-zero</code>
{{math|10 <sup>20</sup>}}

{{ind|general-imported|floating point numbers|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|exponential notation|with base other than 10}}  {{ind|general-imported|gei|as a ternary operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|operands|too many for infix operation}}  {{ind|general-imported|null operator|for infix operations with too many operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|ge'a|for infix operations with too many operands}} Note, however, that although 10 is far and away the most common exponent base, it is not the only possible one. The third operand of
