{{vla|gei}}, therefore, is the base, with 10 as the default value. Most computers internally store so-called 
“floating-point” numbers using 2 as the exponent base. (This has nothing to do with the fact that computers also represent all integers in base 2; the IBM 360 series used an exponent base of 16 for floating point, although each component of the number was expressed in base 2.) Here is a computer floating-point number with a value of 40:

{{dsp|example-random-id-7nMz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-7nMz}}
{{judri|c18e14d4}}
:'''papano bi'eju'u re gei pipanopano bi'eju'u re ge'a re'''
:<code>(one-one-zero base 2) scientific (point-one-zero-one-zero base 2) with-base 2</code>
{{math|.1010<subscript>2</subscript> x 2<sup>110<subscript>2</subscript></sup>}}

{{judri|section-vectors-matrices}}
==Vectors and matrices==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|jo'i}}
:{{s|JOhI}}
:''description''

:{{c|te'u}}
:{{s|TEhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|pi'a}}

:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|sa'i}}

:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|matrix|definition}}  {{ind|general-imported|vector|definition}} A mathematical vector is a list of numbers, and a mathematical matrix is a table of numbers. Lojban considers matrices to be built up out of vectors, which are in turn built up out of operands.

{{ind|general-imported|vector indicator|terminator for}}  {{ind|general-imported|vector|components of}}  {{ind|general-imported|jo'i|precedence of}}  {{ind|general-imported|vector indicator}} 
{{vla|jo'i}}, the only cmavo of selma'o JOhI, is the vector indicator: it has a syntax reminiscent of a forethought operator, but has very high precedence. The components must be simple operands rather than full expressions (unless parenthesized). A vector can have any number of components; 

{{vla|te'u}} is the elidable terminator. An example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-IVDJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-IVDJ}}
{{judri|c18e15d1}}
:'''li jo'i paboi reboi te'u su'i jo'i ciboi voboi du li jo'i voboi xaboi'''
:<code>The-number array (one, two) plus array (three, four) equals the-number array (four, six).</code>
{{math|(1,2) + (3,4) = (4,6)}}

{{ind|general-imported|matrix|with ge'a for more than 2 rows/columns}}  {{ind|general-imported|matrix|as combination of vectors}}  {{ind|general-imported|matrix column operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|matrix row operator}} Vectors can be combined into matrices using either 
{{vla|pi'a}}, the matrix row operator, or 

{{vla|sa'i}}, the matrix column operator. The first combines vectors representing rows of the matrix, and the second combines vectors representing columns of the matrix. Both of them allow any number of arguments: additional arguments are tacked on with the null operator 

{{vla|ge'a}}.

Therefore, the 
“magic square” matrix

<table>
<tr>
<td>8</td><td>1</td><td>6</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3</td><td>5</td><td>7</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4</td><td>9</td><td>2</td>
</tr>
</table>
can be represented either as:

{{dsp|example-random-id-zbJP}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-zbJP}}
{{ind|example|magic square|example}}
{{judri|c18e15d2}}
:'''jo'i biboi paboi xa pi'a jo'i ciboi muboi ze ge'a jo'i voboi soboi re'''
:<code>the-vector (8 1 6) matrix-row the-vector (3 5 7), the-vector (4 9 2)</code>

or as

{{dsp|example-random-id-06dx}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-06dx}}
{{judri|c18e15d3}}
:'''jo'i biboi ciboi vo sa'i jo'i paboi muboi so ge'a jo'i xaboi zeboi re'''
:<code>the-vector (8 3 4) matrix-column the-vector (1 5 9), the-vector (6 7 2)</code>

{{ind|general-imported|matrices|use of parentheses with}}  {{ind|general-imported|vectors|use of parentheses with}}  {{ind|general-imported|matrices|use as operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|vectors|use as operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|inner product}}  {{ind|general-imported|outer product}} The regular mekso operators can be applied to vectors and to matrices, since grammatically both of these are expressions. It is usually necessary to parenthesize matrices when used with operators in order to avoid incorrect groupings. There are no VUhU operators for the matrix operators of inner or outer products, but appropriate operators can be created using a suitable symbolic lerfu word or string prefixed by 
{{vla|ma'o}}.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|xi}}  {{ind|general-imported|subscripts|to form matrices of more than 2 dimensions}}  {{ind|general-imported|matrix|with more than 2 dimensions}} Matrices of more than two dimensions can be built up using either 
{{vla|pi'a}} or 

{{vla|sa'i}} with an appropriate subscript numbering the dimension. When subscripted, there is no difference between 

{{vla|pi'a}} and 

{{vla|sa'i}}.

{{judri|section-reverse-polish-notation}}
==Reverse Polish notation==
The following cmavo is discussed in this section:

:{{c|fu'a}}

:{{s|FUhA}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|RP|as abbreviation for reverse Polish notation}} So far, the Lojban notational conventions have mapped fairly familiar kinds of mathematical discourse. The use of forethought operators may have seemed odd when applied to 
“+”, but when applied to 
“f” they appear as the usual functional notation. Now comes a sharp break. Reverse Polish (RP) notation represents something completely different; even mathematicians don't use it much. (The only common uses of RP, in fact, are in some kinds of calculators and in the implementation of some programming languages.)

{{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|terminator}}  {{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|marker}}  {{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|use of parentheses in}}  {{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|definition}} In RP notation, the operator follows the operands. (Polish notation, where the operator precedes its operands, is another name for forethought mekso of the kind explained in 
[[#section-forethought|this section]].) The number of operands per operator is always fixed. No parentheses are required or permitted. In Lojban, RP notation is always explicitly marked by a 
{{vla|fu'a}} at the beginning of the expression; there is no terminator. Here is a simple example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-V4xe}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-V4xe}}
{{judri|c18e16d1}}
:'''li fu'a reboi ci su'i du li mu'''
:<code>the-number (RP!) two, three, plus equals the-number five.</code>

The operands are 
{{vla|re}} and 
{{vla|ci}}; the operator is 
{{vla|su'i}}.

Here is a more complex example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-PSpq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-PSpq}}
{{judri|c18e16d2}}
:'''li fu'a reboi ci pi'i voboi mu pi'i su'i du li rexa'''
:<code>the-number (RP!) (two, three, times), (four, five, times), plus equals the-number two-six</code>

Here the operands of the first 
{{vla|pi'i}} are 
{{vla|re}} and 
{{vla|ci}}; the operands of the second 
{{vla|pi'i}} are 
{{vla|vo}} and 
{{vla|mu}} (with 
{{vla|boi}} inserted where needed), and the operands of the 
{{vla|su'i}} are 
:{{jbo|reboi ci pi'i}}, or 6, and 
:{{jbo|voboi mu pi'i}}, or 20. As you can see, it is easy to get lost in the world of reverse Polish notation; on the other hand, it is especially easy for a mechanical listener (who has a deep mental stack and doesn't get lost) to comprehend.

{{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|parentheses in operands of}}  {{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|operands of}} The operands of an RP operator can be any legal mekso operand, including parenthesized mekso that can contain any valid syntax, whether more RP or something more conventional.

{{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|with too many operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|with too few operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|reverse Polish notation|number of operands}} In Lojban, RP operators are always parsed with exactly two operands. What about operators which require only one operand, or more than two operands? The null operand 

{{vla|tu'o}} and the null operator 

{{vla|ge'a}} provide a simple solution. A one-operand operator like 
{{vla|va'a}} always appears in a reverse Polish context as 
:{{jbo|tu'o va'a}}. The 

{{vla|tu'o}} provides the second operand, which is semantically ignored but grammatically necessary. Likewise, the three-operand version of 

{{vla|gei}} appears in reverse Polish as 
:{{jbo|ge'a gei}}, where the 

{{vla|ge'a}} effectively merges the 2nd and 3rd operands into a single operand. Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiJp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiJp}}
{{judri|c18e16d3}}
:'''li fu'a ciboi muboi vu'u du li fu'a reboi tu'o va'a'''
:<code>The-number (RP!) (three, five, minus) equals the-number (RP!) two, null, negative-of.</code>
{{math|3 − 5 = -2}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qijY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qijY}}
{{judri|c18e16d4}}
:'''li cinoki'oki'o du li fu'a biboi ciboi panoboi ge'a gei'''
:<code>The-number 30-comma-comma equals the-number (RP!) 8, (3, 10, null-op), exponential-notation.</code>
{{math|30,000,000 = 3 × 10}}

{{judri|section-connectives-within-mekso}}
==Logical and non-logical connectives within mekso==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|.abu}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

:{{c|by}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

:{{c|cy}}
:{{s|BY}}
:''description''

:{{c|fe'a}}
:{{s|VUhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|lo'o}}
:{{s|LOhO}}
:''description''

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|GA selma'o}}  {{ind|lojban-word-imported|A selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought connection|of operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|afterthought connection|of operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|of operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|forethought connection|of operands}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator connection|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator connection|afterthought}}  {{ind|general-imported|operand connection|forethought}}  {{ind|general-imported|operand connection|afterthought}} As befits a logical language, Lojban has extensive provision for logical connectives within both operators and operands. Full details on logical and non-logical connectives are provided in 

[[#chapter-connectives|this chapter]]. Operands are connected in afterthought with selma'o A and in forethought with selma'o GA, just like sumti. Operators are connected in afterthought with selma'o JA and in forethought with selma'o GUhA, just like tanru components. This parallelism is no accident.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|BO selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|connection of operators|grouping}}  {{ind|general-imported|connection of operands|grouping}} In addition, A+BO and A+KE constructs are allowed for grouping logically connected operands, and 
{{vla|ke}}&hellip;{{vla|ke'e}} is allowed for grouping logically connected operators, although there are no analogues of tanru among the operators.

Despite the large number of rules required to support this feature, it is of relatively minor importance in the mekso scheme of things. 
{{linker|example-random-id-e9Xi}} exhibits afterthought logical connection between operands:

{{dsp|example-random-id-e9Xi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-e9Xi}}
{{judri|c18e17d1}}
{{ind|example|three or four people|example}}
:'''vei ci .a vo ve'o prenu cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>( Three or four ) people go-to the market.</code>

{{linker|example-random-id-eiTM}} is equivalent in meaning, but uses forethought connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eiTM}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eiTM}}
{{judri|c18e17d2}}
:'''vei ga ci gi vo ve'o prenu cu klama le zarci'''
:<code>( Either 3 or 4 ) people go-to the market.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|parentheses|for complex mekso used as quantifier}}  {{ind|general-imported|mekso|complex used as quantifier}} Note that the mekso here are being used as quantifiers. Lojban requires that any mekso other than a simple number be enclosed in parentheses when used as a quantifier. This rule prevents ambiguities that do not exist when using 
{{vla|li}}.

{{ind|general-imported|lo'o|effect of logical connective on elidability of}}  {{ind|general-imported|logical connection|effect on elidability of lo'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|li|terminator for}} By the way, 
{{vla|li}} has an elidable terminator, 
{{vla|lo'o}}, which is needed when a 

{{vla|li}} sumti is followed by a logical connective that could seem to be within the mekso. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LXtp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LXtp}}
{{judri|c18e17d3}}
:'''li re su'i re du li vo lo'o .onai lo nalseldjuno namcu'''
:<code>The-number two plus two equals the-number four or else a non-known number.</code>

Omitting the 
{{vla|lo'o}} would cause the parser to assume that another operand followed the 

{{vla|.onai}} and reject 
{{vla|lo}} as an invalid operand.

Simple examples of logical connection between operators are hard to come by. A contrived example is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-YoFg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-YoFg}}
{{judri|c18e17d4}}
:'''li re su'i je pi'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number two plus and times two equals the-number four.</code>
{{math|2 + 2 = 4 and 2 × 2 = 4.}}

The forethought-connection form of 
{{linker|example-random-id-YoFg}} is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ccNn}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ccNn}}
{{judri|c18e17d5}}
:'''li re ge su'i gi pi'i re du li vo'''
:<code>the-number two both plus and times two equals the-number four.</code>
{{math|Both 2 + 2 = 4 and 2 × 2 = 4.}}

Here is a classic example of operand logical connection:

{{dsp|example-random-id-k36J}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k36J}}
{{judri|c18e17d6}}
{{ind|example|quadratic formula|example}}
:'''go li .abu bi'epi'i vei xy. te'a re ve'o su'i by. bi'epi'i xy. su'i cy. du li no gi li xy. du li vei va'a by. ku'e su'i ja vu'u fe'a vei by. bi'ete'a re vu'u vo bi'epi'i .abu bi'epi'i cy. ve'o [ku'e] ve'o fe'i re bi'epi'i .abu'''
:<code>If-and-only-if the-number “a”-times-(“x” power two ) plus “b”-times- “x” plus “c” equals the-number zero then the-number x equals the-number [ the-negation-of( b ) plus or minus the-root-of (“b”-power-2 minus four-times- “a”-times- “c” ) ] divided-by two-times- “a”.</code>
:''Iff ax <sup>2</sup>  + bx + c = 0, then x = -b ± √ <!--sqrt-->(b <sup>2</sup>  − 4ac) <!-- fraction bar --> 2a''

{{ind|general-imported|infix notation mixed with Polish|example}}  {{ind|general-imported|Polish notation mixed with infix|example}}  {{ind|general-imported|infix notation mixed with Polish}}  {{ind|general-imported|Polish notation mixed with infix}} Note the mixture of styles in 
{{linker|example-random-id-k36J}}: the negation of b and the square root are represented by forethought and most of the operator precedence by prefixed 

{{vla|bi'e}}, but explicit parentheses had to be added to group the numerator properly. In addition, the square root parentheses cannot be removed here in favor of simple 

{{vla|fe'a}} and 
{{vla|ku'e}} bracketing, because infix operators are present in the operand. Getting 
{{linker|example-random-id-k36J}} to parse perfectly using the current parser took several tries: a more relaxed style would dispense with most of the 
{{vla|bi'e}} cmavo and just let the standard precedence rules be understood.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|JOI selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|non-logical connection|of operands}} Non-logical connection with JOI and BIhI is also permitted between operands and between operators. One use for this construct is to connect operands with 
{{vla|bi'o}} to create intervals:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Bzf6}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Bzf6}}
{{judri|c18e17d7}}
:'''li no ga'o bi'o ke'i pa'''
:<code>the-number zero (inclusive) from-to (exclusive) one</code>
{{math|[0,1)}}
:''the numbers from zero to one, including zero but not including one''

Intervals defined by a midpoint and range rather than beginning and end points can be expressed by 
{{vla|mi'i}}:

{{dsp|example-random-id-LvBT}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-LvBT}}
{{judri|c18e17d8}}
:'''li pimu ga'o mi'i ke'i pimu'''
:<code>the-number 0.5 ± 0.5</code>

{{ind|general-imported|closed interval|expressed with mi'i}}  {{ind|general-imported|open interval|expressed with mi'i}} which expresses the same interval as 
{{linker|example-random-id-Bzf6}}. Note that the 
{{vla|ga'o}} and 
{{vla|ke'i}} still refer to the endpoints, although these are now implied rather than expressed. Another way of expressing the same thing:

{{dsp|example-random-id-CEvD}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-CEvD}}
{{judri|c18e17d9}}
:'''li pimu su'i ni'upimu bi'o ma'upimu'''
:<code>the-number 0.5 plus [-0.5 from-to +0.5]</code>

{{ind|general-imported|connection of operands|precedence over operator}} Here we have the sum of a number and an interval, which produces another interval centered on the number. As 
{{linker|example-random-id-CEvD}} shows, non-logical (or logical) connection of operands has higher precedence than any mekso operator.

{{ind|general-imported|subscripts|multiple for same base word}}  {{ind|general-imported|compound subscript}} You can also combine two operands with 
{{vla|ce'o}}, the sequence connective of selma'o JOI, to make a compound subscript:

{{dsp|example-random-id-eMsd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-eMsd}}
{{judri|c18e17d10}}
:'''xy. xi vei by. ce'o dy. [ve'o]'''

<code>
“x” sub ( 
“b” sequence 
“d”)</code>
{{math|x<subscript>b,d</subscript>}}

{{judri|section-lojban-within-mekso}}
==Using Lojban resources within mekso==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|na'u}}
:{{s|NAhU}}
:''description''

:{{c|ni'e}}

:{{s|NIhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|mo'e}}

:{{s|MOhE}}
:''description''

:{{c|te'u}}
:{{s|TEhU}}
:''description''

{{ind|general-imported|mo'e|terminator for}}  {{ind|general-imported|ni'e|terminator for}}  {{ind|general-imported|na'u|terminator for}} One of the mekso design goals requires the ability to make use of Lojban's vocabulary resources within mekso to extend the built-in cmavo for operands and operators. There are three relevant constructs: all three share the elidable terminator 
{{vla|te'u}} (which is also used to terminate vectors marked with 
{{vla|jo'i}})

{{ind|general-imported|operator derived from selbri|effect of selbri place structure on}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri place structure|effect on operator formed by}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of selbri into operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator|converting selbri into}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|converting into an operator}} The cmavo 
{{vla|na'u}} makes a selbri into an operator. In general, the first place of the selbri specifies the result of the operator, and the other unfilled places specify the operands:

{{dsp|example-random-id-k38f}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-k38f}}
{{judri|c18e18d1}}
{{ind|example|tan(pi/2) = infinity|example}}
:'''li na'u tanjo te'u vei pai fe'i re [ve'o] du li ci'i'''
:<code>The-number the-operator tangent (π / 2 ) = the-number infinity.</code>

{{math|tan(π/2) = ∞}}

{{vla|tanjo}} is the gismu for 
“x1 is the tangent of x2”, and the 
{{vla|na'u}} here makes it into an operator which is then used in forethought

{{ind|general-imported|formulae|expressing based on pure dimensions}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of selbri into operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|operand|converting selbri into}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|converting into an operand}} The cmavo 
{{vla|ni'e}} makes a selbri into an operand. The x1 place of the selbri generally represents a number, and therefore is often a 

{{vla|ni}} abstraction, since 
{{vla|ni}} abstractions represent numbers. The 
{{vla|ni'e}} makes that number available as a mekso operand. A common application is to make equations relating pure dimensions:

{{dsp|example-random-id-wCJQ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-wCJQ}}
{{judri|c18e18d2}}
{{ind|example|Length * Width * Depth = Volume|example}}
:'''li ni'e ni clani [te'u] pi'i ni'e ni ganra [te'u] pi'i ni'e ni condi te'u du li ni'e ni canlu'''
:<code>The-number quantity-of length times quantity-of width times quantity-of depth equals the-number quantity-of volume.</code>
{{math|Length × Width × Depth = Volume}}

{{ind|general-imported|dimensioned numbers|expressing}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of sumti into operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|operand|converting sumti into}}  {{ind|general-imported|sumti|converting into an operand}} The cmavo 
{{vla|mo'e}} operates similarly to 

{{vla|ni'e}}, but makes a sumti (rather than a selbri) into an operand. This construction is useful in stating equations involving dimensioned numbers:

{{dsp|example-random-id-ETmX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-ETmX}}
{{judri|c18e18d3}}
{{ind|example|2 rats + 2 rabbits = 4 animals|example}}  
:'''li mo'e re ratcu su'i mo'e re ractu du li mo'e vo danlu'''
:<code>The-number two rats plus two rabbits equals the-number four animals.</code>
{{math|2 rats + 2 rabbits = 4 animals.}}

{{ind|general-imported|folk quantifiers|expressing}} Another use is in constructing Lojbanic versions of so-called 
“folk quantifiers”, such as 

“a pride of lions”:

{{dsp|example-random-id-D4y4}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-D4y4}}
{{judri|c18e18d4}}
{{ind|example|pride of lions|example}}
:'''mi viska vei mo'e lo'e lanzu ve'o cinfo'''
:<code>I see ( the-typical family )-number-of lions.</code>
:''I see a pride of lions.''

{{judri|section-other-mekso-uses}}
==Other uses of mekso==
The following cmavo are discussed in this section:

:{{c|me'o}}
:{{s|LI}}
:''description''

:{{c|nu'a}}
:{{s|NUhA}}
:''description''

:{{c|mai}}
:{{s|MAI}}
:''description''

:{{c|mo'o}}
:{{s|MAI}}
:''description''

:{{c|roi}}

:{{s|ROI}}
:''description''

So far we have seen mekso used as sumti (with 
{{vla|li}}), as quantifiers (often parenthesized), and in MOI and ME-MOI selbri. There are a few other minor uses of mekso within Lojban.

{{ind|general-imported|mathematical expression|referring to}}  {{ind|general-imported|li|contrasted with me'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|me'o|contrasted with li}} The cmavo 
{{vla|me'o}} has the same grammatical use as 
{{vla|li}} but slightly different semantics. 
{{vla|li}} means 
“the number which is the value of the mekso ...”, whereas 
{{vla|me'o}} just means 
“the mekso ...” So it is true that:

{{dsp|example-random-id-93Qu}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-93Qu}}
{{judri|c18e19d1}}
:'''li re su'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number two plus two equals the-number four.</code>
{{math|2 + 2 = 4}}

but false that:

{{dsp|example-random-id-Shbg}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-Shbg}}
{{judri|c18e19d2}}
:'''me'o re su'i re du me'o vo'''
:<code>The-mekso two plus two equals the-mekso four.</code>
:''“2 + 2”=“4”''

{{ind|general-imported|me'o|relation to li compared with la/zo relation}}  {{ind|general-imported|li|relation to me'o compared with la/zo relation}} since the expressions 
“2 + 2” and 
“4” are not the same. The relationship between 
{{vla|li}} and 
{{vla|me'o}} is related to that between 
:{{jbo|la djan.}}, the person named John, and 
:{{jbo|zo .djan.}}, the name 
“John”

{{ind|general-imported|selbri|place structure of converted operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of operator into selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator|converting into selbri}}  {{ind|general-imported|selbri|converting operator into}} The cmavo 
{{vla|nu'a}} is the inverse of 
{{vla|na'u}}, and allows a mekso operator to be used as a normal selbri, with the place structure:

:''x1 is the result of applying (operator) to x2, x3, ...''
for as many places as may be required. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-9idi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-9idi}}
{{judri|c18e19d3}}
:'''li ni'umu cu nu'a va'a li ma'umu'''
:<code>The-number -5 is-the-negation-of the-number +5.</code>

uses 
{{vla|nu'a}} to make the operator 
{{vla|va'a}} into a two-place bridi

{{ind|general-imported|nu'a|use in answering operator questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|na'u|use in asking operator questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|answers|to operator questions}}  {{ind|general-imported|questions|operator}} Used together, 
{{vla|nu'a}} and 
{{vla|na'u}} make it possible to ask questions about mekso operators, even though there is no specific cmavo for an operator question, nor is it grammatical to utter an operator in isolation. Consider 
{{linker|example-random-id-qIKp}}, to which 
{{linker|example-random-id-qILi}} is one correct answer:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIKp}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIKp}}
{{judri|c18e19d4}}
:'''li re na'u mo re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number two what-operator? two equals the-number four.</code>
{{math|2 ? 2 = 4}}

{{dsp|example-random-id-qILi}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qILi}}
{{judri|c18e19d5}}
:'''nu'a su'i'''
:''plus''

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-qIKp}}, 
:{{jbo|na'u mo}} is an operator question, because 
{{vla|mo}} is the selbri question cmavo and 
{{vla|na'u}} makes the selbri into an operator. 
{{linker|example-random-id-qILi}} makes the true answer 
{{vla|su'i}} into a selbri (which is a legal utterance) with the inverse cmavo 
{{vla|nu'a}}. Mechanically speaking, inserting 
{{linker|example-random-id-qILi}} into 
{{linker|example-random-id-qIKp}} produces:

{{dsp|example-random-id-M5YX}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-M5YX}}
{{judri|c18e19d6}}
:'''li re na'u nu'a su'i re du li vo'''
:<code>The-number two (the-operator the-selbri plus) two equals the-number four.</code>

where the 
:{{jbo|na'u nu'a}} cancels out, leaving a truthful bridi

{{ind|general-imported|digit string|definition of}}  {{ind|general-imported|section numbering}}  {{ind|general-imported|text|sub-division numbering with -mai}} Numerical free modifiers, corresponding to English 

“firstly”, 

“secondly”, and so on, can be created by suffixing a member of selma'o MAI to a digit string or a lerfu string. (Digit strings are compound cmavo beginning with a cmavo of selma'o PA, and containing only cmavo of PA or BY; lerfu strings begin with a cmavo of selma'o BY, and likewise contain only PA or BY cmavo.) Here are some examples:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qimN}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qimN}}
{{ind|example|firstly|example}}
{{judri|c18e19d7}}
:'''pamai'''
:''firstly''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiMz}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiMz}}
{{judri|c18e19d8}}
:'''remai'''
:''secondly''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qInd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qInd}}
{{judri|c18e19d9}}
:'''romai'''
:<code>all-ly</code>
:''lastly''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIoY}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIoY}}
{{judri|c18e19d10}}
:'''ny.mai'''
:''nth-ly''

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiPq}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiPq}}
{{judri|c18e19d11}}
:'''pasomo'o'''
:''nineteenthly (higher order)''

{{ind|general-imported|chapter numbering}}  {{ind|general-imported|mo'o|contrasted with mai}}  {{ind|general-imported|mai|contrasted with mo'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|text|division numbering with -mai}} The difference between 
{{vla|mai}} and 
{{vla|mo'o}} is that 
{{vla|mo'o}} enumerates larger subdivisions of a text. Each 
{{vla|mo'o}} subdivision can then be divided into pieces and internally numbered with 
{{vla|mai}}. If this chapter were translated into Lojban, each section would be numbered with 
{{vla|mo'o}}. (See [[#section-utterance-ordinals|this section]] for more on these words.)

{{ind|general-imported|tense|numerical}} A numerical tense can be created by suffixing a digit string with 

{{vla|roi}}. This usage generates tenses corresponding to English 

“once”, 
“twice”, and so on. This topic belongs to a detailed discussion of Lojban tenses, and is explained further in 
[[#section-interval-properties|this section]].

{{ind|general-imported|numerical tenses|effect on use of boi}}  {{ind|general-imported|boi|exception before ROI}}  {{ind|general-imported|boi|exception before MAI}}  {{ind|general-imported|MAI selma'o|exception on use of boi before}}  {{ind|general-imported|ROI selma'o|exception on use of boi before}} Note: the elidable terminator 
{{vla|boi}} is not used between a number and a member of MAI or ROI.

{{judri|section-explicit-operator-precedence}}
==Explicit operator precedence==

As mentioned earlier, Lojban does provide a way for the precedences of operators to be explicitly declared, although current parsers do not understand these declarations.

The declaration is made in the form of a metalinguistic comment using 

{{vla|ti'o}}, a member of selma'o SEI. 

{{vla|sei}}, the other member of SEI, is used to insert metalinguistic comments on a bridi which give information about the discourse which the bridi comprises. The format of a 
{{vla|ti'o}} declaration has not been formally established, but presumably would take the form of mentioning a mekso operator and then giving it either an absolute numerical precedence on some pre-established scale, or else specifying relative precedences between new operators and existing operators.

{{ind|general-imported|operator precedence|plans for future}} In future, we hope to create an improved machine parser that can understand declarations of the precedences of simple operators belonging to selma'o VUhU. Originally, all operators would have the same precedence. Declarations would have the effect of raising the specified cmavo of VUhU to higher precedence levels. Complex operators formed with 
{{vla|na'u}}, 
{{vla|ni'e}}, or 

{{vla|ma'o}} would remain at the standard low precedence; declarations with respect to them are for future implementation efforts. It is probable that such a parser would have a set of 
“commonly assumed precedences” built into it (selectable by a special 
{{vla|ti'o}} declaration) that would match mathematical intuition: times higher than plus, and so on.

{{judri|section-miscellany}}
==Miscellany==
A few other points:

{{ind|general-imported|se|use with operators}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion|of operator places}} 
{{vla|se}} can be used to convert an operator as if it were a selbri, so that its arguments are exchanged. For example:

{{dsp|example-random-id-NwYJ}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-NwYJ}}
{{judri|c18e21d1}}
:'''li ci se vu'u vo du li pa'''
:<code>The-number three (inverse) minus four equals the-number one.</code>
:''3 subtracted from 4 equals 1.''

The other converters of selma'o SE can also be used on operators with more than two operands, and they can be compounded to create (probably unintelligible) operators as needed.

{{ind|lojban-word-imported|NAhE selma'o}}  {{ind|general-imported|negation|of operator}} Members of selma'o NAhE are also legal on an operator to produce a scalar negation of it. The implication is that some other operator would apply to make the bridi true:

{{dsp|example-random-id-qIPR}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qIPR}}
{{judri|c18e21d2}}
:'''li ci na'e su'i vo du li pare'''
:<code>The-number 3 non-plus 4 equals the-number 12.</code>

{{dsp|example-random-id-qiqd}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-qiqd}}
{{judri|c18e21d3}}
{{ind|example|opposite-of-minus|example}}
:'''li ci to'e vu'u re du li mu'''
:<code>The-number 3 opposite-of-minus 2 equals the-number 5.</code>

The sense in which 
“plus” is the opposite of 
“minus” is not a mathematical but rather a linguistic one; negated operators are defined only loosely.

{{ind|general-imported|negation|of operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|symbol|for operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|referent|of operand}} 
{{vla|la'e}} and 
{{vla|lu'e}} can be used on operands with the usual semantics to get the referent of or a symbol for an operand. Likewise, a member of selma'o NAhE followed by 
{{vla|bo}} serves to scalar-negate an operand, implying that some other operand would make the bridi true:

{{dsp|example-random-id-3het}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-3het}}
{{judri|c18e21d4}}
:'''li re su'i re du li na'ebo mu'''
:<code>The-number 2 plus 2 equals the-number non-5.</code>
:''2 + 2 = something other than 5.''

{{ind|general-imported|digits|names from}}  {{ind|general-imported|digits|rafsi for}} The digits 0-9 have rafsi, and therefore can be used in making lujvo. Additionally, all the rafsi have CVC form and can stand alone or together as names:

{{dsp|example-random-id-hvGK}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-hvGK}}
{{judri|c18e21d5}}
:'''la zel. poi gunta la tebes. pu nanmu'''
:<code>Those-named “Seven” who attack that-named “Thebes” [past] are-men.</code>
:''The Seven Against Thebes were men.''

Of course, there is no guarantee that the name 
{{cmevla|zel.}} is connected with the number rafsi: an alternative which cannot be misconstrued is:

{{dsp|example-random-id-pf3n}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-pf3n}}
{{judri|c18e21d6}}
:'''la zemei poi gunta la tebes. pu nanmu'''
:<code>Those-named-the Sevensome who attack Thebes [past] are-men.</code>

{{ind|general-imported|rafsi|conventional meaning for frinu}}  {{ind|general-imported|PA selma'o|members with rafsi}} Certain other members of PA also have assigned rafsi: 
{{vla|so'a}}, 

{{vla|so'e}}, 

{{vla|so'i}}, 

{{vla|so'o}}, 

{{vla|so'u}}, 

{{vla|da'a}}, 
{{vla|ro}}, 
{{vla|su'e}}, 

{{vla|su'o}}, 
{{vla|pi}}, and 
{{vla|ce'i}}. Furthermore, although the cmavo 

{{vla|fi'u}} does not have a rafsi as such, it is closely related to the gismu 

{{vla|frinu}}, meaning 
“fraction”; therefore, in a context of numeric rafsi, you can use any of the rafsi for 
{{vla|frinu}} to indicate a fraction slash.

{{ind|general-imported|rafsi|conventional meaning for cu'o}} A similar convention is used for the cmavo 
{{vla|cu'o}} of selma'o MOI, which is closely related to 

{{vla|cunso}} (probability); use a rafsi for 
{{vla|cunso}} in order to create lujvo based on 
{{vla|cu'o}}. The cmavo 

{{vla|mei}} and 
{{vla|moi}} of MOI have their own rafsi, two each in fact: 
{{raf|mem}}/ 
{{raf|mei}} and 
{{raf|mom}}/ 
{{raf|moi}} respectively.

{{ind|general-imported|operand|converting from operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|operator|converting into operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of operator into operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|algebra of functions|operator and operand distinction in}}  {{ind|general-imported|lambda calculus|operator and operand distinction in}} The grammar of mekso as described so far imposes a rigid distinction between operators and operands. Some flavors of mathematics (lambda calculus, algebra of functions) blur this distinction, and Lojban must have a method of doing the same. An operator can be changed into an operand with 

:{{jbo|ni'enu'a}}, which transforms the operator into a matching selbri and then the selbri into an operand.

{{ind|general-imported|operator|converting from operand}}  {{ind|general-imported|operand|converting into operator}}  {{ind|general-imported|conversion of operand into operator}} To change an operand into an operator, we use the cmavo 
{{vla|ma'o}}, already introduced as a means of changing a lerfu string such as 
{{vla|fy.}} into an operator. In fact, 
{{vla|ma'o}} can be followed by any mekso operand, using the elidable terminator 
{{vla|te'u}} if necessary.

{{ind|general-imported|ma'o|potential ambiguity caveat}} There is a potential semantic ambiguity in 
:{{jbo|ma'o fy. [te'u]}} if 
{{vla|fy.}} is already in use as a variable: it comes to mean 
“the function whose value is always f”. However, mathematicians do not normally use the same lerfu words or strings as both functions and variables, so this case should not arise in practice.

{{judri|section-four-score-and-seven}}
==Four score and seven: a mekso problem==

{{ind|general-imported|mekso|and literary translation}} Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address begins with the words 

“Four score and seven years ago”. This section exhibits several different ways of saying the number 

“four score and seven”. (A 
“score”, for those not familiar with the term, is 20; it is analogous to a 
“dozen” for 12.) The trivial way:

{{dsp|example-random-id-DzMH}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-DzMH}}
{{judri|c18e22d1}}
:'''li bize'''
:<code>eight seven</code>
{{math|87}}

{{linker|example-random-id-DzMH}} is mathematically correct, but sacrifices the spirit of the English words, which are intended to be complex and formal.

{{dsp|example-random-id-HNyL}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-HNyL}}
{{judri|c18e22d2}}
:'''li vo pi'i reno su'i ze'''
:<code>four times twenty plus seven</code>
{{math|4 × 20 + 7}}

{{ind|general-imported|score|as 20-year span}} 
{{linker|example-random-id-HNyL}} is also mathematically correct, but still misses something. 
“Score” is not a word for 20 in the same way that 
“ten” is a word for 10: it contains the implication of 20 objects. The original may be taken as short for 
“Four score years and seven years ago”. Thinking of a score as a twentysome rather than as 20 leads to:

{{dsp|example-random-id-iwba}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-iwba}}
{{judri|c18e22d3}}
{{ind|example|Four score and seven|example}}
{{ind|example|Gettysburg Address|example}}  
:'''li mo'e voboi renomei te'u su'i ze'''
:<code>the-number-of four twentysomes plus seven</code>

In 
{{linker|example-random-id-iwba}}, 
:{{jbo|voboi renomei}} is a sumti signifying four things each of which are groups of twenty; the 
{{vla|mo'e}} and 

{{vla|te'u}} then make this sumti into a number in order to allow it to be the operand of 
{{vla|su'i}}.

{{ind|general-imported|base-20 arithmetic|remnants of}}  {{ind|general-imported|score|as alternate base for years}} Another approach is to think of 
“score” as setting a representation base. There are remnants of base-20 arithmetic in some languages, notably French, in which 87 is 

“quatre-vingt-sept”, literally 
“four-twenties-seven”. (This fact makes the Gettysburg Address hard to translate into French!) If 

“score” is the representation base, then we have:

{{dsp|example-random-id-2C3I}}{{example|interlinear-gloss-example|example-random-id-2C3I}}
{{judri|c18e22d4}}
:'''li vo pi'e ze ju'u reno'''
:<code>four ; seven base 20</code>
{{math|47}}

Overall, 
{{linker|example-random-id-iwba}} probably captures the flavor of the English best. 
{{linker|example-random-id-DzMH}} and 
{{linker|example-random-id-HNyL}} are too simple, and 
{{linker|example-random-id-2C3I}} is too tricky. Nevertheless, all four examples are good Lojban. Pedagogically, these examples illustrate the richness of lojbau mekso: anything that can be said at all, can probably be said in more than one way.
